        In plain words: a small change in x makes a small change in g(x), which makes a small change in f(g(x)). No jumps anywhere along the chain means no jump at the end.

        Limit of a composition

        • lim_(x→a) g(x) = b and f continuous at b  ⇒  lim_(x→a) f(g(x)) = f(lim_(x→a) g(x)) = f(b)
        • Substitution: lim_(x→a) g(x) = b, g(x) ≠ b near a, lim_(t→b) f(t) = L  ⇒  lim_(x→a) f(g(x)) = L

        The limit goes inside a continuous function: lim_(x→0) cos(x² + π) = cos π = −1. The second line is why a help variable t works.

        Example with a help variable: lim_(x→0) (sin(3x))/(3x): let t = 3x; as x → 0, t → 0, and it becomes lim_(t→0) (sin t)/(t) = 1.

        8Intermediate value theorem

        Intermediate value theorem

        f continuous on [a, b] and y between f(a) and f(b)  ⇒  ∃c ∈ [a, b] : f(c) = y

        A continuous graph can't get from f(a) to f(b) without crossing every level in between.

        Example: a temperature goes from 10° at 8:00 to 20° at noon, changing continuously. At some moment in between it was exactly 15°, even if no one saw it.

        Why continuity is needed: a function with a jump can skip a value. The sign function jumps from −1 to 1 and never equals 0.5.

        A root between a sign change

        f continuous on [a, b] and f(a)·f(b) < 0  ⇒  ∃c ∈ (a, b) : f(c) = 0

        Says a root exists — not where, not how many. Continuity on the whole [a, b] is a must: 1/x on [−1, 1] changes sign with no root.

        Example: does x³ + x − 1 = 0 have a solution? f(0) = −1 < 0 and f(1) = 1 > 0, and a polynomial is continuous. So a root lies between 0 and 1. Steps: the method "Prove an equation has a root (IVT)".

        1What is a derivative

        Derivative at a point

        f'(a) = lim_(h→0) (f(a + h) − f(a))/h

        Same limit, written with x = a + h:

        f'(a) = lim_(x→a) (f(x) − f(a))/(x − a)

        If this limit exists and is finite, f is differentiable at a and the limit is the derivative. The derivative function f' gives this number at every x where it exists. Other notation: y', df/dx.

        The quotient is the slope of the secant (green) through two points of the graph. As h → 0 the second point slides to the first, and the secant turns into the tangent (dashed). Try it live in Precalc › Derivatives › Secant → tangent.

        In plain words: the derivative is the slope of the graph at one point: how steep it is right there, and whether it's going up or down. You get it by taking the slope between two very close points and letting them merge.

        Example: f(x) = x² at a = 3: (f(3 + h) − f(3))/h = (6h + h²)/h = 6 + h → 6. So f'(3) = 6: at x = 3 the parabola climbs 6 units for every 1 unit to the right.

        What the derivative tells you

        • Slope: f'(a) is the slope of the tangent to the graph at a.
        • Tangent line: y = f(a) + f'(a)·(x − a)
        • Rate of change: how fast f changes at a. Near a: f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)·h
        • Direction: f' > 0 on an interval → rising; f' < 0 → falling; f'(a) = 0 → horizontal tangent (Derivatives › 7).

        From the definition: for f(x) = x², (f(x + h) − f(x))/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h → 2x. So f'(x) = 2x: the slope at each point of the parabola.

        Tangent line example: for f(x) = x² at a = 3: f(3) = 9, f'(3) = 6, so the tangent is y = 9 + 6(x − 3), which is y = 6x − 9.

        Rate of change example: if s(t) is distance (in metres) after t seconds, s'(t) is the speed at that moment, in metres per second.

        2Differentiation formulas

        Powers, polynomials and roots

        • (c)' = 0  ·  (c·f)' = c·f'  ·  (f + g)' = f' + g'
        • (xⁿ)' = n·xⁿ⁻¹
        • (√x)' = 1/(2√x)  (x > 0)
        • (ⁿ√x)' = 1/(n·ⁿ√(xⁿ⁻¹))
        • Any real power, x > 0: (xʳ)' = r·xʳ⁻¹. A root or a fraction is a power: 1/x² = x⁻², so (1/x²)' = −2x⁻³ = −2/x³
        • Polynomial, term by term: (4x³ − 5x + 7)' = 12x² − 5

        The slope grows with x: the derivative of x² is the straight line 2x. Differentiating lowers a power by one.

        Why, from the definition

        • Powers: by the binomial formula (x + h)ⁿ = xⁿ + n·xⁿ⁻¹·h + h²·(…), so
        • ((x + h)ⁿ − xⁿ)/h = n·xⁿ⁻¹ + h·(…) → n·xⁿ⁻¹
        • Root (multiply by the conjugate, Limits › 3):
        • With s = √(x + h) + √x: (√(x + h) − √x)/h = ((x + h) − x)/(h·s) = 1/s
        • As h → 0, s → 2√x, so the limit is 1/(2√x).
        • Sum and constant: split the quotient and use the arithmetic of limits.
        • Real power: xʳ = er·ln x, so by the chain rule (xʳ)' = xʳ·(r/x) = r·xʳ⁻¹.

        In plain words: bring the exponent down in front and lower it by one. For roots and fractions, first rewrite them as powers: √x = x^(1/2), 1/(x³) = x⁻³.

        Product and quotient

        • Product: (f·g)' = f'·g + f·g'
        • Quotient: (f/g)' = (f'·g − f·g')/g²  (g ≠ 0)
        • Reciprocal: (1/g)' = −g'/g²

        Example: (x²·sin x)' = 2x·sin x + x²·cos x

        Think of f·g as an area. When both sides grow, the area gains two strips, Δf·g and f·Δg. The small corner Δf·Δg disappears in the limit. That is the two terms of the product rule.

        Why, from the definition

        • Product: add and subtract f(x + h)·g(x) in the numerator:
        • f(x + h)g(x + h) − f(x)g(x)
        • = f(x + h)·(g(x + h) − g(x)) + (f(x + h) − f(x))·g(x)
        • Divide by h and let h → 0. Since f is differentiable it is continuous, so f(x + h) → f(x), and the result is f·g' + f'·g.
        • Reciprocal: (1/g(x + h) − 1/g(x))/h = −(g(x + h) − g(x))/h · 1/(g(x + h)·g(x)) → −g'/g²
        • Quotient: f/g = f·(1/g), so (f/g)' = f'/g − f·g'/g² = (f'·g − f·g')/g²

        Quotient example, step by step: ((x)/(x² + 1))': top f = x, f' = 1; bottom g = x² + 1, g' = 2x. So (1 · (x² + 1) − x · 2x)/((x² + 1)²) = (1 − x²)/((x² + 1)²).

        Order matters in the quotient rule: it's top′ · bottom minus top · bottom′. Swapping them flips the sign of the answer.

        Composite functions (chain rule)

        (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x))·g'(x)

        The derivative of the outer function, at the inner function, times the derivative of the inner function.

        • ((3x² + 1)⁵)' = 5(3x² + 1)⁴·6x
        • (√(x² + 1))' = 2x/(2√(x² + 1)) = x/√(x² + 1)
        • (sin(x³))' = cos(x³)·3x²

        A small change in x is multiplied by g' on the way through g, and that result is multiplied by f' on the way through f. Rates multiply.

        Why, from the definition

        • Write t = g(x + h) and b = g(x). Multiply by 1, as long as t ≠ b:
        • (f(t) − f(b))/h = (f(t) − f(b))/(t − b) · (t − b)/h
        • t → b because g is continuous. The first quotient → f'(g(x)), the second → g'(x).
        • The case g(x + h) = g(x) near x needs a small extra argument in a full proof; the formula stays the same.

        How to use it: find the layers (outside and inside, like peeling an onion). Differentiate the outside, keep the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. With more layers, keep multiplying: (sin²(3x))' = 2 sin(3x) · cos(3x) · 3.

        Trigonometric functions

        • (sin x)' = cos x
        • (cos x)' = −sin x
        • (tan x)' = 1/cos²x = 1 + tan²x
        • With an inner function g: (sin g)' = cos g·g'  ·  (cos g)' = −sin g·g'  ·  (tan g)' = g'/cos²g

        The green curve is the slope of the blue one. At the top of sin x the tangent is flat, and cos x = 0 there.

        Why, from the definition

        • Two base limits: lim_(h→0) (sin h)/h = 1 and lim_(h→0) (cos h − 1)/h = 0
        • Sine: use sin(x + h) = sin x·cos h + cos x·sin h (Trig base › Identities):
        • (sin(x + h) − sin x)/h = sin x·(cos h − 1)/h + cos x·(sin h)/h → cos x
        • Cosine: use cos(x + h) = cos x·cos h − sin x·sin h:
        • (cos(x + h) − cos x)/h = cos x·(cos h − 1)/h − sin x·(sin h)/h → −sin x
        • Tangent: the quotient rule on sin x / cos x gives (cos²x + sin²x)/cos²x = 1/cos²x

        Example: (cos(5x))' = −sin(5x) · 5 = −5 sin(5x). The angle must be in radians for these formulas.

        Inverse trig: (arctan x)' = 1/(1 + x²). More in Functions › 6 (and arcsin, arccos in Functions › 7).

        Exponential and logarithmic functions

        • (eˣ)' = eˣ
        • (aˣ)' = aˣ·ln a  (a > 0)
        • (ln x)' = 1/x  (x > 0)
        • (log_a x)' = 1/(x·ln a)
        • With an inner function f: (ef)' = ef·f'  ·  (af)' = af·ln a·f'  ·  (ln f)' = f'/f

        eˣ and ln x mirror each other in y = x. eˣ has slope 1 at x = 0, and ln x has slope 1 at x = 1.

        Why, from the definition

        • eˣ: (eˣ⁺ʰ − eˣ)/h = eˣ·(eʰ − 1)/h → eˣ, because lim_(h→0) (eʰ − 1)/h = 1. That is what makes e special: the tangent at 0 has slope 1 (Precalc › Exp & log calculus).
        • aˣ: aˣ = ex·ln a, so the chain rule gives aˣ·ln a.
        • ln x: (ln(x + h) − ln x)/h = ln(1 + h/x)/h. With t = h/x this is (1/x)·ln(1 + t)/t → 1/x, because lim_(t→0) ln(1 + t)/t = 1.
        • log_a x: log_a x = ln x / ln a, a constant times ln x.
        • ln f: the chain rule with outer ln and inner f.

        Examples: (e^(x²))' = e^(x²) · 2x. (ln(3x + 1))' = 3/(3x + 1). (2ˣ)' = 2ˣ ln 2.

        3Differentiability

        Differentiable at a point

        f differentiable at a  ⇔  lim_(h→0) (f(a + h) − f(a))/h exists and is finite.

        One-sided derivatives:

        • f'₋(a) = lim_(h→0⁻) (f(a + h) − f(a))/h
        • f'₊(a) = lim_(h→0⁺) (f(a + h) − f(a))/h
        • f differentiable at a  ⇔  f'₋(a) = f'₊(a), both finite

        Differentiable on (a, b): at every point. On [a, b]: also one-sided at the ends.

        In plain words: "differentiable at a" means the graph has one clear, non-vertical tangent there: no corner, no jump, no vertical spike.

        Example: f(x) = |x| at 0. From the right the graph is y = x, slope 1; from the left it's y = −x, slope −1. The one-sided derivatives differ, so |x| isn't differentiable at 0.

        Differentiable implies continuous

        f differentiable at a  ⇒  f continuous at a

        The other way is false: f(x) = |x| is continuous at 0 and not differentiable there.

        Proof: f(x) − f(a) = (f(x) − f(a))/(x − a) · (x − a) → f'(a)·0 = 0, so f(x) → f(a).

        Use it backwards: not continuous at a ⇒ not differentiable at a. No calculation needed.

        In plain words: to have a tangent at a point, the graph must at least be unbroken there. But unbroken isn't enough: a corner is unbroken and still has no single tangent.

        Where a function is not differentiable

        Four ways the limit of the quotient can fail:

        • Not continuous: a jump or a hole. Example: f(x) jumps at a.
        • Corner: f'₋(a) ≠ f'₊(a). Example: |x| at 0.
        • Vertical tangent or cusp: the quotient → ±∞. Examples: ∛x and ∛(x²) at 0.
        • Oscillation: the quotient has no limit. Example: x·sin(1/x) at 0, with f(0) = 0.

        Also, of course: a point outside the domain.

        Limit of the derivative

        f continuous at a, differentiable for x ≠ a near a, and lim_(x→a) f'(x) = L:

        • L finite  ⇒  f differentiable at a and f'(a) = L
        • L = ±∞  ⇒  f not differentiable at a
        • One-sided too: lim_(x→a⁻) f'(x) = f'₋(a) and lim_(x→a⁺) f'(x) = f'₊(a)

        Consequence: if f'(a) exists and lim_(x→a) f'(x) exists, then the two are equal, so f' is continuous at a. A derivative function can't have a hole or a jump.

        Why: by the mean value theorem (Derivatives › 7), (f(x) − f(a))/(x − a) = f'(c) for some c between a and x. As x → a, c → a, so the quotient has the same limit as f'.

        Continuity of f at a is required. If lim_(x→a) f'(x) does not exist, the theorem says nothing: go to the definition. Example: x²·sin(1/x), f(0) = 0, has f'(0) = 0, yet lim_(x→0) f'(x) does not exist.

        Example: f(x) = x² for x < 1, 2x − 1 for x ≥ 1. It's continuous at 1 (both pieces give 1). f'(x) = 2x → 2 from the left and f'(x) = 2 from the right. Both are 2, so f'(1) = 2.

        When the derivative formula is undefined at a point

        If the formula for f' has a denominator that is 0 at a, or is undefined at a in any other way, treat it as a warning sign. It is not yet a verdict: the formula only holds where the rules were allowed.

        • Usually not differentiable: f = ∛x, f' = 1/(3∛(x²)) → +∞ at 0. Not differentiable.
        • But not always: f = √(x⁴), f' = 4x³/(2√(x⁴)) is undefined at 0, yet f = x² is differentiable there.

        Decide with the limit of the derivative (if f is continuous at a), or with the definition.

        Method: Is a function differentiable at a point?

        4Arithmetic of differentiability

        Arithmetic of differentiable functions

        f, g differentiable at a  ⇒  these are differentiable at a:

        • f ± g, with (f ± g)'(a) = f'(a) ± g'(a)
        • c·f, with (c·f)'(a) = c·f'(a)
        • f·g, with (f·g)'(a) = f'(a)·g(a) + f(a)·g'(a)
        • f/g, if g(a) ≠ 0, with (f/g)'(a) = (f'(a)·g(a) − f(a)·g'(a))/g(a)²

        Composition: g differentiable at a and f differentiable at g(a)  ⇒  f∘g differentiable at a, with (f∘g)'(a) = f'(g(a))·g'(a)

        Differentiable on their whole domain: polynomials, sin, cos, tan, eˣ, aˣ, ln. Roots: on x > 0, not at 0. |x|: everywhere except 0.

        When you can't use the arithmetic

        The theorem only works in one direction: all parts differentiable ⇒ the result is differentiable. If one part is not differentiable at a, the theorem says nothing. Go to the definition.

        • Sum: f differentiable, g not ⇒ f + g not. If it were, g = (f + g) − f would be differentiable.
        • Both not differentiable, sum is: |x| + (−|x|) = 0
        • Product is differentiable: x·|x| at 0, and |x|·|x| = x²
        • Product is not: 1·|x| at 0
        • Composition: |x|² is differentiable at 0, |sin x| and sin|x| are not.

        The factor x flattens the corner: x·|x| has tangent slope 0 from both sides of 0.

        5Local extrema

        Local extremum point

        • Local maximum at a: ∃δ > 0 : |x − a| < δ ⇒ f(x) ≤ f(a)
        • Local minimum at a: ∃δ > 0 : |x − a| < δ ⇒ f(x) ≥ f(a)

        "Local" means compared only with nearby points. A local maximum can be lower than a local minimum somewhere else.

        In plain words: a local maximum is a hilltop: the highest point in its neighbourhood, not necessarily the highest point of the whole graph. A local minimum is a valley floor.

        Example: f(x) = x³ − 3x has a local maximum at x = −1 (f = 2) and a local minimum at x = 1 (f = −2), though the graph goes higher and lower further out.

        Fermat's theorem

        f has a local extremum at an interior point a and f is differentiable at a  ⇒  f'(a) = 0

        The other way is false: f(x) = x³ has f'(0) = 0 and no extremum at 0.

        Proof (maximum): near a, f(x) − f(a) ≤ 0. So the quotient (f(x) − f(a))/(x − a) is ≥ 0 from the left and ≤ 0 from the right. Both one-sided limits equal f'(a), so f'(a) = 0.

        In plain words: at the top of a smooth hill or the bottom of a smooth valley, the tangent is flat.

        How it's used: to find extrema, solve f'(x) = 0. The theorem guarantees every smooth extremum is among the answers, though some answers may not be extrema (like x³ at 0).

        Critical points and the first derivative test

        A critical point is an interior point of the domain where f'(a) = 0 or f'(a) does not exist. Every local extremum is at a critical point, but not every critical point is an extremum.

        First derivative test (f continuous at a):

        • f' changes from + to − at a ⇒ local maximum
        • f' changes from − to + at a ⇒ local minimum
        • No sign change ⇒ no extremum

        The test works because the sign of f' tells where f rises and falls (Derivatives › 7, Monotonicity).

        Example: f(x) = x³ − 3x, f'(x) = 3(x − 1)(x + 1). Critical points: ±1. Signs of f': + before −1, − between, + after. So −1 is a maximum and 1 a minimum. Full steps: the method "Find the local extrema".

        Don't forget points where f' doesn't exist: |x| has its minimum at 0, where f'(0) doesn't exist.

        6Absolute extrema

        Absolute extremum point

        • Absolute maximum of f on D at a ∈ D: ∀x ∈ D : f(x) ≤ f(a)
        • Absolute minimum of f on D at a ∈ D: ∀x ∈ D : f(x) ≥ f(a)
        • The value is unique on a given domain: one largest value, one smallest value.
        • The point need not be: sin x reaches its maximum 1 at infinitely many points.
        • It may not exist.
        • Where to look: a critical point inside the domain, or an end of the domain.

        Local vs absolute: local = highest in the neighbourhood; absolute = highest on the whole domain. An absolute extremum inside the domain is also a local one.

        Extreme value theorem

        f continuous on a closed interval [a, b]  ⇒  ∃c, d ∈ [a, b] : ∀x ∈ [a, b] : f(c) ≤ f(x) ≤ f(d)

        A continuous function on a closed interval reaches an absolute minimum and an absolute maximum.

        Both conditions are needed. Functions with no absolute extremum:

        • Open interval: f(x) = x on (0, 1) has neither.
        • Open at one end: f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1] has no maximum.
        • Not bounded domain: f(x) = eˣ on ℝ has neither.
        • Not continuous: f(x) = x on [0, 1), f(1) = 0, has no maximum.

        In plain words: a graph you can draw without lifting your pen, from one end of a closed interval to the other, must have a highest and a lowest point.

        Example: f(x) = x² − 2x on [0, 3]. Critical point x = 1: f(1) = −1. Ends: f(0) = 0, f(3) = 3. Absolute minimum −1 at x = 1, absolute maximum 3 at x = 3. Steps: the method "Absolute extrema on a closed interval".

        Functions that go to infinity at both ends

        f continuous on (a, b) (a, b may be ±∞):

        • lim_(x→a⁺) f(x) = lim_(x→b⁻) f(x) = +∞  ⇒  absolute minimum, no absolute maximum
        • lim_(x→a⁺) f(x) = lim_(x→b⁻) f(x) = −∞  ⇒  absolute maximum, no absolute minimum

        Why: take any point x₀. Near the ends f > f(x₀), so outside some closed interval [c, d] containing x₀ the function is above f(x₀). On [c, d] the extreme value theorem gives a minimum, and it is the minimum everywhere.

        Same idea with a finite limit: if both end limits are finite and some f(x₀) is below both, there is an absolute minimum (above both: an absolute maximum).

        Example: f(x) = x + 1/(x) on (0, ∞) goes to +∞ at both ends, so it has an absolute minimum. f'(x) = 1 − 1/(x²) = 0 at x = 1: the minimum is f(1) = 2.

        7Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem

        Rolle's theorem

        If:

        1. f is continuous on [a, b]
        2. f is differentiable on (a, b)
        3. f(a) = f(b)

        then ∃c ∈ (a, b) : f'(c) = 0

        A graph that leaves a height and comes back must turn around somewhere, and at the turn the tangent is horizontal.

        Proof: by the extreme value theorem, f reaches a maximum and a minimum on [a, b]. If both are at the ends, f is constant and any c works. Otherwise one is at an interior point c, and Fermat's theorem gives f'(c) = 0.

        Example: f(x) = x² − 4x on [0, 4]: continuous, differentiable, f(0) = f(4) = 0. So some c has f'(c) = 0: 2c − 4 = 0, c = 2.

        When a condition of Rolle's theorem fails

        Drop any one condition and the conclusion can fail:

        • Not continuous at an end: f(x) = x on [0, 1), f(1) = 0. Then f(0) = f(1), but f' = 1 everywhere inside.
        • Not differentiable inside: f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1]. Then f(−1) = f(1), but f' = ±1.
        • Different end values: f(x) = x on [0, 1]. Then f' = 1 everywhere.

        The conditions are sufficient, not necessary: when one fails, a point with f' = 0 may still exist. The theorem just doesn't promise it.

        Mean value theorem

        f continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b)  ⇒  ∃c ∈ (a, b) : f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)

        Somewhere the tangent is parallel to the chord: the instant rate equals the average rate. Rolle's theorem is the case f(a) = f(b).

        Proof: apply Rolle's theorem to h(x) = f(x) − (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)·(x − a), which has h(a) = h(b) = f(a).

        In plain words: if a car drives 100 km in one hour, at some moment its speedometer showed exactly 100 km/h. The average speed is reached at least once.

        Example: f(x) = x² on [1, 3]: the chord's slope is (9 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 4. f'(c) = 2c = 4 at c = 2, which is inside (1, 3) ✓.

        Monotonicity

        f continuous on an interval I and differentiable inside it:

        • f' > 0 inside I ⇒ f strictly increasing on I
        • f' < 0 inside I ⇒ f strictly decreasing on I
        • f' = 0 inside I ⇒ f constant on I
        • f' = g' inside I ⇒ f = g + c on I
        • Comparing: f(a) ≥ g(a) and f' > g' for x > a ⇒ f(x) > g(x) for x > a

        Why: for x₁ < x₂ the mean value theorem gives f(x₂) − f(x₁) = f'(c)·(x₂ − x₁). The sign of f'(c) decides.

        It must be an interval. 1/x has f' < 0 on its domain but is not decreasing there. The converse is weaker: x³ is strictly increasing with f'(0) = 0. A f' that is 0 only at single points doesn't spoil strict increase.

        Example: f(x) = eˣ − x: f'(x) = eˣ − 1, negative for x < 0 and positive for x > 0. So f decreases on (−∞, 0] and increases on [0, ∞).

        Roots of f and roots of f'

        • Between two roots of f there is a root of f' (Rolle).
        • f has n roots ⇒ f' has at least n − 1 roots
        • f' has k roots ⇒ f has at most k + 1 roots
        • f' has no roots ⇒ f has at most one root
        • A polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots; if n is odd, at least one.

        These count at most. To show a root really exists, use the intermediate value theorem (Limits › 8). All of this assumes f is differentiable on the whole interval.

        Example: how many roots does x³ + x − 1 have? Its derivative 3x² + 1 is never 0, so at most one root. And it changes sign on [0, 1], so exactly one. Steps: the method "Prove an equation has exactly one root".

        8Convexity and concavity

        Convex and concave

        The second derivative is the derivative of the derivative: f'' = (f')'.

        f differentiable on an interval I:

        • Convex on I: f' increasing. The graph bends upward, lies above its tangents and below its chords.
        • Concave on I: f' decreasing. The graph bends downward, lies below its tangents and above its chords.

        Test: f'' > 0 on I ⇒ convex  ·  f'' < 0 on I ⇒ concave

        On a convex stretch the slope keeps growing; on a concave stretch it keeps shrinking. That is why the sign of f'', the rate of change of the slope, decides.

        In plain words: convex is shaped like a cup (holds water, ∪), concave like a cap (spills it, ∩). x² is convex everywhere, −x² concave everywhere.

        Example: f(x) = x³: f''(x) = 6x. Concave for x < 0, convex for x > 0.

        Inflection point

        a is an inflection point of f if f is continuous at a, has a tangent there, and changes from convex to concave (or the other way) at a.

        • Candidates: f''(a) = 0 or f''(a) undefined, with a in the domain.
        • f''(a) = 0 is not enough: x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 and is convex on both sides. The sign of f'' must change.
        • f'' may be undefined at an inflection point: ∛x at 0, with a vertical tangent.
        • A sign change at a point outside the domain is not an inflection point: 1/x at 0.

        At an inflection point the graph crosses its own tangent.

        Example: f(x) = x³ − 3x: f''(x) = 6x changes sign at 0, so (0, 0) is an inflection point: the graph switches from cap to cup there. Steps: the method "Find convexity and inflection points".

        Second derivative test

        f'(a) = 0 and f''(a) exists:

        • f''(a) > 0 ⇒ local minimum
        • f''(a) < 0 ⇒ local maximum
        • f''(a) = 0 ⇒ no conclusion: x⁴ (minimum), −x⁴ (maximum), x³ (neither)

        A horizontal tangent on a convex stretch can only be a bottom, on a concave stretch only a top.

        Example: f(x) = x³ − 3x: f''(x) = 6x. At x = 1, f''(1) = 6 > 0: minimum. At x = −1, f''(−1) = −6 < 0: maximum.

        Inequalities from convexity

        • Convex on I, a ∈ I: f(x) ≥ f(a) + f'(a)·(x − a) for all x ∈ I
        • Concave on I, a ∈ I: f(x) ≤ f(a) + f'(a)·(x − a) for all x ∈ I
        • Convex on [a, b]: below the chord between a and b. Concave: above it.

        The right side is the tangent line at a. If one side of an inequality is a line, it is often a tangent or a chord of the other side.

        Example: eˣ is convex ((eˣ)'' = eˣ > 0), and its tangent at 0 is y = 1 + x. So eˣ ≥ 1 + x for every x. Steps: the method "Prove an inequality with convexity".

        9Implicit differentiation and differentials

        Implicit differentiation

        When y is tied to x by an equation (like x² + y² = 25) instead of a formula y = f(x): differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x, then solve for y'.

        Every time y is differentiated, the chain rule adds a factor y': (y²)' = 2y · y', (sin y)' = cos y · y', (xy)' = y + x y'.

        Why it's needed: a circle isn't the graph of one function (it fails the vertical line test), but near each point it is: the top half is y = √(25 − x²). Implicit differentiation gives the slope without splitting into halves.

        Example: x² + y² = 25. Differentiate: 2x + 2y · y' = 0, so y' = −x/(y). At (3, 4): y' = −3/4. (Check: the radius has slope 4/3, and the tangent is perpendicular to it.)

        Careful: the answer usually contains both x and y. To get a number, plug in a point that lies on the curve.

        Differentials and linear approximation

        • Δy = f(x + Δx) − f(x): the real change in y.
        • The differential dy = f'(x) dx: the change along the tangent line (dx = Δx).
        • For small Δx: Δy ≈ dy, so f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + f'(a) · h (the linear approximation).

        In words: close to a point, a smooth curve looks like its tangent line. So to estimate a value near a point you know, follow the tangent instead of the curve. The smaller the step, the smaller the gap between Δy and dy.

        Example: √(4.1). Use f(x) = √x, a = 4, h = 0.1: f(4) = 2, f'(4) = 1/(2√4) = 1/4. So √(4.1) ≈ 2 + 0.1/4 = 2.025. (Calculator: 2.02485.)

        Error estimates: a side of a cube measured as 10 cm with a possible error of 0.1 cm: V = s³, dV = 3s² ds = 300 · 0.1 = 30 cm³ is the possible error in the volume.

        10Related rates

        Related rates

        When two quantities are linked by an equation and both change with time t, differentiate the equation with respect to t. The result links their rates (dx/dt, dy/dt), so knowing one rate gives the other.

        Why it works: both x and y are functions of time, so the chain rule gives (x²)' = 2x · dx/dt. The equation that holds at every moment also holds for the rates.

        Example: a 5 m ladder slides; its foot moves away from the wall at 0.5 m/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the foot is 3 m from the wall? x² + y² = 25 → 2x · dx/dt + 2y · dy/dt = 0. At x = 3, y = 4: 3 · 0.5 + 4 · dy/dt = 0, so dy/dt = −0.375 m/s: the top slides down at 0.375 m/s.

        The usual mistake: plugging in the numbers (like x = 3) before differentiating. Then x looks constant and its rate disappears. Differentiate first, plug in after. Steps: the method "Solving a related-rates problem".

        11Optimization problems

        Optimization problems

        A word problem that asks for the largest or smallest value (area, volume, cost, distance): write the quantity as a function of one variable, find the allowed interval, and find its absolute maximum or minimum there (Derivatives › 6).

        Example: cut equal squares of side x from the corners of a 12 × 12 sheet and fold an open box. V(x) = x(12 − 2x)² for 0 < x < 6. V'(x) = (12 − 2x)(12 − 6x) = 0 at x = 2 (and x = 6, outside). V(2) = 2 · 64 = 128; near the ends V → 0. Largest box: x = 2, volume 128.

        One critical point is enough on an interval: if a continuous function has only one critical point there and it's a local maximum, it's the absolute maximum (likewise for a minimum).

        The hard part is the setup: draw a sketch, name the variables, use the given condition (the "constraint") to remove all variables but one. Steps: the method "Solving an optimization problem".

        12Newton's method

        Newton's method

        To approximate a root of f(x) = 0: start from a guess x₁ and repeat

        x_(n+1) = x_(n) − (f(x_(n)))/(f'(x_(n)))

        The idea: at your guess, replace the curve by its tangent line, and take the place where the tangent crosses the x-axis as the next guess. Near a root the tangent hugs the curve, so the guesses close in very fast: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step.

        Example, √2: f(x) = x² − 2, f'(x) = 2x, so x_(n+1) = x_(n) − (x_(n)² − 2)/(2x_(n)). From x₁ = 2: 1.5, 1.41667, 1.414216 (true value 1.414214).

        When it fails: if f'(x_(n)) = 0 (a flat tangent never meets the axis), or the start is too far from the root, the guesses can jump away. Start close: use the intermediate value theorem to find an interval with a sign change first (Limits › 8).

        13Motion along a line

        Position, velocity and acceleration

        • Position s(t) on a line; velocity v(t) = s'(t); acceleration a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t).
        • Speed = |v(t)|. v > 0: moving in the positive direction; v < 0: the negative direction; v = 0: stopped (maybe turning around).
        • Speeding up when v and a have the same sign; slowing down when they have opposite signs.

        In words: velocity is how fast the position changes (with a direction), acceleration is how fast the velocity changes. A slope on the position graph is a velocity.

        Example: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3), a(t) = 6t − 12. It moves forward until t = 1, backwards until t = 3, then forward again. At t = 2: v = −3, a = 0. At t = 0.5: v = 3.75 > 0, a = −9 < 0: slowing down.

        Going backwards (from acceleration to velocity to position) is integration: Integrals › 17.

        1What an integral is

        Integrals and antiderivatives

        F is an antiderivative of f when F'(x) = f(x). Then

        ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C

        Integration is differentiation run backwards: F' = f  ⇔  ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C

        In words: differentiating asks "how fast is this function changing?". Integrating asks the reverse: "which function changes like this?". If you know the speed at every moment, the integral gives you back the position.

        Why the + C: a constant has derivative 0, so x², x² + 1 and x² − 7 all have derivative 2x. The derivative can't tell them apart, so the integral gives the whole family: ∫ 2x dx = x² + C, where C is any number.

        Check any answer by differentiating it: you must get the function under the integral back.

        Every antiderivative is the same curve moved up or down. Moving a curve up doesn't change its slope, so all of them have the same derivative.

        The integral sign and its bounds

        • Indefinite integral: ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C. No bounds. The answer is a family of functions.
        • Definite integral: ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx. The answer is one number.

        Reading the symbol: ∫ is a stretched S, for "sum". f(x) is the integrand, the function being integrated. a is the lower bound and b the upper bound: where the sum starts and ends on the x-axis. dx says that x is the variable.

        What the number means: the definite integral is the signed area between the graph and the x-axis from a to b. Area above the axis counts plus, area below counts minus (Integrals › 7).

        The two kinds are tied together by Newton–Leibniz (Integrals › 2): find F from the indefinite integral, then ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

        What dx means

        dx names the variable you integrate by, and stands for a very thin width along the x-axis.

        The picture: cut the area under the graph into very thin vertical slices. One slice at x is almost a rectangle: height f(x), width dx, area f(x) dx. The integral adds up all these slices from a to b. That is why f(x) and dx are written next to each other, like a multiplication.

        Which variable: in ∫ x·t dt the variable is t, so x is treated as a constant. Change the letter after d and you change the question.

        How thin is "very thin"? Darboux and Riemann sums (next card) make it exact: the slices get thinner and thinner, and the integral is what the sum tends to.

        Darboux and Riemann sums

        Split [a, b] into n strips of width Δx = (b − a)/(n), with points x_(0) = a < x_(1) < … < x_(n) = b.

        • Lower sum L: each strip's rectangle is as high as the lowest value of f on it.
        • Upper sum U: each rectangle is as high as the highest value of f on it.
        • Riemann sum: any point c_(i) in each strip: ∑_(i=1)^(n) f(c_(i))·Δx. It always lies between L and U.
        • f is integrable on [a, b] when L and U come together as the strips get thinner. Then ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx = lim_(n→∞) ∑_(i=1)^(n) f(c_(i))·Δx
        • Theorem: every function continuous on [a, b] is integrable on it.

        In words: we can't measure a curved area directly, but we can measure rectangles. The lower sum is too small, the upper sum is too big, and the true area is squeezed between them. Make the strips thinner and the two estimates close in on the same number: that number is the integral.

        For f(x) = x² on [0, 1]: the green rectangles are the lower sum, the outlined ones the upper sum. With 4, 8, 16 strips the gap between them shrinks towards the exact area 1/3.

        2The fundamental theorem and Newton–Leibniz

        Fundamental theorem of calculus

        f continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = ∫_(a)^(x) f(t) dt  ⇒  F'(x) = f(x) for every x ∈ (a, b)

        The area function is an antiderivative of the function under it. This is the theorem that links integrals and derivatives.

        What F is: the area under f from the fixed start a up to a moving end x. Move x and the area changes, so F is a function of x. The letter inside is t only because x is already taken by the end.

        Why it is true: move the end from x to x + h. The area grows by a thin strip of width h and height about f(x), so F(x + h) − F(x) ≈ f(x)·h. Divide by h: (F(x + h) − F(x))/h ≈ f(x). As h → 0 the strip becomes an exact rectangle, and the left side is the derivative F'(x) (Derivatives › 1). The area grows at the rate f(x).

        The shaded area is F(x). The thin outlined strip is what moving to x + h adds: about f(x)·h.

        Example: F(x) = ∫_(0)^(x) sin t dt has F'(x) = sin x, without calculating the integral at all. With an inner function, add the chain rule: (∫_(0)^(x²) sin t dt)' = sin(x²) · 2x.

        Newton–Leibniz theorem

        f continuous on [a, b] and F any antiderivative of f  ⇒  ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)

        Written: ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx = [F(x)]_(a)^(b) = F(b) − F(a)

        Where it comes from: by the fundamental theorem, the area function A(x) = ∫_(a)^(x) f(t) dt is an antiderivative of f. Any other antiderivative differs from it by a constant: F = A + C (Derivatives › 7, Monotonicity). So F(b) − F(a) = A(b) − A(a) = A(b) − 0, which is the whole area.

        In words: the change in a function between two points equals the area under its derivative over that interval: ∫_(a)^(b) f'(x) dx = f(b) − f(a). If f' is a speed, the area under it is the distance covered.

        Signed area: the result is the signed area. It equals the geometric area only where the function under the integral is ≥ 0.

        The + C doesn't matter here: (F(b) + C) − (F(a) + C) = F(b) − F(a), so any antiderivative gives the same answer.

        Left: the area under f'(x) = x from 1 to 3 is 4. Right: f(x) = x²/2 rises from 1/2 to 9/2, also by 4.

        Example, step by step: ∫_(1)^(3) x² dx. An antiderivative is F(x) = (x³)/3. Then F(3) − F(1) = 27/3 − 1/3 = 26/3.

        3Linear properties

        Sums and constants

        • ∫ (f(x) + g(x)) dx = ∫ f(x) dx + ∫ g(x) dx
        • ∫ k·f(x) dx = k·∫ f(x) dx  (k a constant)
        • The same with bounds: ∫_(a)^(b) (α·f(x) + β·g(x)) dx = α∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx + β∫_(a)^(b) g(x) dx

        Why: the derivative has the same rules: (F + G)' = F' + G' and (k·F)' = k·F'. Run them backwards and you get these.

        Use: split a long integrand into simple pieces and integrate each one: ∫ (3x² − 4x + 5) dx = 3·∫ x² dx − 4·∫ x dx + ∫ 5 dx = x³ − 2x² + 5x + C

        There is no such rule for products or quotients: ∫ f·g dx is not ∫ f dx·∫ g dx. Products need substitution or parts (Integrals › 5, 6).

        Properties of the definite integral

        • Same bounds: ∫_(a)^(a) f(x) dx = 0
        • Swapping the bounds flips the sign: ∫_(b)^(a) f(x) dx = −∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx
        • Splitting the interval: ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx = ∫_(a)^(c) f(x) dx + ∫_(c)^(b) f(x) dx

        In words: no width, no area. Walking the interval backwards counts every slice with the opposite sign. And an area can be cut into two pieces at any point c and added back together.

        Splitting is what lets you integrate a piecewise function or an absolute value: cut at each breakpoint (Integrals › 7).

        Example: if ∫_(0)^(2) f(x) dx = 5 and ∫_(2)^(3) f(x) dx = −1, then ∫_(0)^(3) f(x) dx = 5 + (−1) = 4 and ∫_(3)^(0) f(x) dx = −4.

        4Basic integration techniques

        Polynomials and roots

        • Power rule: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C  (n ≠ −1)
        • The missing case: ∫ 1/(x) dx = ln|x| + C
        • Constants: ∫ k dx = k·x + C
        • Roots are powers: √x = x^(1/2), ∛x = x^(1/3), 1/√x = x^(−1/2)

        Why: differentiating lowers the power by one and multiplies by it. Integrating does the opposite: raise the power by one, then divide by the new power. Check: (xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1))' = xⁿ.

        Why n ≠ −1: for n = −1 the rule would divide by 0. That case is ln|x|. The absolute value is there so it also works for x < 0, where ln x is not defined but (ln|x|)' = 1/x still holds.

        Examples: ∫ √x dx = ∫ x^(1/2) dx = (x^(3/2))/(3/2) + C = (2/3)·x√x + C  ·  ∫ 1/(x³) dx = ∫ x⁻³ dx = (x⁻²)/(−2) + C = −1/(2x²) + C

        A linear function to a power

        • ∫ (ax + b)ⁿ dx = ((ax + b)ⁿ⁺¹)/(a(n + 1)) + C  (n ≠ −1, a ≠ 0)
        • ∫ 1/(ax + b) dx = (1/a)·ln|ax + b| + C

        Why the extra 1/a: differentiating (ax + b)ⁿ⁺¹ gives (n + 1)(ax + b)ⁿ·a. The inside's derivative a appears (chain rule, Derivatives › 2), so we divide by it in advance.

        Example: ∫ (3x − 1)⁴ dx = ((3x − 1)⁵)/(3·5) + C = ((3x − 1)⁵)/(15) + C

        This works only when the inside is linear. For (x² + 1)⁴ the inside's derivative 2x is not a constant: expand it, or use substitution if x is also there (Integrals › 5).

        Integrals that give ln

        ∫ f'(x)/(f(x)) dx = ln|f(x)| + C

        Why: by the chain rule, (ln|f(x)|)' = f'(x)/f(x) (Derivatives › 2).

        How to spot it: the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, maybe up to a constant.

        Examples: ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx = ln(x² + 1) + C (no |·| needed: x² + 1 > 0)  ·  ∫ cos x/sin x dx = ln|sin x| + C

        Almost the right numerator? Fix it first: the method "Bring a quotient to the form f′/f".

        Not ln: a constant over a square plus a number gives arctan: ∫ 1/(1 + x²) dx = arctan x + C (Functions › 6).

        Sine and cosine

        • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C
        • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C
        • ∫ sin(ax + b) dx = −(1/a)·cos(ax + b) + C
        • ∫ cos(ax + b) dx = (1/a)·sin(ax + b) + C

        Why: (cos x)' = −sin x, so (−cos x)' = sin x, and (sin x)' = cos x (Derivatives › 2). Watch the minus sign: it belongs to the integral of sin.

        Example: ∫ cos(2x + 1) dx = (1/2)·sin(2x + 1) + C. Check: ((1/2)·sin(2x + 1))' = (1/2)·cos(2x + 1)·2 = cos(2x + 1)

        When the inside is not linear, like sin(x²), these rules don't work. Substitution does, when the inside's derivative is also there: ∫ x·sin(x²) dx (Integrals › 5).

        Exponential functions

        • ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C
        • ∫ e^(ax + b) dx = (1/a)·e^(ax + b) + C  (a ≠ 0)

        Why: eˣ is its own derivative (Derivatives › 2). With a linear inside, the chain rule brings out an a, so we divide by it.

        Example: ∫ e^(−2x) dx = −(1/2)·e^(−2x) + C

        5Substitution

        What the substitution does

        ∫ f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫ f(t) dt, with t = g(x) and dt = g'(x) dx

        With bounds: ∫_(a)^(b) f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫_(g(a))^(g(b)) f(t) dt

        Where it comes from: it is the chain rule run backwards. If F' = f, the chain rule gives (F(g(x)))' = f(g(x))·g'(x). So the integral of the right side is F(g(x)) + C = F(t) + C, which is exactly ∫ f(t) dt.

        What dt = g'(x) dx means: a thin slice of width dx on the x-axis becomes a slice of width dt = g'(x)·dx on the t-axis. Where g changes fast, the slices are stretched, and the integrand is rescaled to match, so the area stays the same.

        How to spot it: a function inside another function (the inside is g(x)), and the inside's derivative g'(x) is also multiplying, maybe up to a constant.

        ∫_(0)^(1) 2x·e^(x²) dx with t = x² becomes ∫_(0)^(1) eᵗ dt. The graphs look different, but the areas are the same: e − 1 ≈ 1.72.

        Example, step by step: ∫ x · sin(x²) dx. The inside is x², so t = x² and dt = 2x dx, which means x dx = (dt)/2. The integral becomes (1/2) ∫ sin t dt = −(1/2) cos t + C = −(1/2) cos(x²) + C. Full steps: the method "Integration by substitution".

        6Integration by parts

        Integration by parts formula

        ∫ u·v' dx = u·v − ∫ u'·v dx

        With bounds: ∫_(a)^(b) u·v' dx = [u·v]_(a)^(b) − ∫_(a)^(b) u'·v dx

        Where it comes from, step by step:

        1. Product rule (Derivatives › 2): (u·v)' = u'·v + u·v'
        2. Integrate both sides: u·v = ∫ u'·v dx + ∫ u·v' dx. The left side is an antiderivative of its own derivative.
        3. Move one integral across: ∫ u·v' dx = u·v − ∫ u'·v dx

        What it buys you: it swaps one integral for another. It helps when the new one, ∫ u'·v dx, is easier: you choose u as the factor that gets simpler when you differentiate it.

        The big rectangle minus the small one is u₂v₂ − u₁v₁. The curve splits that L-shaped region into the area under it, ∫ v du, and the area beside it, ∫ u dv. So ∫ u dv = [uv] − ∫ v du.

        Example, step by step: ∫ x · eˣ dx. Choose u = x (it gets simpler when differentiated: u' = 1) and v' = eˣ, so v = eˣ. Then x eˣ − ∫ 1 · eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C. Full steps: the method "Integration by parts".

        7Definite integrals and area

        Integral value and area

        • Value of the integral: ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx. Parts below the x-axis count negative.
        • Area between the graph and the x-axis: ∫_(a)^(b) |f(x)| dx. Everything counts positive.

        In words: the integral adds heights times widths, and a height below the axis is a negative number. So a piece below the axis subtracts. The area is a geometric size, never negative: you flip the negative pieces before adding.

        When they are equal: only when f ≥ 0 on the whole interval.

        For sin x on [0, 2π] the two humps cancel in the integral but add up in the area. Try other functions live in Precalc › Integrals.

        Example: f(x) = x on [−1, 2]. The value is ∫_(−1)^(2) x dx = 4/2 − 1/2 = 3/2. The area is the triangle below the axis (1/2) plus the one above (2): 5/2.

        Area between two curves

        Where f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b]:  area = ∫_(a)^(b) (f(x) − g(x)) dx

        In words: each thin slice now goes from the lower curve up to the upper curve, so its height is top − bottom. This works anywhere, even below the x-axis, because the difference is still the slice's height.

        When the curves cross inside the interval, the top one changes. Split at the crossing points and use top − bottom on each piece.

        y = x and y = x³ cross at −1, 0 and 1. On (0, 1) the line is on top, on (−1, 0) the cubic is.

        Example: between y = x and y = x³ on [0, 1], the line is on top: ∫_(0)^(1) (x − x³) dx = 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4.

        Even and odd functions on a symmetric interval

        • Even (f(−x) = f(x), mirror image in the y-axis): ∫_(−a)^(a) f(x) dx = 2∫_(0)^(a) f(x) dx
        • Odd (f(−x) = −f(x), symmetric about the origin): ∫_(−a)^(a) f(x) dx = 0, but the area is 2∫_(0)^(a) |f(x)| dx

        Examples: x², cos x, |x| are even. x³, sin x, x are odd.

        Why: an even graph has two equal halves, so do one and double it. An odd graph's left half is the right half flipped below the axis, so their signed values cancel. The areas don't cancel: both halves have the same size.

        8Estimating integrals

        Comparison of integrals

        f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ∈ [a, b] (a < b)  ⇒  ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx ≤ ∫_(a)^(b) g(x) dx

        In words: if one graph is never above the other, the area under it can't be bigger. Each thin slice of f is no taller than the matching slice of g.

        Use it to estimate an integral you can't calculate: put it between two simpler functions whose integrals you can calculate.

        Example: on [0, 1], x² ≤ x (squaring a number between 0 and 1 makes it smaller). So ∫_(0)^(1) x² dx ≤ ∫_(0)^(1) x dx: indeed 1/3 ≤ 1/2.

        Bounds from the minimum and maximum

        f continuous on [a, b], with minimum m and maximum M there  ⇒  m(b − a) ≤ ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx ≤ M(b − a)

        Why: compare f with the two constant functions m ≤ f(x) ≤ M. A constant's integral is a rectangle: height times width.

        Finding m and M: check the two ends and the critical points inside (Derivatives › 6). Only when f is monotone on the interval are they simply f(a) and f(b).

        The integral is the area under the curve. It is more than the low rectangle (green) and less than the high one (blue). Here the maximum is inside the interval, not at an end.

        Example: ∫_(0)^(1) e^(−x²) dx has no simple antiderivative. On [0, 1], e^(−x²) falls from 1 to 1/e, so the integral is between 1/e ≈ 0.37 and 1. Steps: the method "Estimating an integral you can't calculate".

        9Improper integrals

        What an improper integral is

        • ∫_(a)^(∞) f(x) dx = lim_(r→∞) ∫_(a)^(r) f(x) dx
        • ∫_(−∞)^(b) f(x) dx = lim_(r→−∞) ∫_(r)^(b) f(x) dx
        • Both bounds infinite: split at any point c: ∫_(−∞)^(∞) f(x) dx = ∫_(−∞)^(c) f(x) dx + ∫_(c)^(∞) f(x) dx. Both pieces must converge.

        It converges if the limit is a finite number, and diverges otherwise (infinite, or no limit).

        In words: we can't plug in ∞, so we stop at a finite end r, calculate as usual, and then let r run off to infinity (limits at infinity: Limits › 1). An area that goes on forever can still add up to a finite number, if the graph falls towards 0 fast enough.

        ∫_(1)^(r) 1/(x²) dx = 1 − 1/r → 1: the endless area under 1/x² from 1 on is exactly 1.

        A divergent example: ∫_(1)^(r) 1/(x) dx = ln r → ∞. The graph of 1/x falls towards 0 too, but too slowly: the area keeps growing.

        Improper integrals of unbounded functions

        If f blows up at the end a (continuous on (a, b]):

        ∫_(a)^(b) f(x) dx = lim_(r→a⁺) ∫_(r)^(b) f(x) dx

        The same at the end b with r → b⁻. A blow-up inside the interval: split there.

        In words: the bound is finite, but the graph shoots up to infinity at it, so we can't plug it in. Stop just before it at r, calculate, and let r slide to the bad point. Converges or diverges exactly as before.

        ∫_(r)^(1) 1/(√x) dx = 2 − 2√r → 2: the graph has no top near 0, yet the area is 2.

        A divergent example: ∫_(r)^(1) 1/(x²) dx = 1/(r) − 1 → ∞ as r → 0⁺. Near 0, 1/x² shoots up too steeply for the area to be finite.

        Harmonic integral (p-integral)

        • ∫_(1)^(∞) 1/(x^(p)) dx converges when p > 1 and diverges when p ≤ 1
        • Near 0, the other way round: ∫_(0)^(1) 1/(x^(p)) dx converges when p < 1 and diverges when p ≥ 1

        Why, for p ≠ 1: ∫_(1)^(r) x^(−p) dx = (r^(1 − p) − 1)/(1 − p). If p > 1 the power 1 − p is negative, so r^(1 − p) → 0 and the limit is 1/(p − 1). If p < 1 it grows to infinity.

        The harmonic case p = 1 diverges: ∫_(1)^(r) 1/(x) dx = ln r → ∞. It is the border: 1/x falls, but just too slowly.

        Why it matters: these are the reference functions for the comparison test (next card).

        1/x (blue) and 1/x² (green) look alike, but the area under 1/x is infinite and the area under 1/x² is 1.

        Comparison test for improper integrals

        0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ≥ a:

        • ∫_(a)^(∞) g(x) dx converges  ⇒  ∫_(a)^(∞) f(x) dx converges
        • ∫_(a)^(∞) f(x) dx diverges  ⇒  ∫_(a)^(∞) g(x) dx diverges

        In words: under a finite area, a smaller area is finite too. Above an infinite area, a bigger area is infinite too.

        What tells you nothing: the bigger one diverges, or the smaller one converges. Something below an infinite area can be finite or infinite, and something above a finite area too. If you land there, compare with a different function, in the other direction.

        Both conditions matter: f ≥ 0 (no negative parts) and the inequality on the whole [a, ∞), or at least from some point on.

        The same works for unbounded functions near a bad point, with ∫_(0)^(1) 1/(x^(p)) dx as the reference.

        Example: does ∫_(1)^(∞) 1/(x² + 1) dx converge? For x ≥ 1, 1/(x² + 1) ≤ 1/(x²), and ∫_(1)^(∞) 1/(x²) dx converges (p = 2 > 1). The smaller one is under a finite area, so it converges too.

        10Trig integrals

        Powers of sin and cos

        ∫ sinᵐx cosⁿx dx:

        • One power is odd (say n): save one cos x, turn the rest into sin with cos²x = 1 − sin²x, and substitute u = sin x. (Odd m: the same with the roles swapped, u = cos x.)
        • Both powers are even: lower them with sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 and cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2.

        Why saving one factor works: the saved cos x dx is exactly du when u = sin x, and everything else becomes a polynomial in u.

        Example (odd): ∫ sin³x dx = ∫ (1 − cos²x) sin x dx; with u = cos x, du = −sin x dx: −∫ (1 − u²) du = −cos x + (cos³x)/3 + C.

        Example (even): ∫ cos²x dx = ∫ (1 + cos 2x)/2 dx = x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + C.

        Products like sin 3x cos 5x become sums: sin A cos B = (1/2)(sin(A − B) + sin(A + B)), and each piece is easy.

        Powers of tan and sec

        • ∫ tan x dx = −ln|cos x| + C  ·  ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C
        • ∫ 1/(cos²x) dx = ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + C
        • Even power of sec: save sec²x, turn the rest into tan with sec²x = 1 + tan²x, substitute u = tan x.
        • Odd power of tan: save sec x tan x, turn the rest into sec, substitute u = sec x.

        Why ∫ tan x dx is a log: tan x = (sin x)/(cos x), and the top is minus the derivative of the bottom: the f'/f pattern (Integrals › 4).

        Example: ∫ tan²x dx = ∫ (sec²x − 1) dx = tan x − x + C.

        Example: ∫ sec⁴x dx = ∫ (1 + tan²x) sec²x dx, u = tan x: tan x + (tan³x)/3 + C.

        11Trig substitution

        Trig substitution

        The integral hasSubstituteBecause
        √(a² − x²)x = a sin θa² − a²sin²θ = a²cos²θ
        √(a² + x²)x = a tan θa² + a²tan²θ = a²sec²θ
        √(x² − a²)x = a sec θa²sec²θ − a² = a²tan²θ

        The idea: a root of "square plus or minus square" is a Pythagoras leftover. Choosing x as a trig function of an angle turns the inside into a perfect square, and the root disappears.

        Going back to x: draw the right triangle that matches your substitution (above, for x = a sin θ) and read any trig function of θ from it.

        Example: ∫ 1/(x²√(4 − x²)) dx, x = 2 sin θ, dx = 2 cos θ dθ: ∫ (2 cos θ)/(4 sin²θ · 2 cos θ) dθ = (1/4) ∫ csc²θ dθ = −(1/4) cot θ + C. From the triangle, cot θ = (√(4 − x²))/(x), so the answer is −(√(4 − x²))/(4x) + C.

        12Partial fractions

        Partial fractions

        To integrate a fraction of polynomials (P(x))/(Q(x)):

        • If the top's degree is ≥ the bottom's, first divide (long division).
        • Factor the bottom into linear factors (ax + b) and quadratics with no real roots.
        • Each factor gets its own simple fraction: (x − r) → A/(x − r); (x − r)² → A/(x − r) + B/((x − r)²); (x² + px + q) → (Ax + B)/(x² + px + q).
        • Find the constants, then integrate each piece: they give ln, powers, or arctan.

        The idea: it's adding fractions backwards. 1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1) makes 2/(x² − 1); partial fractions takes the single fraction apart into pieces that are each easy to integrate.

        Example: (5x − 1)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 2). Multiply out: 5x − 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x − 1). Put x = 1: 4 = 3A, A = 4/3. Put x = −2: −11 = −3B, B = 11/3. So the integral is (4/3) ln|x − 1| + (11/3) ln|x + 2| + C.

        Quick trick: plugging in each root of a linear factor kills every other term, as in the example. Steps: the method "Integrating with partial fractions".

        13Other substitutions

        Substitutions that remove roots

        • A root of a linear expression, ⁿ√(ax + b): let u = ⁿ√(ax + b), so x = (uⁿ − b)/a. The integral becomes a fraction of polynomials.
        • Several roots of x (√x and ∛x): let x = u⁶ (6 = the least common multiple of the root orders).
        • A fraction of sin x and cos x: u = tan(x/2) turns it into a fraction of polynomials, with sin x = (2u)/(1 + u²), cos x = (1 − u²)/(1 + u²), dx = (2 du)/(1 + u²).

        Example: ∫ 1/(1 + √x) dx: u = √x, x = u², dx = 2u du. It becomes ∫ (2u)/(1 + u) du = ∫ (2 − 2/(1 + u)) du = 2u − 2 ln|1 + u| + C = 2√x − 2 ln(1 + √x) + C.

        When to try it: after the basic techniques fail. The goal is always to land on something you know: a polynomial, a fraction of polynomials, or a standard integral.

        14Numerical integration

        The trapezoid rule and Simpson's rule

        Split [a, b] into n equal steps of width Δx = (b − a)/n, with points x₀, x₁, …, xₙ and values yᵢ = f(xᵢ).

        • Trapezoid: T = (Δx)/2 (y₀ + 2y₁ + 2y₂ + … + 2yₙ₋₁ + yₙ)
        • Simpson (n even): S = (Δx)/3 (y₀ + 4y₁ + 2y₂ + 4y₃ + … + 4yₙ₋₁ + yₙ)

        The idea: when there's no antiderivative to use, add up simple shapes. The trapezoid rule joins neighbouring points with straight chords; Simpson's rule fits a parabola through each three points, which follows a curve much more closely.

        Example: ∫_(1)^(3) 1/(x) dx = ln 3 ≈ 1.0986. With n = 4, Δx = 0.5, values 1, 0.667, 0.5, 0.4, 0.333: trapezoid 0.25(1 + 1.333 + 1 + 0.8 + 0.333) ≈ 1.1167; Simpson (0.5/3)(1 + 2.667 + 1 + 1.6 + 0.333) ≈ 1.1000. Simpson is much closer.

        Error bounds: trapezoid ≤ ((b − a)³ M₂)/(12n²) with M₂ ≥ |f''|; Simpson ≤ ((b − a)⁵ M₄)/(180n⁴) with M₄ ≥ |f⁽⁴⁾|. Doubling n cuts the trapezoid error by about 4 and Simpson's by about 16.

        15Volumes

        Volumes by slicing: disks and washers

        • Cross-sections of area A(x): V = ∫_(a)^(b) A(x) dx
        • Disks (turning y = f(x) around the x-axis): V = ∫_(a)^(b) π f(x)² dx
        • Washers (the region between f ≥ g ≥ 0): V = ∫_(a)^(b) π (f(x)² − g(x)²) dx

        The idea: cut the solid into thin slices of width dx. Each slice is almost a flat disk with volume π · radius² · dx, and the integral adds them up, exactly like area adds thin rectangles.

        Example: turn y = √x, 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, around the x-axis: V = ∫_(0)^(4) π x dx = 8π.

        Washer: when the region doesn't touch the axis, each slice has a hole: outer radius f, inner radius g. Subtract the squares, not the radii: π(f² − g²), not π(f − g)².

        Around the y-axis: use y as the variable: V = ∫ π x(y)² dy.

        Volumes by cylindrical shells

        Turning the region under y = f(x) ≥ 0, 0 ≤ a ≤ x ≤ b, around the y-axis:

        V = ∫_(a)^(b) 2π x f(x) dx

        The idea: a thin vertical strip at distance x from the axis sweeps out a thin tube (a shell). Unrolled, it's almost a flat sheet: length 2πx (the circumference), height f(x), thickness dx.

        When to use it: when slicing the other way would need x as a function of y and that's hard. Example: y = x − x³ on [0, 1] around the y-axis: V = ∫_(0)^(1) 2π x(x − x³) dx = 2π(1/3 − 1/5) = (4π)/15.

        Disks or shells? Disks: slices perpendicular to the axis of rotation. Shells: strips parallel to it. Steps: the method "Setting up a volume of revolution".

        16Arc length and surface area

        Arc length

        The length of y = f(x) from x = a to x = b (with f' continuous):

        L = ∫_(a)^(b) √(1 + f'(x)²) dx

        Where it comes from: a tiny piece of the curve is almost straight: by Pythagoras its length is √(dx² + dy²). Take out dx: √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx. Add up all the pieces.

        Example: y = (2/3)x^(3/2) on [0, 3]: f'(x) = √x, so L = ∫_(0)^(3) √(1 + x) dx = (2/3)(4^(3/2) − 1) = 14/3.

        Warning: the root usually makes the integral impossible to do exactly. Textbook examples are chosen so 1 + f'² is a perfect square; otherwise use numerical integration (Integrals › 14).

        Surface area of revolution

        Turning y = f(x) ≥ 0, a ≤ x ≤ b, around the x-axis:

        S = ∫_(a)^(b) 2π f(x) √(1 + f'(x)²) dx

        The idea: each tiny piece of curve, of length ds, sweeps a thin band: circumference 2π f(x) times width ds.

        Example, a sphere: f(x) = √(r² − x²) on [−r, r]. Then f · √(1 + f'²) = r, so S = ∫_(−r)^(r) 2πr dx = 4πr² ✓.

        17Motion, work and fluid force

        Motion: from velocity to position

        • s(t) = ∫ v(t) dt  ·  v(t) = ∫ a(t) dt (each with a constant from the starting values)
        • Displacement: ∫_(t₁)^(t₂) v(t) dt  ·  Distance travelled: ∫_(t₁)^(t₂) |v(t)| dt

        Displacement or distance? Displacement is where you end up compared with where you started: going forward 5 and back 3 is 2. Distance counts every step: 8. It's the same difference as "integral value vs area" (Integrals › 7).

        Example: v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 = (t − 1)(t − 3) on [0, 3]. Displacement: ∫_(0)^(3) v dt = 9 − 18 + 9 = 0. Distance: ∫_(0)^(1) v dt − ∫_(1)^(3) v dt = 4/3 + 4/3 = 8/3.

        Free fall: a = −g gives v = v₀ − gt and s = s₀ + v₀t − (1/2)gt². (Derivatives › 13 goes the other way.)

        Work

        A force F(x) moving an object along a line from a to b does work W = ∫_(a)^(b) F(x) dx. (A constant force: W = F · d.)

        Why an integral: over a tiny step dx the force is almost constant, so the work there is F(x) dx. Add up the steps.

        Example, a spring (Hooke's law F = kx): a spring with k = 200 N/m, stretched from its natural length by 0.1 m to 0.3 m: W = ∫_(0.1)^(0.3) 200x dx = 100(0.09 − 0.01) = 8 J.

        Pumping a liquid: slice the liquid into thin horizontal layers; each layer's weight times the distance it's lifted gives its work; integrate over the depth. Steps: the method "Solving a work problem".

        Fluid pressure and force

        • Pressure at depth h: p = ρ h (ρ = weight density of the liquid)
        • Force on a vertical plate whose width at depth h is w(h): F = ∫_(a)^(b) ρ h w(h) dh

        The idea: pressure grows with depth, so you can't just multiply. A thin horizontal strip at depth h has almost one pressure: force ρ h · w(h) dh. Add up the strips.

        Example: a rectangular gate 2 m wide, from depth 1 m to 3 m, in water (ρ ≈ 9810 N/m³): F = ∫_(1)^(3) 9810 · h · 2 dh = 9810 · 8 ≈ 78,500 N.

        18Differential equations

        What a differential equation is

        An equation with an unknown function and its derivatives, like y' = 2y. A solution is a function that makes it true. The order is the highest derivative.

        The general solution has an arbitrary constant; an initial condition like y(0) = 5 fixes it (an initial value problem).

        Example: y' = 2y. Try y = Ce^(2x): y' = 2Ce^(2x) = 2y ✓. With y(0) = 5: C = 5, so y = 5e^(2x).

        Why they matter: nature usually tells you how fast something changes, not what it is. "A population grows in proportion to its size" is y' = ky; solving it tells you the population at any time.

        The simplest kind, y' = f(x), is just integration: y = ∫ f(x) dx.

        Separable equations

        An equation that can be written dy/dx = g(x) h(y) is separable. Move everything with y to one side and everything with x to the other, then integrate both sides:

        ∫ (dy)/(h(y)) = ∫ g(x) dx

        Example: y' = xy². Separate: (dy)/(y²) = x dx. Integrate: −1/(y) = (x²)/2 + C, so y = −2/(x² + 2C). Only one constant is needed (put both constants on one side).

        Don't lose solutions: dividing by h(y) assumes h(y) ≠ 0. Constant solutions with h(y) = 0 (here y = 0) must be checked separately.

        First-order linear equations

        y' + p(x) y = q(x). Multiply by the integrating factor μ(x) = e^(∫ p(x) dx); the left side becomes (μ y)', so

        μ y = ∫ μ q dx,  i.e.  y = (1/μ) ∫ μ(x) q(x) dx

        Why it works: by the product rule, (μy)' = μy' + μ'y, and μ' = pμ by its definition. So μ(y' + py) = (μy)', which you can integrate directly.

        Example: y' + 2y = 4. μ = e^(2x); (e^(2x) y)' = 4e^(2x), so e^(2x) y = 2e^(2x) + C and y = 2 + Ce^(−2x). Every solution settles at 2.

        Growth, decay and cooling

        • Growth or decay: y' = ky → y = y₀ e^(kt) (k > 0 grows, k < 0 decays)
        • Half-life: T = (ln 2)/(|k|)  ·  doubling time: (ln 2)/k
        • Newton's law of cooling: T' = −k(T − Tₛ) → T = Tₛ + (T₀ − Tₛ) e^(−kt)

        In words: when the rate of change is proportional to the amount, you get exponential growth or decay. Cooling is the same idea applied to the difference from room temperature: the bigger the gap, the faster it closes.

        Example: coffee at 90° in a 20° room is 60° after 10 minutes. 40 = 70e^(−10k) → k = (ln(7/4))/10 ≈ 0.056. After 20 minutes: 20 + 70e^(−20k) = 20 + 70 · (4/7)² ≈ 42.9°.

        Example: a substance has half-life 5 years: k = −(ln 2)/5. After 15 years, (1/2)³ = 1/8 is left.

        1Sequences

        What a sequence is

        A sequence is an endless list of numbers in order: a_(1), a_(2), a_(3), …. Written {a_(n)}_(n=1)^(∞) or just {a_(n)}.

        Formally, it's a function whose domain is the natural numbers: a_(n) = f(n), n = 1, 2, 3, …

        In words: a_(n) is "the term in place n". A formula for a_(n) tells you any term straight away: for a_(n) = 1/(n), the 5th term is 1/5.

        Finding the formula from the first terms: compare each term with its place number. 1/3, 2/4, 3/5, 4/6, …: the top is the place n, the bottom is n + 2, so a_(n) = n/(n + 2). Signs that switch (+, −, +, −) come from a factor (−1)^(n+1).

        Defined step by step: a sequence can also be given by its first term and a rule that builds each term from the one before (a recursive formula). Example: a_(1) = 2, a_(n+1) = 3a_(n) − 1 gives 2, 5, 14, 41, …

        The graph of a sequence is separate dots at n = 1, 2, 3, …, not a connected curve (next card).

        Limit of a sequence

        lim_(n→∞) a_(n) = L  ⇔  ∀ε > 0 ∃N : n ≥ N ⇒ |a_(n) − L| < ε

        Then the sequence converges to L. A sequence with no finite limit diverges.

        In words: the terms get as close to L as you like and stay that close. However thin a band someone draws around L, from some place N on, every term is inside it. The first few terms don't matter at all.

        Three ways to diverge: grow without end (n + 1, limit +∞); jump between values ((−1)^(n): −1, 1, −1, …); or wander without settling.

        Example: a_(n) = n/(n + 1): 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, … gets closer and closer to 1. Dividing top and bottom by n: 1/(1 + 1/(n)) → 1/(1 + 0) = 1.

        Limit laws and the squeeze theorem

        If a_(n) → L₁ and b_(n) → L₂ (finite), then a_(n) ± b_(n) → L₁ ± L₂, c · a_(n) → c · L₁, a_(n) b_(n) → L₁ L₂, and (a_(n))/(b_(n)) → (L₁)/(L₂) when L₂ ≠ 0.

        • From a function: if lim_(x→∞) f(x) = L and a_(n) = f(n), then lim_(n→∞) a_(n) = L. So you may use L'Hôpital's rule on f(x).
        • Squeeze: b_(n) ≤ a_(n) ≤ c_(n) from some place on, and b_(n) → L, c_(n) → L ⇒ a_(n) → L.
        • Even and odd places: a_(n) → L ⇔ the terms in the even places and the terms in the odd places both tend to L.

        Why L'Hôpital needs a function: a sequence only lives at whole numbers, so it has no derivative. Replace n by a real x, find the limit of f(x), and the sequence has the same limit.

        Example (function): (ln n)/(n). Look at (ln x)/(x): it's ∞/∞, and L'Hôpital gives (1/(x))/(1) → 0. So (ln n)/(n) → 0.

        Example (even and odd): (−1)^(n) · n/(n + 1): the even places tend to 1, the odd places to −1. They disagree, so the sequence diverges.

        Example (squeeze): (sin n)/(n) is between −1/(n) and 1/(n), and both tend to 0, so it tends to 0 too.

        Standard limits

        • lim_(n→∞) 1/(nᵖ) = 0  (p > 0)
        • lim_(n→∞) rⁿ = 0 when |r| < 1; rⁿ diverges when |r| > 1 or r = −1
        • lim_(n→∞) ⁿ√n = 1  ·  lim_(n→∞) ⁿ√a = 1 (a > 0)
        • lim_(n→∞) (xⁿ)/(n!) = 0 for every real x
        • lim_(n→∞) (1 + 1/(n))ⁿ = e

        Who wins: as n grows, ln n << nᵖ << aⁿ (a > 1) << n!. A slower one over a faster one tends to 0: n¹⁰/(2ⁿ) → 0, (5ⁿ)/(n!) → 0.

        Why ⁿ√n → 1: write it as n^(1/n) = e^((ln n)/n). The exponent (ln n)/(n) → 0, so the whole thing tends to e⁰ = 1.

        Why (xⁿ)/(n!) → 0: from some place on, each new factor x/(n) is less than 1/2, so each step at least halves the term.

        2Monotone sequences

        Increasing, decreasing and bounded

        • Increasing: a_(1) ≤ a_(2) ≤ a_(3) ≤ …  ·  strictly increasing: with <
        • Decreasing: a_(1) ≥ a_(2) ≥ a_(3) ≥ …  ·  strictly decreasing: with >
        • Either kind is monotone.
        • Bounded above by M: a_(n) ≤ M for every n. Bounded below by m: a_(n) ≥ m for every n.
        • Monotone from some place on: monotone once you ignore the first few terms.

        Examples: 1, 1/2, 1/3, … is strictly decreasing, bounded below by 0. 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, … is increasing, but not strictly. 1, −1/2, 1/3, −1/4, … is not monotone: it goes down, up, down.

        From some place on: (10ⁿ)/(n!) grows at first (10, 50, 166.7, …), but from n = 10 on, each term is smaller than the one before.

        Three ways to test monotonicity

        TestIncreasingDecreasing
        Differencea_(n+1) − a_(n) ≥ 0a_(n+1) − a_(n) ≤ 0
        Ratio (positive terms)(a_(n+1))/(a_(n)) ≥ 1(a_(n+1))/(a_(n)) ≤ 1
        Derivative, a_(n) = f(n)f'(x) ≥ 0 for x ≥ 1f'(x) ≤ 0 for x ≥ 1

        With strict inequalities (> 0, > 1) the sequence is strictly monotone.

        Which to pick: the difference is good for fractions and sums; the ratio for factorials and powers like (2ⁿ)/(n!), where a lot cancels; the derivative when a_(n) is a nice formula in n.

        Example, all three: a_(n) = n/(n + 1). Difference: (n + 1)/(n + 2) − n/(n + 1) = 1/((n + 1)(n + 2)) > 0. Ratio: (n² + 2n + 1)/(n² + 2n) > 1. Derivative: f(x) = x/(x + 1), f'(x) = 1/((x + 1)²) > 0. All say: strictly increasing.

        Monotone convergence theorem

        • An increasing sequence that is bounded above by M converges, to some L ≤ M. If it isn't bounded above, it tends to +∞.
        • A decreasing sequence that is bounded below by M converges, to some L ≥ M. If it isn't bounded below, it tends to −∞.
        • The same holds for a sequence that is monotone from some place on.

        In words: a sequence that only goes up but can never pass a ceiling has to level off somewhere. It can't jump around (it's monotone) and can't escape (it's bounded).

        What it does and doesn't tell you: it proves the limit exists, but doesn't say what it is. To find it, a trick often works: if a_(n+1) = g(a_(n)) and a_(n) → L, then a_(n+1) → L too, so L = g(L).

        Example: a_(n) = (5ⁿ)/(n!) is decreasing from n = 5 on and bounded below by 0, so it converges. Its terms satisfy a_(n+1) = 5/(n + 1) · a_(n); let n → ∞: L = 0 · L, so L = 0. Full steps: the method "Showing a sequence converges (monotone and bounded)".

        3Infinite series

        Partial sums and convergence

        An infinite series is an endless sum ∑_(k=1)^(∞) u_(k) = u_(1) + u_(2) + u_(3) + …

        The n-th partial sum is s_(n) = u_(1) + u_(2) + … + u_(n). If the sequence of partial sums {s_(n)} converges to S, the series converges and its sum is S. Otherwise it diverges and has no sum.

        In words: you can't add infinitely many numbers directly. So add the first n, then ask what those running totals head for as n grows. That target is the sum. In the sketch, 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + …: the totals 0.5, 0.75, 0.875, … climb towards 1.

        A sequence vs a series: a sequence is a list of numbers; a series is the sum of a list. The terms 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, … tend to 0, but their sum is 1.

        Example of a divergent series: 1 − 1 + 1 − 1 + … has partial sums 1, 0, 1, 0, …, which never settle, so it has no sum. Grouping the terms differently can't fix that: the ordinary rules of addition don't automatically hold for endless sums.

        Geometric series

        a + ar + ar² + ar³ + … = ∑_(k=0)^(∞) arᵏ  (a ≠ 0)

        • |r| < 1: it converges, and its sum is (a)/(1 − r).
        • |r| ≥ 1: it diverges.

        a is the first term, r the ratio: each term is the one before times r.

        Where (a)/(1 − r) comes from: s_(n) = a + ar + … + arⁿ⁻¹ and r · s_(n) = ar + … + arⁿ. Subtract: almost everything cancels, leaving (1 − r)s_(n) = a − arⁿ. When |r| < 1, rⁿ → 0, so s_(n) → (a)/(1 − r).

        Example: 4 + 4/3 + 4/9 + … has a = 4, r = 1/3, so the sum is (4)/(1 − 1/3) = 6.

        Repeating decimals are geometric series: 0.454545… = 0.45 + 0.0045 + …, with a = 0.45, r = 0.01: (0.45)/(0.99) = 45/99 = 5/11.

        Watch where it starts: ∑_(k=1)^(∞) (2/3)ᵏ starts at 2/3, so a = 2/3 and the sum is (2/3)/(1/3) = 2. Always take a = the first term actually written.

        Telescoping series

        When each term is a difference u_(k) = b_(k) − b_(k+1), the partial sum collapses: s_(n) = b_(1) − b_(n+1). The series converges exactly when b_(n) has a limit, and then S = b_(1) − lim_(n→∞) b_(n+1).

        In words: like a folding telescope, each middle piece cancels the next one, and only the very first and the very last parts stay.

        Example: ∑_(k=1)^(∞) 1/(k(k + 1)). Partial fractions: 1/(k(k + 1)) = 1/(k) − 1/(k + 1). So s_(n) = (1 − 1/2) + (1/2 − 1/3) + … + (1/(n) − 1/(n + 1)) = 1 − 1/(n + 1) → 1. The sum is 1. Full steps: the method "Sum of a telescoping series".

        Harmonic series

        ∑_(k=1)^(∞) 1/(k) = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + … diverges, even though its terms tend to 0.

        Why, by grouping: 1/3 + 1/4 > 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2; 1/5 + … + 1/8 > 4 · 1/8 = 1/2; the next 8 terms are again more than 1/2, and so on. You can collect infinitely many groups, each worth more than 1/2, so the total grows without end.

        The lesson: terms that shrink to 0 are not enough. They must shrink fast enough. 1/(k) shrinks too slowly; 1/(k²) shrinks fast enough (Series › 4).

        How slowly: it takes about 12,000 terms for the partial sum to pass 10.

        Sums, constant multiples, and the first terms

        • ∑ u_(k) and ∑ v_(k) converge ⇒ ∑ (u_(k) ± v_(k)) = ∑ u_(k) ± ∑ v_(k).
        • c ≠ 0: ∑ c u_(k) and ∑ u_(k) both converge or both diverge; when they converge, ∑ c u_(k) = c ∑ u_(k).
        • Removing or adding finitely many terms doesn't change whether a series converges. It does change the sum.

        Example: ∑_(k=1)^(∞) (5/(2ᵏ) − 2/(3ᵏ)) is two convergent geometric series: 5 · 1 − 2 · 1/2 = 4.

        Example: ∑_(k=20)^(∞) 1/(k) diverges: it's the harmonic series without its first 19 terms. And ∑ 7/(k) diverges: 7 times the harmonic series.

        Careful: a sum of two divergent series may converge (∑ 1 plus ∑ (−1)). Split a series only when the pieces converge.

        4Convergence tests

        Divergence test (the k-th term)

        lim_(k→∞) u_(k) ≠ 0 (or doesn't exist) ⇒ ∑ u_(k) diverges.

        Equivalently: ∑ u_(k) converges ⇒ u_(k) → 0.

        Why: u_(k) = s_(k) − s_(k−1). If the partial sums tend to S, both s_(k) and s_(k−1) tend to S, so their difference tends to 0.

        Example: ∑ (2k)/(3k + 1): the terms tend to 2/3 ≠ 0, so it diverges. You're adding numbers close to 2/3 forever.

        The trap: u_(k) → 0 does not prove convergence. The harmonic series has 1/(k) → 0 and diverges. This test can only ever say "diverges".

        Integral test

        ∑ u_(k) with positive terms, and f the function you get by putting x for k in u_(k). If f is decreasing and continuous on [a, ∞), then

        ∑_(k=a)^(∞) u_(k) and ∫_(a)^(∞) f(x) dx both converge or both diverge.

        Why: each term u_(k) is the area of a rectangle of width 1 and height f(k). Placed between k − 1 and k, the rectangles sit under the decreasing curve, so u_(2) + u_(3) + … + u_(n) ≤ ∫_(1)^(n) f(x) dx. A finite area on top caps the sum. Shifted one step left, the rectangles stick out above the curve, so an infinite area forces the sum to infinity too.

        Example: ∑ 1/(k²): ∫_(1)^(∞) 1/(x²) dx = 1 converges, so the series converges. (Its sum is π²/6 ≈ 1.645, not 1: the test tells you whether, not how much.)

        Check the conditions: positive, continuous and decreasing (from some point on is enough). Improper integrals: Integrals › 9.

        p-series (generalized harmonic series)

        ∑_(k=1)^(∞) 1/(kᵖ) = 1 + 1/(2ᵖ) + 1/(3ᵖ) + … converges when p > 1 and diverges when p ≤ 1.

        Why: the integral test with f(x) = 1/(xᵖ): ∫_(1)^(∞) 1/(xᵖ) dx converges exactly when p > 1 (Integrals › 9, the harmonic integral). p = 1 is the harmonic series itself.

        Examples: ∑ 1/(k³) converges (p = 3). ∑ 1/(√k) diverges (p = 1/2). ∑ 1/(k√k) converges (p = 3/2). For p ≤ 0 the terms don't even tend to 0.

        Why it matters: together with geometric series, p-series are the yardsticks you compare other series with (next concept).

        Bounded partial sums

        A series with non-negative terms converges exactly when its partial sums are bounded: s_(n) ≤ M for every n. Then S ≤ M.

        Why: with no negative terms, each partial sum is at least the one before, so {s_(n)} is increasing. An increasing sequence converges exactly when it's bounded above (Series › 2).

        Why it matters: it's the reason behind the integral test and the comparison test. For a positive series there are only two options: a finite sum, or +∞.

        5More convergence tests

        Comparison test

        ∑ a_(k) and ∑ b_(k) with non-negative terms, and a_(k) ≤ b_(k) for every k (or from some place on):

        • The bigger one, ∑ b_(k), converges ⇒ the smaller one, ∑ a_(k), converges.
        • The smaller one, ∑ a_(k), diverges ⇒ the bigger one, ∑ b_(k), diverges.

        In words: under a finite sum, a smaller sum is finite too. Above an infinite sum, a bigger sum is infinite too. The other two directions tell you nothing.

        How to use it: first guess the answer by looking at the "main part" of u_(k) (drop small constants, keep the biggest powers). Then compare with a series you know (geometric or p-series), in the direction that proves your guess.

        Example: ∑ 1/(k² + 5): 1/(k² + 5) < 1/(k²), and ∑ 1/(k²) converges, so it converges.

        Example: ∑ 1/(√k − 0.5): 1/(√k − 0.5) > 1/(√k), and ∑ 1/(√k) diverges, so it diverges.

        Limit comparison test

        ∑ a_(k) and ∑ b_(k) with positive terms, and ρ = lim_(k→∞) (a_(k))/(b_(k)).

        If ρ is finite and ρ > 0, the two series both converge or both diverge.

        In words: if two series' terms are roughly proportional far out, they behave the same. You don't have to find an exact inequality, which makes it easier than the plain comparison test.

        Two practical rules for choosing b_(k): constants added to u_(k) usually don't matter; in a fraction of polynomials, keep only the biggest power on the top and on the bottom.

        Example: ∑ (2k² + 3)/(k⁴ − k + 1) behaves like (2k²)/(k⁴) = 2/(k²). Take b_(k) = 1/(k²): ρ = lim (2k⁴ + 3k²)/(k⁴ − k + 1) = 2, finite and positive. ∑ 1/(k²) converges, so the series converges.

        When ρ = 0 or ρ = ∞ the test (in this form) says nothing: choose another b_(k).

        Ratio test

        ∑ u_(k) with positive terms, and ρ = lim_(k→∞) (u_(k+1))/(u_(k)):

        • ρ < 1 ⇒ converges.
        • ρ > 1 or ρ = +∞ ⇒ diverges.
        • ρ = 1 ⇒ no conclusion: try another test.

        Why: if each term is eventually about ρ times the one before, the series behaves like a geometric series with ratio ρ. Below 1 that converges, above 1 it diverges.

        When to use it: terms with factorials (k!) or powers with k in the exponent (3ᵏ): they mostly cancel in (u_(k+1))/(u_(k)).

        Example: ∑ (3ᵏ)/(k!): (3^(k+1))/((k + 1)!) · (k!)/(3ᵏ) = 3/(k + 1) → 0 < 1, so it converges.

        Why ρ = 1 says nothing: both ∑ 1/(k) (diverges) and ∑ 1/(k²) (converges) give ρ = 1. That happens for every fraction of polynomials: use a comparison test there.

        Root test

        ∑ u_(k) with positive terms, and ρ = lim_(k→∞) ᵏ√(u_(k)): the same three cases as the ratio test (ρ < 1 converges, ρ > 1 diverges, ρ = 1 no conclusion).

        When to use it: when the whole term is something to the power k, like ((k)/(2k + 1))ᵏ. The k-th root removes that power.

        Example: ∑ ((3k + 1)/(5k − 2))ᵏ: ᵏ√(u_(k)) = (3k + 1)/(5k − 2) → 3/5 < 1, so it converges.

        Changing where the sum starts (from k = 0 or k = 1) doesn't affect any of these tests: only the far terms matter.

        6Alternating series and absolute convergence

        Alternating series test (Leibniz)

        An alternating series has signs that switch: a_(1) − a_(2) + a_(3) − … or −a_(1) + a_(2) − a_(3) + …, with every a_(k) > 0. It converges if:

        1. a_(1) > a_(2) > a_(3) > … (the sizes decrease)
        2. lim_(k→∞) a_(k) = 0

        Error bound: the sum S is within one term of every partial sum: |S − s_(n)| < a_(n+1).

        Why it converges: each step goes the other way and is shorter than the step before. The partial sums zig-zag, overshooting less each time, and close in on one number. The sum always lies between two neighbouring partial sums, which is where the error bound comes from.

        Example: the alternating harmonic series 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + …: the sizes 1/(k) decrease to 0, so it converges (its sum is ln 2). Without the alternating signs it would be the harmonic series, which diverges.

        Error example: stopping after 9 terms, the error is less than the 10th term, 1/10.

        The decrease needs to hold only from some place on. If the terms don't tend to 0, the series diverges by the divergence test.

        Absolute and conditional convergence

        • ∑ u_(k) converges absolutely if ∑ |u_(k)| converges.
        • Theorem: a series that converges absolutely converges.
        • A series that converges but not absolutely converges conditionally.

        Why absolute convergence is enough: taking absolute values makes every term as big as it can be. If even that sum is finite, letting some terms be negative can only cancel, never blow up.

        The three outcomes for a series with mixed signs: converges absolutely (1 − 1/4 + 1/9 − 1/16 + …, since ∑ 1/(k²) converges); converges conditionally (1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − …: it converges, but ∑ 1/(k) diverges); or diverges.

        Example, signs not alternating: ∑ (cos k)/(k²). |(cos k)/(k²)| ≤ 1/(k²), so it converges absolutely by comparison, and therefore converges.
