        Careful: if ∑ |u_(k)| diverges, the series itself may still converge. Check it separately (Leibniz, if it alternates). Full steps: the method "Absolutely, conditionally, or divergent?".

        Ratio test for absolute convergence

        ∑ u_(k) with non-zero terms (any signs), and ρ = lim_(k→∞) (|u_(k+1)|)/(|u_(k)|):

        • ρ < 1 ⇒ converges absolutely (so converges).
        • ρ > 1 or ρ = +∞ ⇒ diverges.
        • ρ = 1 ⇒ no conclusion.

        Why ρ > 1 means "diverges", not only "not absolutely": then the sizes |u_(k)| grow, so the terms can't tend to 0.

        Example: ∑ (−1)ᵏ (5ᵏ)/(k!): (|u_(k+1)|)/(|u_(k)|) = 5/(k + 1) → 0 < 1. It converges absolutely.

        Summary of all the tests: the method "Choosing a convergence test".

        7Power series

        What a power series is

        A power series in x − a (centred at a) is

        ∑_(k=0)^(∞) c_(k)(x − a)ᵏ = c_(0) + c_(1)(x − a) + c_(2)(x − a)² + …

        The c_(k) are fixed numbers (the coefficients) and x is a variable. With a = 0 it's a power series in x: ∑ c_(k) xᵏ.

        In words: a "polynomial that never ends". For each value of x it's an ordinary series of numbers, which may converge or diverge. So a power series defines a function, but only on the x values where it converges.

        Example: ∑ xᵏ = 1 + x + x² + … is geometric with ratio x. It converges for −1 < x < 1, and there its sum is 1/(1 − x). At x = 1/2: 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … = 2 = 1/(1 − 1/2) ✓.

        The convention x⁰ = 1, also at x = 0, so the first term is always just c_(0).

        Radius and interval of convergence

        For every power series ∑ c_(k)(x − a)ᵏ, exactly one of these holds:

        • It converges only at x = a. (Radius R = 0.)
        • It converges absolutely for every real x. (Radius R = +∞.)
        • There's a number R > 0: it converges absolutely for |x − a| < R and diverges for |x − a| > R. At the two ends x = a ± R anything can happen.

        The set of x where it converges is the interval of convergence, centred at a; R is the radius of convergence.

        How to find R: usually with the ratio test for absolute convergence. x stays as a letter; you get ρ = |x − a| · (something), and ρ < 1 gives the inside of the interval.

        Why the ends need their own check: there the ratio test gives ρ = 1 and says nothing. Put each end into the series and test the ordinary series you get (p-series, Leibniz, divergence test).

        Example: ∑_(k=1)^(∞) ((x − 2)ᵏ)/(k · 3ᵏ): ρ = |x − 2|/3, so |x − 2| < 3: −1 < x < 5. At x = 5: ∑ 1/(k), diverges. At x = −1: ∑ (−1)ᵏ/(k), converges (Leibniz). Interval: [−1, 5), R = 3. Full steps: the method "Finding the interval of convergence".

        8Taylor and Maclaurin series

        Taylor polynomials

        The Taylor polynomial of order n of f about x = a is

        p_(n)(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x − a) + (f''(a))/(2!) (x − a)² + … + (f⁽ⁿ⁾(a))/(n!) (x − a)ⁿ

        It's the polynomial of degree ≤ n whose value and first n derivatives at a equal those of f. With a = 0 it's the Maclaurin polynomial.

        The idea: near a, copy f as closely as possible with a polynomial, which is easy to calculate. p_(1) matches the value and the slope: it's the tangent line. p_(2) also matches the bending. Each extra order fits a little more, over a wider stretch.

        Where the k! comes from: differentiating (x − a)ᵏ k times gives k!. To make the k-th derivative at a equal f⁽ᵏ⁾(a), the coefficient must be (f⁽ᵏ⁾(a))/(k!).

        Example: f(x) = eˣ, a = 0: every derivative is eˣ, which is 1 at 0. So p_(3)(x) = 1 + x + (x²)/2 + (x³)/6. At x = 0.5: p_(3) ≈ 1.6458, while e^(0.5) ≈ 1.6487.

        About another point: ln x about a = 1: f(1) = 0, f'(1) = 1, f''(1) = −1, so p_(2)(x) = (x − 1) − ((x − 1)²)/2.

        Taylor and Maclaurin series

        If f has derivatives of every order at a, its Taylor series about a is

        ∑_(k=0)^(∞) (f⁽ᵏ⁾(a))/(k!) (x − a)ᵏ

        With a = 0 it's the Maclaurin series: ∑_(k=0)^(∞) (f⁽ᵏ⁾(0))/(k!) xᵏ.

        In words: the Taylor polynomials, continued forever. The n-th partial sum of the Taylor series is the Taylor polynomial p_(n).

        Example, sin x: its derivatives at 0 repeat 0, 1, 0, −1, 0, 1, …, so only odd powers survive, with alternating signs: sin x = x − (x³)/(3!) + (x⁵)/(5!) − …

        Careful: writing down the series is one question; whether it actually adds up to f(x) is another. That needs the remainder (next card). For the common functions it does, on the intervals in the table below.

        Only one power series: if f equals some power series in x − a on an open interval around a, that series is the Taylor series of f. So any legal way of finding a power series for f (substitution, differentiation, integration) gives its Taylor series.

        The standard Maclaurin series

        SeriesValid for
        1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + x³ + …−1 < x < 1
        eˣ = 1 + x + (x²)/(2!) + (x³)/(3!) + …every x
        sin x = x − (x³)/(3!) + (x⁵)/(5!) − …every x
        cos x = 1 − (x²)/(2!) + (x⁴)/(4!) − …every x
        ln(1 + x) = x − (x²)/2 + (x³)/3 − …−1 < x ≤ 1
        arctan x = x − (x³)/3 + (x⁵)/5 − …−1 ≤ x ≤ 1
        sinh x = x + (x³)/(3!) + (x⁵)/(5!) + …every x
        cosh x = 1 + (x²)/(2!) + (x⁴)/(4!) + …every x
        (1 + x)ᵐ = 1 + mx + (m(m − 1))/(2!) x² + …−1 < x < 1

        Patterns that help you remember: sin has the odd powers, cos the even ones, both with alternating signs. sinh and cosh are the same without the minus signs (sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2). eˣ has every power. ln(1 + x) and arctan x divide by k instead of k!, so they converge only for |x| ≤ 1.

        The binomial series (last line) works for any real m. When m is a whole number ≥ 0, it stops after m + 1 terms and is the ordinary binomial formula, valid for every x. Example: 1/(√(1 + x)) = (1 + x)^(−1/2) = 1 − (1/2)x + (3/8)x² − …

        New series from these: put something else in place of x: e^(−x²) = 1 − x² + (x⁴)/(2!) − …; 1/(1 + x²) = 1 − x² + x⁴ − … for |x| < 1. Full steps: the method "Building a new series from a known one".

        Taylor's formula with remainder

        f(x) = p_(n)(x) + R_(n)(x), where R_(n) is the remainder (the error of the approximation).

        Lagrange form: if f has n + 1 derivatives on an interval containing a and x, then for some c between a and x:

        R_(n)(x) = (f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c))/((n + 1)!) (x − a)ⁿ⁺¹

        The Taylor series equals f(x) exactly when R_(n)(x) → 0 as n → ∞.

        In words: the error looks just like the next term of the series, except that the derivative is taken at some unknown point c instead of at a. You don't know c, but you can bound the error: if |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| ≤ M between a and x, then |R_(n)(x)| ≤ (M)/((n + 1)!) |x − a|ⁿ⁺¹.

        For n = 0 it's the mean value theorem: f(x) = f(a) + f'(c)(x − a) (Derivatives › 7).

        Example, why eˣ equals its series everywhere: |R_(n)(x)| = (e^(c))/((n + 1)!) |x|ⁿ⁺¹ ≤ e^(|x|) · (|x|ⁿ⁺¹)/((n + 1)!), and (|x|ⁿ⁺¹)/((n + 1)!) → 0 (Series › 1, standard limits). The same argument works for sin and cos, whose derivatives are all at most 1 in size.

        Calculating with Taylor series

        To approximate f(x₀): pick a centre a near x₀ where the derivatives are easy, add terms until the error bound is small enough.

        • Accurate to n decimal places: error less than 0.5 × 10⁻ⁿ.
        • Bound the error with the Lagrange remainder, or, when the series alternates, with the next term (Leibniz).

        Example, e to 3 decimal places: e = 1 + 1 + 1/(2!) + 1/(3!) + … (put x = 1). The error after the xⁿ term is (e^(c))/((n + 1)!) < 3/((n + 1)!). We need it below 0.0005: n = 6 gives 3/5040 ≈ 0.0006, too big; n = 7 gives 3/40320 ≈ 0.00007 ✓. So e ≈ 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/24 + 1/120 + 1/720 + 1/5040 ≈ 2.718.

        Example, cos 0.2: 1 − (0.2²)/2 + (0.2⁴)/24 − … alternates, so stopping after 1 − 0.02 = 0.98 has an error below the next term, (0.0016)/24 ≈ 0.00007. Full steps: the method "Approximating a value to a given accuracy".

        Angles in radians: for sin 2°, use x = 2 · π/180 ≈ 0.0349.

        9Differentiating and integrating power series

        Term-by-term differentiation and integration

        If f(x) = ∑_(k=0)^(∞) c_(k)(x − a)ᵏ with radius of convergence R > 0, then on (a − R, a + R):

        • f'(x) = ∑_(k=1)^(∞) k c_(k)(x − a)ᵏ⁻¹
        • ∫ f(x) dx = ∑_(k=0)^(∞) (c_(k))/(k + 1) (x − a)ᵏ⁺¹ + C

        Both new series have the same radius R (the ends may behave differently).

        In words: inside its interval of convergence, a power series can be treated like a long polynomial: differentiate or integrate each term separately. One + C covers the whole integral.

        Check with known series: differentiating x − (x³)/(3!) + (x⁵)/(5!) − … term by term gives 1 − (x²)/(2!) + (x⁴)/(4!) − …, which is cos x. Just as (sin x)' = cos x.

        Example, ln(1 + x): 1/(1 + x) = 1 − x + x² − … for |x| < 1. Integrate from 0 to x: ln(1 + x) = x − (x²)/2 + (x³)/3 − …

        Example, arctan x: 1/(1 + x²) = 1 − x² + x⁴ − …; integrate: arctan x = x − (x³)/3 + (x⁵)/5 − …

        Integrals you can't do otherwise

        Some functions, like e^(−x²) or (sin x)/(x), have no antiderivative made of ordinary functions. Their integrals can still be calculated: replace the function by its power series and integrate term by term.

        Example: ∫_(0)^(1/2) e^(−x²) dx. e^(−x²) = 1 − x² + (x⁴)/2 − …, so the integral is [x − (x³)/3 + (x⁵)/10 − …]_(0)^(1/2) = 1/2 − 1/24 + 1/320 − …

        How accurate: it's an alternating series with decreasing terms, so stopping after 1/2 − 1/24 ≈ 0.4583 has an error below the next term, 1/320 ≈ 0.003. Add that term: ≈ 0.4615, with an error below (0.5⁷)/42 ≈ 0.0002.

        1Statistics, data and variables

        The stages of a statistical study

        Every study goes through the same steps: ask a question → plan (which data, collected how) → collect the data → organize and present it (tables, charts) → summarize it with measures (a mean, a range…) → report the findings.

        Descriptive statistics is the middle part: organizing, presenting and summarizing data. That is what this subject covers.

        Population and sample

        The population is everyone (or everything) the question is about. A sample is the part of it you actually measure.

        Why samples: measuring a whole population is usually too expensive or impossible (all the children in the world, every light bulb a factory will make). So we measure a sample and describe it.

        Inference: going from what the sample shows to a claim about the whole population is statistical inference. It needs probability (subjects Probability and Random variables) and is the topic of a later course.

        Example: to learn the average height of 12th graders in the country, measure 500 of them (the sample) and use their average to estimate the average of all of them (the population).

        Variables and values

        A variable is a property that changes from one case to another (height, blood type, number of siblings). Each case has a value of it. A constant is the same for every case.

        • Discrete variable: between two values there are only finitely many possible values. Usually a count: number of children 0, 1, 2, …
        • Continuous variable: any value in between is possible, at least in principle. Usually a measurement: weight, time, temperature.

        Names: variables get capital or small letters such as x, y; the value of case number i is x_(i), and n is the number of cases (observations).

        2Measurement scales

        The four scales

        The scale of a variable says what its numbers really mean, and so which calculations make sense.

        Each scale has everything the one above it has, plus one more thing. Nominal: = and ≠. Ordinal: also < and >. Interval: also differences. Ratio: also ratios.

        Why 0 matters: 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C, because 0 °C is not "no heat" (interval). But 20 kg really is twice 10 kg, because 0 kg is "no weight" (ratio).

        Which measure fits which scale

        • Nominal: only the mode (the most common value) means something. The "average blood type" is nonsense.
        • Ordinal: also the median (the middle value) and percentiles.
        • Interval and ratio: also the mean, the variance and the standard deviation.

        A trap: numbers that are only codes (shirt number 10, area code 03) are nominal. You can compute their mean, but it means nothing.

        3Frequency tables

        Frequency and the frequency table

        The frequency f(x) of a value x is how many times it appears in the data. A frequency table lists each value with its frequency. The frequencies add up to n: ∑ f(x) = n.

        Reading it: 20 students took a quiz; 6 of them scored 7, which is the most common score. The table shows the distribution of the scores at a glance, much better than a list of 20 numbers.

        Grouping into classes

        With many different values, group them into classes (intervals) and count how many fall in each. The classes must be disjoint (no value in two classes) and exhaustive (every value in some class).

        • Apparent limits are the limits as written: 50–59, 60–69.
        • Real limits close the gaps between classes: split each gap in half, 49.5–59.5, 59.5–69.5. Each class ends exactly where the next begins.
        • Class width a = L₁ − L₀, the upper real limit minus the lower one (here 10). Use the real limits, not the apparent ones: 59 − 50 = 9 would be wrong.
        • Midpoint m_(x) = (L₀ + L₁)/2, the average of the class's two real limits: (49.5 + 59.5)/2 = 54.5. It stands for the whole class in calculations.
        • Open class: one with only one limit, such as "90 and up".

        How many classes: too few hide the shape, too many leave single cases in each class. About 5 to 10 is usual. The width is roughly (largest − smallest)/(number of classes), rounded to a convenient number.

        Where the width and the midpoint are used: see the card Discrete or continuous: which table? below, which builds the full table row by row.

        Cumulative and relative frequency

        • Cumulative frequency F(x): how many observations are at most x (up to the upper real limit of a class). The last one is always n.
        • Relative frequency (proportion): f(x)/n, the share of the data with this value. Times 100, it's a percentage.
        • Cumulative relative frequency: F(x)/n, the share at most x.

        Reading F: F = 16 at 69.5 says 16 of the 40 students scored below 69.5. The relative frequencies always add up to 1.

        Discrete or continuous: which table?

        First ask what kind of variable you have (Variables and values, in Statistics, data and variables):

        • Discrete: separate values you can list (0, 1, 2 siblings). The same values come up again and again, so count each value: a table with 3 rows.
        • Continuous: any value in a range (a time, a weight). Two people rarely have exactly the same value, so group the values into classes: a table with 6 rows.

        Discrete: siblings of 20 students.

        Continuous: the commute of 40 workers, in minutes. The last class is three times as wide as the others.

        • x, the class: the interval, written with its real limits L₀–L₁, so each class ends exactly where the next begins. Everything below is built from it.
        • f(x), the frequency: how many observations fall in the class. Used for the mean, the variance and the density.
        • F(x), the cumulative frequency: how many observations are at most L₁, the class's upper real limit. Used to find the median, the quartiles and the percentiles.
        • m_(x), the midpoint: (L₀ + L₁)/2, the value that stands for the whole class. Used for the mean and the variance of grouped data: x̄ = (∑ m_(x) f(x))/n.
        • a, the class width: L₁ − L₀. Used for the density, and in the median, quartile and percentile formulas.
        • d, the density: f(x)/a, the frequency per unit (here, workers per minute). It is the height of the histogram bar.

        Why the density row matters here: the class 30–60 has 9 workers, not far below the 12 of 20–30, but they are spread over 30 minutes instead of 10. Per minute it holds only 0.3 workers, the thinnest class of all. Compare classes by d, not by f, when the widths differ.

        A discrete table has no width or density row: each value is a single point, so there is nothing to spread over.

        4Charts and the shape of a distribution

        Bar chart and histogram

        A bar chart (stick diagram) draws one stick per value, as tall as its frequency. A histogram draws one rectangle per class, standing on the class's real limits, with no gaps.

        The height of each bar is the density d = f(x)/a, and so the area of the bar is the frequency: d · a = f(x).

        Why not draw the height as f? The eye judges a bar by its area. Drawn with height 9, the 30–60 bar would be 30 wide and tall: the biggest block in the picture, although it holds fewer workers than 10–20 or 20–30. With height d, its 9 workers are spread thinly over 30 minutes, and the picture tells the truth.

        Equal widths: then every d is f divided by the same number, so drawing f as the height gives the same shape (the grades histogram above). The table with all the rows: Discrete or continuous: which table? (Frequency tables).

        Other charts: a pie chart gives each class a slice with angle 360° · f/n (good for nominal data); a frequency polygon joins the tops of the sticks, or the midpoints of the rectangles' tops, with straight lines.

        Shapes of distributions

        • Symmetric bell: most values near the middle, few at the ends, the same on both sides.
        • Positive (right) skew: a long tail toward the large values (incomes: most are moderate, a few are huge).
        • Negative (left) skew: a long tail toward the small values (scores on an easy exam).

        Density: as the data grows and the classes get thinner, the histogram's outline becomes a smooth curve. Its height is the density, frequency per unit; the area under the curve between two values is the share of the data between them.

        5Summation notation

        The sigma sign

        ∑_(i=1)^(n) x_(i) = x_(1) + x_(2) + … + x_(n)

        Read it as a loop: let i run from the bottom number to the top number, write what's after the sign for each i, and add everything up.

        Example: with x_(1) = 1, x_(2) = 4, x_(3) = 5: ∑_(i=1)^(3) x_(i) = 10 and ∑_(i=1)^(3) x_(i)² = 1 + 16 + 25 = 42.

        Rules for sums

        • ∑_(i=k)^(m) c = (m − k + 1) c
        • ∑ c x_(i) = c ∑ x_(i)
        • ∑ (x_(i) + y_(i)) = ∑ x_(i) + ∑ y_(i)

        In words: a constant added n times is n times the constant; a common factor comes out of the sum; a sum of two things splits into two sums.

        Traps: ∑ x_(i)² ≠ (∑ x_(i))² and ∑ x_(i) y_(i) ≠ ∑ x_(i) · ∑ y_(i). With 1, 4, 5: 42 ≠ 100.

        Example: ∑_(i=1)^(3) (2x_(i) + 1) = 2 ∑ x_(i) + 3 · 1 = 2 · 10 + 3 = 23.

        6Measures of center

        A center as the best single guess

        A measure of center is one number x̃ that stands for all the data. Which number is "best" depends on how you count a wrong guess: a loss function adds up the errors x_(i) − x̃, and the best center is the one with the smallest loss.

        So no center is "the right one": each is the best answer to a different question. A shop ordering one shoe size wants the mode; someone who hates big mistakes wants the mid-range.

        Mode, mid-range and median

        • Mode Mo: the value with the highest frequency. In a grouped table, the midpoint of the class with the highest frequency.
        • Mid-range MR = (x_(max) + x_(min))/2, halfway between the largest and the smallest.
        • Median Md: the middle value once the data is sorted. Half the data is below it, half above.
        • n odd: Md = x_((n+1)/2)
        • n even: Md = (x_(n/2) + x_(n/2+1))/2

        Example: 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10 (9 values): Md is the 5th, 7. Add a 4 (10 values): the 5th and 6th are 6 and 7, so Md = 6.5.

        The median of a grouped table

        Md = L₀ + (n/2 − F(x_(m−1)))/(f(x_(m))) · (L₁ − L₀)

        The parts: the median class x_(m) is the first class where F reaches n/2; L₀, L₁ are its real limits and f(x_(m)) its frequency; F(x_(m−1)) is the cumulative frequency up to the end of the class before it.

        The width a: L₁ − L₀ = a is the width of the median class (not of any other class). The fraction says what part of the class to cross; times the width, it becomes a distance in the data's units.

        Why it works: the cases inside a class are taken as spread evenly over it. We need n/2 − F(x_(m−1)) more cases out of the class's f(x_(m)), so we go that fraction of the way across it: start at L₀ and move that fraction of a. It is the point that cuts the histogram's area in half.

        Example: the commute table (Discrete or continuous: which table?): place 20, class 20–30, F(x_(m−1)) = 19, f(x_(m)) = 12: Md = 20 + (20 − 19)/12 · 10 ≈ 20.83 minutes.

        The mean

        • x̄ = (∑_(i=1)^(n) x_(i))/n
        • x̄ = (∑ x f(x))/n (a frequency table)
        • x̄ = (∑ m_(x) f(x))/n (a table of classes, m_(x) the midpoint)

        With classes the exact values are lost, so each case is counted at its class's midpoint. The result is an estimate. Commute table: (5 · 5 + 15 · 14 + 25 · 12 + 45 · 9)/40 = 940/40 = 23.5 minutes.

        Example: the quiz table (Frequency tables): (4 · 1 + 5 · 3 + 6 · 5 + 7 · 6 + 8 · 3 + 9 · 2)/20 = 133/20 = 6.65.

        The balance point: the deviations from the mean always cancel, ∑ (x_(i) − x̄) = 0. If the values were weights on a ruler, the ruler would balance at x̄.

        Skew and how the centers sit

        • Symmetric: mode, median and mean coincide.
        • Positive skew: usually Mo < Md < x̄. The few large values pull the mean toward the tail.
        • Negative skew: the other way round, x̄ < Md < Mo.

        Why: the mean uses the size of every value, so one extreme value moves it a lot. The median only cares about order, so it barely moves. For skewed data such as income, the median describes a typical case better.

        Changing units: y = bx + a

        If every value is multiplied by b and then a is added, every measure of center does the same: ȳ = b x̄ + a, and likewise for Md, Mo and MR.

        Example: the mean temperature is 20 °C. In Fahrenheit, F = 1.8C + 32, so the mean is 1.8 · 20 + 32 = 68 °F. No need to convert every value first.

        Why: the book calls y = bx + a a linear transformation. Every value goes through the same rule, so the middle value stays in the middle and the most common stays the most common; for the mean, the rules for sums give (∑ (b x_(i) + a))/n = b x̄ + a. Other changes (adding or removing values, changing one value): How changes in the data affect the measures.

        7Measures of spread

        What a measure of spread must do

        Two distributions can have the same center and still be very different: one tightly packed, one spread out. A measure of spread says how far the values are from each other, or from the center.

        • It is never negative.
        • It is 0 exactly when all the values are equal.
        • Adding the same constant to every value doesn't change it (shifting the data doesn't spread it).

        Error rate, largest error and range

        • Error rate (percentage error): the percentage of values not equal to the mode, (1 − f(Mo)/n) · 100%. The only spread measure for nominal data.
        • Largest error (maximum deviation) from the mid-range: (x_(max) − x_(min))/2.
        • Range: x_(max) − x_(min).

        Their weakness: the last two use only the two most extreme values. One odd value makes them huge even when everything else is packed together.

        Quartiles and the interquartile range

        The lower quartile Q₁ has 25% of the data below it; the upper quartile Q₃ has 75% below it. The interquartile range IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ is the width of the middle half of the data.

        • Q₁ = L₀ + (n/4 − F(x_(m−1)))/(f(x_(m))) · (L₁ − L₀)
        • Q₃ = L₀ + ((3n)/4 − F(x_(m−1)))/(f(x_(m))) · (L₁ − L₀)

        Same idea as the median (Measures of center), with n/4 and 3n/4 in place of n/2. Here x_(m) is the class the quartile falls in, and L₁ − L₀ = a is that class's width: you cross a fraction of the class, so the fraction is multiplied by its width.

        A plain list (not grouped): sort it, compute n/4 and 3n/4, and round to the nearest whole number to get the places. n = 39: 9.75 → 10th value and 29.25 → 29th value.

        Strength: the extremes don't affect it at all.

        Mean absolute deviation

        (∑_(i=1)^(n) |x_(i) − Md|)/n

        In words: the average distance of a value from the median. It uses every value. It is measured from the median because that is where the sum of distances is smallest.

        A grouped table: (∑ |m_(x) − Md| f(x))/n, with m_(x) the class midpoint.

        Why not just average x_(i) − x̄? Those always add up to 0: the positive and negative deviations cancel. Taking absolute values (here) or squares (variance) stops the cancelling.

        Variance and standard deviation

        • s_(x)² = (∑_(i=1)^(n) (x_(i) − x̄)²)/n
        • s_(x)² = (∑ (x − x̄)² f(x))/n (a frequency table; with classes, m_(x) in place of x)
        • s_(x) = √(s_(x)²)

        In words: the variance is the average squared distance from the mean. Its units are squared (cm²), so we take the root: the standard deviation s_(x) is back in the data's own units and is the usual measure of spread.

        Notation: s is for data you have (a sample); σ is for a whole population. In this course both divide by n.

        The shortcut formula for the variance

        s_(x)² = (∑ x_(i)²)/n − x̄²

        In words: the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean. It's quicker by hand: no deviations to compute.

        Where it comes from: open the square, (x_(i) − x̄)² = x_(i)² − 2x̄ x_(i) + x̄², and sum with the rules for sums using ∑ x_(i) = n x̄: ∑ x_(i)² − 2n x̄² + n x̄² = ∑ x_(i)² − n x̄². Divide by n.

        Example: the quiz table: ∑ x² f(x) = 919, so s² = 919/20 − 6.65² = 45.95 − 44.2225 = 1.7275 and s ≈ 1.31.

        Spread after y = bx + a

        • s_(y) = |b| s_(x)
        • s_(y)² = b² s_(x)²

        In words: adding a shifts the data and changes no spread at all; multiplying by b stretches every distance by |b|. The same goes for the range, the IQR and the mean absolute deviation.

        Example: s = 5 °C becomes 1.8 · 5 = 9 °F; the variance 25 becomes 1.8² · 25 = 81.

        Every kind of change in one table: Summary: what each change does (How changes in the data affect the measures).

        8Combining groups

        Weighted mean

        x̄_(T) = (∑_(j=1)^(k) n_(j) x̄_(j))/N,   N = n_(1) + … + n_(k)

        In words: the mean of all groups together is the average of the group means, each weighted by its size. A group of 30 counts three times as much as a group of 10.

        Only when the groups are the same size is it the plain average of the means.

        Pooled variance

        s_(T)² = (∑ n_(j) s_(j)²)/N + (∑ n_(j) (x̄_(j) − x̄_(T))²)/N

        Two parts: the first is the average spread inside the groups (the weighted mean of their variances). The second is the spread between the groups (how far the group means are from the overall mean). The total spread is both together.

        So: even if each group is tightly packed, the whole is spread out when the groups sit far apart.

        9Relative position: percentiles and z-scores

        Why relative position

        A grade of 70 in math and 75 in English can't be compared directly: the exams differ in difficulty and in spread. A relative measure places each value inside its own distribution, so values from different distributions (even different units) become comparable.

        Percentiles

        The k-th percentile C_(k) is the value with k% of the data below it and (100 − k)% above it.

        • C_(k) = L₀ + ((n · k)/100 − F(x_(m−1)))/(f(x_(m))) · (L₁ − L₀)
        • k = (F(x_(m−1)) + (C − L₀)/(L₁ − L₀) · f(x_(m))) · 100/n

        The first finds the value for a given percent (the same steps as the median); the second goes back, from a value C to its percent.

        The width a = L₁ − L₀ is the width of the class x_(m) the percentile falls in. In the first formula it turns "this fraction of the class" into a distance; in the second, (C − L₀)/a is the fraction of the class below C, so that fraction of its cases is added. With unequal widths this matters: in the commute table, C_(90) falls in 30–60, so C_(90) = 30 + (36 − 31)/9 · 30 ≈ 46.67, with a = 30, not 10.

        Familiar ones: C_(25) = Q₁, C_(50) = Md, C_(75) = Q₃.

        Limit: percentiles keep the order but not the distances. The gap from C_(50) to C_(60) can be tiny in the middle and wide in the tails.

        z-scores

        z_(x) = (x − x̄)/(s_(x))

        In words: how many standard deviations a value is above (z > 0) or below (z < 0) the mean. It has no units.

        Example: math 70 with x̄ = 65, s = 3: z = 5/3 ≈ 1.67. English 75 with ȳ = 70, s = 4: z = 5/4 = 1.25. Compared with their classmates, the math grade is the better one.

        Always: the z-scores of a whole data set have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Turning values into z-scores is the linear change y = (1/(s_(x))) x − (x̄)/(s_(x)), so it keeps distances in proportion (percentiles don't).

        10Correlation

        Scatter diagrams and linear relations

        With two variables measured on each case, draw one point (x_(i), y_(i)) per case: a scatter diagram. If the points lie close to a straight line, there is a linear relation between x and y.

        • Positive relation: large x goes with large y (height and weight).
        • Negative relation: large x goes with small y (speed and travel time).
        • Perfect when the points lie exactly on a line: y = bx + a.

        Covariance: the numerator of r

        • cov(x, y) = (∑_(i=1)^(n) (x_(i) − x̄)(y_(i) − ȳ))/n
        • cov(x, y) = (∑ x_(i) y_(i))/n − x̄ ȳ (shortcut)

        In words: the covariance (in the book: שונות משותפת, "shared variance") is the average product of the distances from the two means. The shortcut reads: the mean of the products minus the product of the means, just like the variance's shortcut.

        Why it measures a relation: draw lines at x̄ and ȳ. A point above both means, or below both, adds a positive product; a point in one of the other two corners adds a negative one; a point on a line adds 0. Mostly "+" corners: the covariance is positive, and y tends to rise with x.

        Example (the points drawn): x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5, x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4. Distances −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and −2, 0, 1, 0, 1; products 4, 0, 0, 0, 2: cov = 6/5 = 1.2. Shortcut: 66/5 − 3 · 4 = 1.2.

        The variance is the covariance of a variable with itself: cov(x, x) = (∑ (x_(i) − x̄)²)/n = s_(x)².

        Why r divides by s_(x) s_(y): the covariance depends on the units. Measure x in mm instead of cm and it becomes 10 times bigger (in general cov(bx + a, cy + d) = bc cov(x, y)), although the relation is the same. Dividing by the two standard deviations, which grow by the same factors, cancels the units, and the result r is always between −1 and 1.

        Not the pooled variance: the pooled variance (Combining groups) is the variance of several groups put together, one variable. The covariance is about two variables measured on the same cases.

        The same idea for random variables: Covariance in Random variables, with averages replaced by expectations.

        Pearson's correlation coefficient

        • r = (cov(x, y))/(s_(x) s_(y))
        • r = (∑ z_(x) z_(y))/n (one product per case)
        • r = (∑ (x_(i) − x̄)(y_(i) − ȳ))/(n s_(x) s_(y))
        • r = ((∑ x_(i) y_(i))/n − x̄ ȳ)/(s_(x) s_(y))

        The numerator is the covariance cov(x, y) (Covariance: the numerator of r, above), and the denominator is the product of the two standard deviations (not the variances). All four forms are the same number: the last three just write the covariance out.

        Why it works: a point above both means, or below both, gives a positive product of z-scores; a point above one mean and below the other gives a negative one. If most points are of the first kind, r comes out positive.

        The last form is the shortcut for hand calculation, like the shortcut for the variance. Step by step: the method Computing Pearson's r.

        Properties of r

        • −1 ≤ r ≤ 1.
        • r = 1 or r = −1 exactly when all the points lie on one line (rising or falling).
        • The sign of r is the direction of the relation; its size is how close the points are to a line.
        • Changing units (bx + a with b > 0) doesn't change r; a negative b flips its sign.

        Two warnings: r = 0 means no linear relation; the points can still lie on a curve (a parabola gives r = 0). And a strong correlation doesn't show that one variable causes the other. Always look at the scatter diagram first.

        11How changes in the data affect the measures

        Adding or multiplying by a constant

        • Add a to every value (y = x + a): every measure of center moves by a. No measure of spread changes.
        • Multiply every value by b (y = bx): every measure of center is multiplied by b; the range, IQR, mean absolute deviation and s by |b|; the variance by b².

        Why: adding a slides the whole data along the line. Everything moves together, so the center moves, but no distance between two values changes. Multiplying by b stretches every distance by |b| (distances are never negative); the variance is made of squared distances, so it grows by b².

        Example: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 has x̄ = Md = 6, range 8, s² = 8. Add 5: x̄ = Md = 11, range still 8, s² still 8. Multiply by −2: x̄ = Md = −12, range 16, s² = 4 · 8 = 32.

        Both at once (y = bx + a, a linear transformation): the cards Changing units: y = bx + a (Measures of center) and Spread after y = bx + a (Measures of spread), and the method Measures after a change of units.

        Adding one observation

        • New mean: x̄_(new) = (n x̄ + x)/(n + 1). It moves toward the new value x, and doesn't move at all if x = x̄.
        • A value equal to the mean: the variance gets smaller: s_(new)² = (n s²)/(n + 1). The sum of squared distances stays the same (the new value adds 0), but it is divided by a bigger n.
        • A value far from the mean: the mean moves toward it and s grows. "Far" means more than about one standard deviation away: exactly, s grows when |x − x̄| > s √((n + 1)/n). If the value is outside the old smallest–largest, the range grows too.
        • The median moves at most half a place in the sorted list, toward the new value (or stays).
        • The mode changes only if the new value's frequency catches up with (two modes) or overtakes the old mode's.

        Example: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (x̄ = 6, s² = 8, s ≈ 2.83). Add 6: x̄ = 6, s² = 40/6 ≈ 6.67, smaller. Add 20: x̄ = 50/6 ≈ 8.33, s² ≈ 33.89, range 18. Add 9 (only 3 from the mean, under 2.83 · √(6/5) ≈ 3.10): s² ≈ 7.92, still smaller, although 9 is above the mean.

        Adding two observations around the mean

        Add x̄ − c and x̄ + c (the same distance below and above the mean):

        • x̄_(new) = x̄
        • s_(new)² = (n s² + 2c²)/(n + 2)
        • c > s: the variance grows.   c = s: it stays the same.   c < s: it shrinks.

        Why: the two new values cancel in the sum, so the mean stays. Each adds c² to the sum of squared distances, which was n s², and n grows by 2. The new variance is the average of n squares of size s² on average and two of size c²: bigger than s² exactly when c² > s².

        Example: 4, 4, 8, 8 has x̄ = 6, s = 2. Add 4 and 8 (c = 2 = s): s² = (4 · 4 + 2 · 4)/6 = 4, the same. Add 3 and 9 (c = 3): (16 + 18)/6 ≈ 5.67, bigger. Add 5 and 7 (c = 1): (16 + 2)/6 = 3, smaller.

        The median stays the same when one new value lands below the middle of the data and the other above it (as in the example, Md = 6 each time).

        Removing an observation

        The same rules, in reverse. New mean x̄_(new) = (n x̄ − x)/(n − 1): it moves away from the removed value.

        • Remove a value equal to the mean: the mean stays; the variance grows, s_(new)² = (n s²)/(n − 1) (the same sum of squares, divided by a smaller n).
        • Remove an extreme value: the mean moves away from it; s and the range shrink.
        • Remove two values x̄ ± c: the mean stays; the variance shrinks if c > s and grows if c < s.

        Example: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (s² = 8). Remove 6: x̄ = 6, s² = 40/4 = 10, bigger. Remove 10: x̄ = 5, s² = 5, range 6.

        Changing one value: robust and sensitive measures

        • Make an extreme value more extreme (the largest larger, or the smallest smaller): the mean, the range and s grow (the mean moves toward it). The median, the mode and the IQR don't change.
        • Change a value without it crossing the median: the median stays the same. The mean always changes, by (new − old)/n.

        Robust vs. sensitive: a robust measure barely notices a few extreme values, because it uses only the order or the middle of the data: the median, the mode and the IQR. A sensitive measure uses the size of every value, so one wild value moves it: the mean, the range, the variance and s. That's why the median is preferred for skewed data such as income.

        Example: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 → 2, 4, 6, 8, 30: the mean 6 → 10, the range 8 → 28, s ≈ 2.83 → 10.2; the median stays 6. Change 4 to 5 instead: the median stays 6, the mean becomes 6.2.

        Changing frequencies or classes in a table

        • Raise the frequency of one value: the mean moves toward that value, and the value may become the mode.
        • Move frequency toward the center (from the ends to the middle values): the spread shrinks. Move it to the ends: the spread grows.
        • Group the same data into different classes (other widths or limits): the grouped mean, median, mode and the histogram can all change, because they are estimates built from the classes (each case counted at its class's midpoint, or spread evenly inside its class). The real data hasn't changed.

        Reading it: the first three rows are symmetric around 2, so the mean stays 2; only the spread changes. In the last row the 3s outnumber the rest: the mean moves toward 3, and 3 becomes the mode.

        Classes: the values 1, 2, 2, 9 have mean 3.5. In the classes 0–5 and 5–10 they are counted as 2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 7.5: grouped mean 3.75.

        Combining groups, z-scores and r

        • Combining groups: the overall mean is the weighted mean of the group means, so it lies between the smallest and the largest of them. The overall variance is at least the average variance inside the groups, more when the group means differ (Pooled variance, Combining groups).
        • z-scores after y = bx + a: unchanged when b > 0, sign flipped when b < 0. A value 1.5 standard deviations above the mean in °C is 1.5 above in °F.
        • r after x' = bx + a, y' = cy + d: unchanged when b and c have the same sign, sign flipped when they differ (Properties of r, Correlation).

        Why z and r ignore units: both measure distances in standard deviations. Multiplying by b stretches a distance and the standard deviation by the same |b|, which cancels; only the direction (the sign of b) survives.

        Summary: what each change does

        • ? = it depends on the actual data, so it can't be determined from the rule alone; the numbered notes say what it depends on. “max” is the largest value.
        • ¹ Unless that value was itself the mode.
        • ² Grows when the new value is more than s √((n + 1)/n) from x̄, shrinks when it is closer (Adding one observation).
        • ³ When one new value lands below the middle and the other above it.
        • ⁴ Shrinks when the value is near the mean, grows when it is at an end.
        • ⁵ Grows if c > s, stays the same if c = s, shrinks if c < s (Adding two observations around the mean).

        "It depends" (can't be determined) is a real answer on a test: say what it depends on, and show two tiny data sets where it goes each way (the method How does a change in the data affect a measure?).

        1Sets

        Sets and members

        A set is a collection of things, its members. x ∈ A: x is a member of A; x ∉ A: it isn't.

        • List it: A = {2, 4, 6}. Order and repeats don't matter.
        • Give a rule: B = {x | x is even and 3 < x < 12} = {4, 6, 8, 10}. Read "|" as "such that".

        Subset: A ⊆ B when every member of A is also in B. Two sets are equal when each is a subset of the other: they have exactly the same members.

        Two special sets: the empty set ∅ has no members (it is a subset of every set); the universal set W holds everything under discussion, and every other set is part of it.

        Operations on sets

        • Union A ∪ B: in A or in B (or both).
        • Intersection A ∩ B: in A and in B.
        • Complement Aᶜ: everything in W that is not in A.
        • Difference A ∖ B: in A but not in B. It equals A ∩ Bᶜ.

        Disjoint sets: A ∩ B = ∅, no common members; their circles don't overlap.

        Example: W = {1, …, 10}, A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, B = {3, 4, 5}: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; A ∩ B = {3, 4}; A ∖ B = {1, 2}; Bᶜ = {1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10}.

        Laws of set operations

        • A ∪ B = B ∪ A,  A ∩ B = B ∩ A
        • (A ∪ B) ∪ D = A ∪ (B ∪ D),  (A ∩ B) ∩ D = A ∩ (B ∩ D)
        • A ∩ (B ∪ D) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ D)
        • A ∪ (B ∩ D) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ D)
        • (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ,  (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ
        • (Aᶜ)ᶜ = A,  A ∪ Aᶜ = W,  A ∩ Aᶜ = ∅

        Names: order doesn't matter (commutative); grouping doesn't matter (associative); one operation spreads over the other (distributive, both ways round, unlike numbers); the last pair of the fifth line are De Morgan's laws.

        De Morgan in words: "not (A or B)" is "not A and not B"; "not (A and B)" is "not A or not B". Taking a complement swaps ∪ and ∩.

        Check any law by shading both sides in a Venn diagram: if they shade the same region, the law holds.

        2Sample space and events

        Experiments and the sample space

        A random experiment is something whose result we can't know in advance (tossing a coin, choosing a student). Each possible result is an outcome (a sample point). The set of all outcomes is the sample space Ω.

        • One die: Ω = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
        • Two coins: Ω = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, a pair (first, second)
        • Rolling until a 6 shows: Ω = {1, 2, 3, …} (number of rolls), endless but countable

        Choose the outcomes carefully: exactly one of them must happen each time, and they should be detailed enough for the question. For "the sum of two dice", list the pairs (3, 5), not just the sums.

        Events

        An event is a set of outcomes, a subset A ⊆ Ω. The event occurs when the outcome is one of its members.

        • "An even number" on a die: A = {2, 4, 6}.
        • An elementary event has a single outcome: {5}.
        • Ω is the certain event; ∅ the impossible one.

        Words become set operations: "A or B" is A ∪ B; "A and B" is A ∩ B; "not A" is Aᶜ; "A but not B" is A ∖ B; "A and B can't both happen" is A ∩ B = ∅ (mutually exclusive, disjoint).

        Example: one die, A = even, B = more than 4 = {5, 6}: "even and more than 4" = {6}; "even or more than 4" = {2, 4, 5, 6}.

        3The probability function

        From relative frequency to probability

        Repeat an experiment N times and count how often A happens, f(A). The relative frequency f(A)/N jumps around at first, then settles near a fixed number as N grows. That number is what probability describes.

        A model: probability theory is a mathematical model of this settling. A good model gives numbers close to the long-run frequencies; if a coin's heads settle near 0.5, the model "P(heads) = 1/2" fits it.

        The three properties of a probability function

        A probability function P on Ω gives every event A a number P(A) so that:

        • 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1
        • P(Ω) = 1
        • A ∩ B = ∅ ⇒ P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)

        In words: a probability is between 0 and 1; something surely happens; for events that can't happen together, the chances add. Relative frequencies behave exactly like this, which is why these three are chosen. Everything else in probability follows from them.

        Probability space: Ω together with P, written (Ω, P).

        Subjective probability: a person's degree of belief ("70% it rains tomorrow") is a probability too, as long as it keeps the three properties.

        Discrete spaces: add up the points

        When Ω is finite or countable (its points can be numbered 1, 2, 3, …) it is discrete, and

        P(A) = ∑_(ω ∈ A) P(ω)

        So it's enough to give each single outcome its probability (non-negative, adding up to 1); every event's probability is then the sum over its outcomes.

        Example: a loaded die with P(6) = 1/2 and 1/10 for each other face. P(even) = P(2) + P(4) + P(6) = 1/10 + 1/10 + 1/2 = 7/10.

        4Rules of probability

        The complement and monotone rules

        • P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A)
        • P(∅) = 0
        • A ⊆ B ⇒ P(A) ≤ P(B)
        • P(A ∖ B) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B)

        Why the first: A and Aᶜ are disjoint and together make Ω, so P(A) + P(Aᶜ) = 1.

        Use it for "at least one": the complement of "at least one six in 4 rolls" is "no six at all", usually much easier to compute.

        The addition rule

        P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

        Why: P(A) + P(B) counts the overlap A ∩ B twice, once in each circle; subtracting it once fixes that. When A and B are disjoint the overlap is empty and this is the third property.

        Three events: P(A ∪ B ∪ D) = P(A) + P(B) + P(D) − P(A ∩ B) − P(A ∩ D) − P(B ∩ D) + P(A ∩ B ∩ D): add the singles, take off the pairs, put the triple back.

        Example: 60% of students read the news, 30% listen to the radio, 20% do both. "At least one": 0.6 + 0.3 − 0.2 = 0.7; "neither": 1 − 0.7 = 0.3.

        5Uniform probability space

        Equally likely outcomes

        A probability space is uniform when all N outcomes of Ω have the same probability. Then

        • P(ω) = 1/N for each outcome
        • P(A) = (N(A))/N,   N(A) = the number of outcomes in A

        In words: favorable cases over all cases. Probability turns into counting, which is what Combinatorics is for.

        Where it comes from: fair coins, fair dice, shuffled cards, and above all random sampling: choosing so that every person (or every group of 50 people) has the same chance.

        Two dice: 36 equally likely pairs

        Rolling two fair dice, the outcomes are the 36 ordered pairs (first, second), all equally likely. The table shows each pair's sum:

        Reading it: a sum of 7 appears 6 times, so P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6; a sum of 12 only once, 1/36.

        A classic trap: the 11 possible sums are not equally likely, so P(sum = 7) ≠ 1/11. Always count in a space whose outcomes really are equally likely: here, the pairs.

        6Conditional probability

        Probability given new information

        P(A | B) = (P(A ∩ B))/(P(B)),   when P(B) > 0

        Read P(A | B) as "the probability of A given B": we learned that B happened, and update the chance of A.

        Why the formula: once we know B happened, B is the whole new world. Of it, only the part A ∩ B is still A; dividing by P(B) scales the new world back up to a total of 1.

        In a uniform space it is counting inside B: P(A | B) = (N(A ∩ B))/(N(B)). One die, given "even": P(6 | even) = 1/3, since only {2, 4, 6} are left.

        Reading conditional probabilities off a table

        A two-way table of counts holds every conditional probability: restrict to the row or column you're given, and divide by its total.

        Example: P(smokes | man) = 30/100 = 0.3 (the "Men" row). P(man | smokes) = 30/50 = 0.6 (the "Smokes" column). The same cell, divided by different totals: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are usually different.

        The multiplication formula

        • P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B | A) = P(B) · P(A | B)
        • P(A ∩ B ∩ D) = P(A) · P(B | A) · P(D | A ∩ B)

        In words: the chance that both happen is the chance of the first times the chance of the second given the first. It is the definition, turned around.

        Example: 4 white and 2 red balls, two drawn without replacement. P(both white) = 4/6 · 3/5 = 2/5: after a white one, 3 of the 5 left are white.

        A conditional probability is a probability: with B fixed, every rule still holds. For instance P(Aᶜ | B) = 1 − P(A | B).

        7Independence

        Independent events

        • P(A | B) = P(A)
        • P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B)

        In words: A is independent of B when knowing that B happened doesn't change the chance of A. The two lines say the same thing (when P(B) > 0); the second is symmetric, so independence goes both ways, and it is the usual test.

        Example: one card from a deck. "Heart" (1/4) and "picture card" (12/52 = 3/13): P(both) = 3/52 = 1/4 · 3/13. Independent: knowing the suit says nothing about the picture.

        Then the complements are independent too: A and Bᶜ, Aᶜ and B, Aᶜ and Bᶜ.

        Disjoint is not independent

        If A and B can't happen together (A ∩ B = ∅) and both have positive probability, they are strongly dependent: knowing B happened tells you for sure that A didn't, P(A | B) = 0 ≠ P(A).

        Tell them apart: disjoint is about the sets (no overlap, a picture); independent is about the numbers (P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), a calculation).

        Independent stages

        When the stages of an experiment don't influence each other (two separate dice, repeated coin tosses, drawing with replacement), events about different stages are independent, and their probabilities multiply.

        Example: a red and a green die. P(red 3 and green 5) = 1/6 · 1/6 = 1/36, the same as counting pairs.

        Example: a test passed with probability 0.8 each time, taken 3 times independently: P(passes all 3) = 0.8³ = 0.512; P(fails all 3) = 0.2³ = 0.008; P(passes at least once) = 1 − 0.008 = 0.992.

        8Total probability and Bayes

        The law of total probability

        If B₁, …, Bₙ are disjoint and together make up Ω (a partition), then

        P(A) = P(A | B₁) P(B₁) + ⋯ + P(A | Bₙ) P(Bₙ)

        With two parts B and Bᶜ: P(A) = P(A | B) P(B) + P(A | Bᶜ) P(Bᶜ).

        In words: split by the cases, find the chance of A in each case, and take the weighted average, weighted by how likely each case is.

        Why: A is the disjoint union of its pieces A ∩ Bᵢ, and each piece is P(A | Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ) by the multiplication formula.

        Bayes' formula

        P(Bⱼ | A) = (P(A | Bⱼ) P(Bⱼ))/(∑ᵢ P(A | Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ))

        What it does: turns the condition around. We know how likely the evidence A is in each case (P(A | Bᵢ)); Bayes gives how likely each case is once we've seen the evidence (P(Bⱼ | A)).

        Example: a test finds 90% of the sick, but also wrongly flags 2% of the healthy; 0.5% of people are sick. A positive result:

        P(sick | +) = (0.9 · 0.005)/(0.9 · 0.005 + 0.02 · 0.995) ≈ 0.184

        Only 18%! The sick are so rare that the few false alarms among the many healthy outnumber the true positives. Ignoring how rare the case is (the base rate) is the classic mistake.

        9Multi-stage experiments: the tree and table methods

        The tree method

        Draw the first stage's outcomes as branches, and under each one the next stage's outcomes, each branch with its probability given the path so far.

        • Multiply along a path to get the chance of that whole path (multiplication formula). The numbers under the leaves are these products.
        • Add the paths that end in the event you want (total probability): P(defective) = 0.018 + 0.02 = 0.038.
        • Bayes from the tree: one path divided by the sum of the paths with the same ending: P(machine I | defective) = 0.018/0.038 ≈ 0.47.

        Checks: the branches out of each point add up to 1, and so do all the leaves.

        The table method

        Put the first stage's outcomes in the rows and the second stage's in the columns. Each cell is the chance of that pair: P(row) · P(column | row).

        • Row totals give back the first stage: 0.6, 0.4.
        • Column totals are total probability: P(defective) = 0.038.
        • Bayes: a cell divided by its column total: P(I | defective) = 0.018/0.038 ≈ 0.47.

        Tree or table? Same numbers, two pictures. The tree shows the order of the stages; the table shows both ways of conditioning at once (rows and columns) and suits two stages best.

        1The multiplication rule

        Counting in stages

        If a first stage has n₁ possible results and, whatever happened, a second stage has n₂, then the two stages together have n₁ · n₂ results. With k stages: n₁ · n₂ · … · nₖ.

        Why: each of the n₁ branches splits into n₂ new ones, so the tree ends in n₁ · n₂ leaves, one per combined result. A table with n₁ rows and n₂ columns shows the same thing.

        Example: a code of 2 letters (26 choices each) and then 3 digits (10 each): 26 · 26 · 10 · 10 · 10 = 676,000 codes.

        What matters is that the number of choices at a stage doesn't depend on earlier choices; which choices they are may change.

        2Ordered samples

        With repeats: n to the k

        Choosing k times out of n items, in order, where an item may come up again (with replacement): nᵏ ways.

        Why: the multiplication rule with n choices at every one of the k stages.

        Examples: 4 coin tosses: 2⁴ = 16 results. A 4-digit PIN: 10⁴ = 10,000. 3 dice: 6³ = 216.

        Without repeats: (n)ₖ and n!

        • (n)ₖ = n(n − 1)(n − 2) ⋯ (n − k + 1) = (n!)/((n − k)!)
        • n! = n(n − 1) ⋯ 2 · 1,   0! = 1

        In words: (n)ₖ counts ordered choices of k different items out of n (without replacement): n choices for the first, one fewer for the second, and so on, k factors in all.

        Permutations: arranging all n items in a row is the case k = n: n! ways ("n factorial").

        Examples: gold, silver and bronze among 8 runners: (8)₃ = 8 · 7 · 6 = 336. Ranking 7 teachers: 7! = 5040.

        3Unordered samples

        Combinations: n choose k

        binom(n,k) = ((n)ₖ)/(k!) = (n!)/(k! (n − k)!)

        In words: the number of groups of k different items out of n, when order doesn't matter (a committee, a hand of cards).

        Why divide by k!: counting in order, each group shows up k! times, once for every way to arrange its members. {a, b, c} is counted as abc, acb, bac, bca, cab, cba.

        Example: 4 electives out of 10: binom(10,4) = (10 · 9 · 8 · 7)/(4 · 3 · 2 · 1) = 210.

        Properties of n choose k

        • binom(n,k) = binom(n,n−k)
        • binom(n,0) = binom(n,n) = 1,   binom(n,1) = n

        Why the first: choosing who goes on the committee is the same as choosing who stays out. So binom(10,8) = binom(10,2) = 45: compute with the smaller one.

        Which formula: a summary

        Two questions decide it: does the order matter (a ranking, a code: yes; a group, a hand: no)? Can the same item come up twice (with replacement: yes)?

        4Arrangements with repeated items

        Repeated letters and splitting into groups

        (n!)/(n₁! n₂! ⋯ nₖ!),   n₁ + n₂ + ⋯ + nₖ = n

        Arranging items with repeats: n items, of which n₁ are alike, n₂ are alike, and so on. Arranging them as if all were different gives n!; swapping alike items among themselves changes nothing, so divide by each nᵢ!.

        Example: STATISTICS has 10 letters: S ×3, T ×3, I ×2, A, C. Different words: (10!)/(3! 3! 2!) = 50,400.

        The same count splits a group: dividing n people into named groups of sizes n₁, …, nₖ. 10 people into teams of 5, 3 and 2: (10!)/(5! 3! 2!) = 2520. With two groups it is binom(n,n₁).

        5Counting for probability

        Choosing special items

        A group of N items has K special ones. Choose n at random without replacement. The chance of exactly j special ones:

        (binom(K,j) binom(N−K,n−j))/(binom(N,n))

        Why: every group of n is equally likely: binom(N,n) of them. A favorable group takes j of the special items and the other n − j from the rest: multiply the two counts.

        Example: 7 black balls and 1 gold; draw 3. P(gold drawn) = (binom(1,1) binom(7,2))/(binom(8,3)) = 21/56 = 3/8. Or by the complement: 1 − binom(7,3)/binom(8,3) = 1 − 35/56 = 3/8.

        All different

        Choosing k times from n with replacement, every one of the nᵏ ordered results is equally likely, and

        P(all different) = ((n)ₖ)/(nᵏ)

        Example: 4 people in an elevator each pick one of 8 floors: P(all different floors) = (8 · 7 · 6 · 5)/(8⁴) = 1680/4096 ≈ 0.41.

        The birthday problem: with 365 days, ((365)ₖ)/(365ᵏ) drops below 1/2 already at k = 23: in a class of 23, two share a birthday more often than not.

        When n is huge compared with k this is close to 1: sampling with or without replacement then gives almost the same answers.

        Keep the counting consistent

        Top and bottom must be counted the same way: both ordered, or both unordered. Mixing them is the most common mistake.

        Example: 3 cards from a deck, all hearts. Unordered: binom(13,3)/binom(52,3). Ordered: (13 · 12 · 11)/(52 · 51 · 50). Both equal 11/850 ≈ 0.013.

        Tip: when order doesn't matter in the question, the unordered count is usually shorter. Order still helps for questions about "the first one" or "the third one".

        1Random variables

        What a random variable is

        A random variable X gives a number to every outcome of an experiment: X(ω). Its value is random because the outcome is.

        Example: toss a coin 3 times; X = the number of heads. The outcome HTH gets X = 2; TTT gets X = 0. Many outcomes can share a value.

        Events from values: {X = 2} is the event "the outcome gives 2" = {HHT, HTH, THH}. Writing P(X = 2) is short for its probability.

        Discrete: X is discrete when its possible values can be listed, x₁, x₂, … (finitely many or countably many). Counts are discrete; lengths and times are continuous (later).

        2Probability function and cumulative distribution

        The probability function

        The probability function of a discrete X gives each value its probability, P(X = x). Usually a table:

        It must have: every P(X = x) ≥ 0, and they add up to 1 (the table's total). That is how to check a table you built.

        The probability of a range is the sum over the values in it: P(X ≥ 2) = 3/8 + 1/8 = 1/2.

        The cumulative distribution function

        F(x) = P(X ≤ x)

        • A staircase for a discrete X: flat between values, jumping at each value by P(X = x); the filled dot shows the value at the jump.
        • Never decreases; starts at 0 far left and reaches 1 far right.
        • P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a).

        Example: heads in 3 tosses: F(1) = 1/8 + 3/8 = 1/2; F(1.7) = 1/2 too (no value between 1 and 2); P(1 < X ≤ 3) = F(3) − F(1) = 1/2.

        3Special discrete distributions

        Discrete uniform: X ~ U(a, b)

        P(X = k) = 1/(b − a + 1),   k = a, a + 1, …, b

        When: every whole number from a to b is equally likely. A fair die is U(1, 6); a random digit is U(0, 9).

        Binomial: X ~ B(n, p)

        P(X = k) = binom(n,k) pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ,   k = 0, 1, …, n,   q = 1 − p

        When: n independent repetitions of the same yes/no trial (a Bernoulli trial: "success" with probability p, "failure" with q), and X counts the successes.

        Why the formula: one particular order with k successes, like SS…FF, has probability pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ (independent trials multiply). There are binom(n,k) ways to choose which of the n trials are the successes.

        Example: 10 multiple-choice questions with 4 options, all guessed: X ~ B(10, 1/4); P(X = 3) = binom(10,3) (1/4)³ (3/4)⁷ ≈ 0.25.

        Geometric: X ~ G(p)

        P(X = k) = qᵏ⁻¹ p,   k = 1, 2, 3, …

        When: repeat a Bernoulli trial until the first success; X is the number of trials needed (the success included).

        Why: X = k means k − 1 failures and then a success.

        Useful: P(X > k) = qᵏ (the first k all failed).

        No memory: P(X > n + k | X > k) = P(X > n). After k failures the wait starts over, as if nothing had happened; the dice don't "owe" you a six.

        Poisson: X ~ P(λ)

        P(X = k) = (λᵏ)/(k!) e^(−λ),   k = 0, 1, 2, …,   λ > 0

        When: counting how many times something happens in a stretch of time (or space) when it happens at random at a steady average rate, independently, one at a time: calls to a center in a minute, typos on a page. λ is the average count in that stretch.

        Example: 5 calls a minute on average: P(no call in a minute) = e^(−5) ≈ 0.0067.

        Approximating the binomial: many trials, each very unlikely (n large, p small): B(n, p) ≈ P(np).

        4Expectation

        The expected value

        E(X) = ∑ x P(X = x)

        In words: each value weighted by its probability. It is the long-run average: repeat the experiment many times, and the mean of the results settles near E(X). Like the mean of a frequency table, with probabilities in place of relative frequencies. Also written μ.

        Example: a fair die: E(X) = (1 + 2 + ⋯ + 6)/6 = 3.5, a value the die never shows. It is a balance point, not a "most likely" value.

        Rules for expectation

        • E(c) = c
        • E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b
        • E(g(X)) = ∑ g(x) P(X = x)

        The third means: to find the expectation of something computed from X (like X²), apply it to each value and keep the same probabilities.

        A trap: usually E(X²) ≠ (E(X))², and E(1/X) ≠ 1/(E(X)). Only straight-line changes pass through E.

        Example: a prize of 5X for a die roll: E(5X) = 5 · 3.5 = 17.5.

        5Variance and standard deviation

        Variance of a random variable

        • V(X) = E[(X − μ)²],   μ = E(X)
        • V(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²
        • σ(X) = √(V(X))

        In words: the expected squared distance from the mean: how spread out the values are, weighted by probability. The second form (the mean of the square minus the square of the mean) is the quicker one, the same shortcut as for data.

        Example: heads in 3 tosses: E(X) = 1.5, E(X²) = (0 + 3 + 12 + 9)/8 = 3, V(X) = 3 − 2.25 = 0.75, σ ≈ 0.87.

        Rules for variance

        • V(aX + b) = a² V(X)
        • σ(aX + b) = |a| σ(X)
        • V(c) = 0

        Why: adding b shifts every value and the mean together, so no distance changes; multiplying by a stretches every distance by |a|, and squares by a².

        The variance is the smallest expected squared distance: E[(X − c)²] is smallest at c = E(X), as the mean is for data.

        Expectation and variance of the special distributions

        Make sense of them: 100 fair coin tosses average np = 50 heads. Waiting for a six takes 1/p = 6 rolls on average. For a Poisson count the mean and the variance are the same number.

        6Two random variables

        The joint probability function

        For two discrete variables on the same experiment, the joint probability function gives each pair of values its probability: P_(XY)(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y). Write it as a table: rows for X, columns for Y.

        The example: two coin tosses; X = number of heads, Y = 1 if the first toss is heads. The cell (1, 1) is "one head, and it came first": HT, 1/4.

        All the cells add up to 1 (the corner of the table).

        Marginal distributions

        • P_(X)(x) = ∑_(y) P_(XY)(x, y)
        • P_(Y)(y) = ∑_(x) P_(XY)(x, y)

        In words: the distribution of X alone is the row totals; that of Y alone, the column totals. They sit in the margins of the table, hence the name. Above: X: 1/4, 1/2, 1/4; Y: 1/2, 1/2.

        The other way doesn't work: the margins alone don't tell you the cells, unless the variables are independent.

        Independent random variables

        X and Y are independent when every cell is the product of its margins:

        P_(XY)(x, y) = P_(X)(x) · P_(Y)(y)   for all x, y

        To show they are dependent one cell that fails is enough. Above: P_(XY)(0, 1) = 0 but P_(X)(0) P_(Y)(1) = 1/4 · 1/2 = 1/8. A zero cell with non-zero margins always means dependent.

        Functions of two variables such as X + Y or XY are random variables too: go over the cells, compute the new value in each, and add the probabilities of the cells with the same value.

        7Covariance and correlation

        Expectation of a sum and of a product

        • E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y)   always
        • E(XY) = E(X) · E(Y)   when X, Y are independent

        The sum rule needs nothing: no independence, no table. The product rule can fail for dependent variables. Above: E(XY) = 1 · 1/4 + 2 · 1/4 = 3/4, but E(X) E(Y) = 1 · 1/2 = 1/2.

        Covariance

        cov(X, Y) = E(XY) − E(X) · E(Y)

        Meaning: positive when large X tends to come with large Y, negative when with small Y. It measures how the two move together, like the numerator of Pearson's r for data.

        Example: above, cov(X, Y) = 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4 > 0: a head first makes more heads likelier.

        Variance of a sum: V(X + Y) = V(X) + V(Y) + 2cov(X, Y); for independent (or just uncorrelated) variables, the variances simply add.

        Uncorrelated is not independent

        X and Y are uncorrelated when cov(X, Y) = 0. Independent ⇒ uncorrelated, but not the other way.

        Example: X is −1, 0, 1 with probability 1/3 each, and Y = X². E(X) = 0 and E(XY) = E(X³) = 0, so cov = 0. Yet Y is completely decided by X. Covariance only sees a straight-line relation.

        The correlation coefficient

        ρ(X, Y) = (cov(X, Y))/(σ(X) · σ(Y))

        • −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1; symmetric, ρ(X, Y) = ρ(Y, X).
        • Not changed by changing units (βX + α, γY + δ with βγ > 0).
        • ρ = 1 when Y = βX + α with β > 0; ρ = −1 when β < 0.
        • ρ = 0 exactly when uncorrelated.

        Example: above, V(X) = 1/2, V(Y) = 1/4: ρ = (1/4)/(√(1/2) · 1/2) = 1/(√2) ≈ 0.71.

        8Continuous random variables

        The density function

        A continuous variable (a length, a time) can take any value in an interval. Its probabilities are described by a density function g(x) ≥ 0:

        P(a < X < b) = the area under g between a and b

        • The total area under g is 1.
        • P(X = a) = 0 for every single value (a line has no area), so < and ≤ give the same probabilities.
        • g(x) itself is not a probability: it can be larger than 1. It is probability per unit, like the height of a histogram.

        Example: the triangle above (area 1/2 · 2 · 1 = 1 ✓). P(X < 0.5) is the shaded small triangle: 1/2 · 0.5 · 0.5 = 0.125.

        The cumulative distribution of a continuous variable

        F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = the area under g to the left of x

        • A smooth rising curve from 0 to 1 (no jumps, unlike the discrete staircase).
        • P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a).

        Piecewise-linear densities: when g is made of straight pieces, every area is a rectangle, a triangle or a trapezoid, so no integrals are needed. Triangle above: F(x) = x²/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

        Expectation and variance are defined as for discrete variables (the limit of finer and finer histograms) and follow the same rules: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b, V(aX + b) = a²V(X). A symmetric density has its expectation at the center of symmetry (the triangle: E(X) = 1).

        Continuous uniform: X ~ U(a, b)

        g(x) = 1/(b − a) for a < x < b, and 0 elsewhere

        • P(c < X < d) = (d − c)/(b − a)   (inside [a, b])
        • E(X) = (a + b)/2,   V(X) = ((b − a)²)/12

        In words: a flat density; the probability of a stretch is just its share of the whole length. A bus every 10 minutes, arriving at a random moment: the wait is U(0, 10), P(wait > 7) = 3/10, average wait 5 minutes.

        9The normal distribution

        X ~ N(μ, σ²)

        The normal distribution has a symmetric bell-shaped density centered at μ = E(X), with spread σ = σ(X). Heights, measurement errors and many sums of small effects are close to normal.

        • About 68% of the area is within 1σ of μ, 95% within 2σ, and almost all (99.7%) within 3σ.
        • A linear change keeps it normal: Y = βX + α ~ N(βμ + α, β²σ²).

        Note the second parameter is the variance σ²: N(100, 225) has σ = 15.

        The standard normal and Φ

        Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1),   Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z)

        • P(X ≤ x) = Φ((x − μ)/σ)
        • Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z),   Φ(0) = 0.5
        • P(a < X < b) = Φ((b − μ)/σ) − Φ((a − μ)/σ)

        Why one table is enough: turning X into its z-score (Descriptive statistics) gives the standard normal Z, the same for every normal. The table of Φ at the end of the course book lists the area to the left of z for z ≥ 0; symmetry gives the negative side.

        Worth remembering: 1.645 leaves 5% above it, 1.96 leaves 2.5%.

        1Measurement and units

        Physical quantities and SI units

        Physics describes the world with measurements. Every physical quantity is a number times a unit: 5 m, 4.2 kg, 2 × 10⁻³ s. The number alone means nothing: "the table is 2 long" could be 2 metres or 2 centimetres.

        The SI system (Système International) is the agreed set of units used in science. Mechanics needs only the first three: metre, kilogram, second (sometimes called the MKS system). Every other unit is built from them.

        Scientific notation: a very large or very small number is written as a number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten: the electron's charge is 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the Earth–Sun distance 1.496 × 10¹¹ m. Powers of ten: Powers & Logs.

        Always write the unit next to every number in a calculation. It catches mistakes, and an answer without a unit is not an answer.

        Derived units and prefixes

        A derived unit is made of base units. Some have their own names:

        A prefix multiplies a unit by a power of ten:

        Reading them: 1 km = 10³ m, 1 ns = 10⁻⁹ s, 5 MΩ = 5 × 10⁶ Ω. Never stack two prefixes: a thousandth of a gram is a milligram, not a "milli-kilo-gram".

        Before putting numbers into a formula, turn every quantity into plain SI units (m, kg, s): 30 kV = 30 × 10³ V, 2 cm = 2 × 10⁻² m. Then the answer comes out in SI units too.

        Units of area and volume

        • 1 cm² = (10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m²
        • 1 km² = (10³ m)² = 10⁶ m²
        • 1 cm³ = (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³
        • 1 L = 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³

        The trap: a square centimetre is not a hundredth of a square metre. A square 1 m on a side holds 100 × 100 = 10,000 squares of 1 cm, so the power of ten is squared too (cubed for volume).

        Safest way: convert each length to metres first, then multiply: a sheet 80 cm by 120 cm is 0.8 m × 1.2 m = 0.96 m².

        Area and volume formulas (rectangle, triangle, circle, sphere, cylinder, cone…): Geometry base. The sphere: S = 4πR², V = (4/3)πR³.

        Dimensions

        The dimension of a quantity says what it is made of, whatever units are used: [L] length, [T] time, [M] mass.

        • [area] = [L]²,   [volume] = [L]³
        • [velocity] = ([L])/([T]),   [acceleration] = ([L])/([T]²)
        • [force] = ([M][L])/([T]²)

        The rule: both sides of an equation, and every term added or subtracted, must have the same dimension. You can't add metres to seconds.

        Why it's useful: it checks a formula you half remember. x = v₀t + (1/2)at²: [L/T][T] = [L] and [L/T²][T²] = [L], both length, as x is. But v = at² would give [L] for a velocity, so it must be wrong.

        Numbers have no dimension, and neither does an angle in radians (arc length over radius, ([L])/([L])). A derivative dy/dx has dimension ([y])/([x]), an integral ∫ f(x) dx has [f][x].

        2Motion in one dimension

        Position, velocity and acceleration

        A body moves along a straight line. Pick a point as the origin and a positive direction. Its position x(t) is its distance from the origin at time t, positive on one side and negative on the other.

        • v_(avg) = (Δx)/(Δt) = (x₂ − x₁)/(t₂ − t₁)
        • v(t) = (dx)/(dt) = lim_(Δt→0) (x(t + Δt) − x(t))/(Δt)
        • a(t) = (dv)/(dt) = (d²x)/(dt²)

        In words: the average velocity is the change in position over the time it took. The instantaneous velocity is the same thing over a tiny time: the derivative of the position. The acceleration is how fast the velocity changes: the derivative of the velocity. Units: m/s and m/s².

        Signs matter: v > 0 means moving in the positive direction, v < 0 the other way. a and v with the same sign: speeding up. Opposite signs: slowing down (decelerating).

        Displacement vs. distance: x₂ − x₁ is the displacement; the distance travelled is the whole path. Drive 100 km north and 50 km back south: displacement 50 km, distance 150 km. The average velocity uses the displacement.

        Reading motion graphs

        • Position graph x(t): its slope at a point is the velocity there. Steeper means faster; going down means moving backwards.
        • Velocity graph v(t): its slope is the acceleration. The area between it and the time axis is the displacement (area below the axis counts as negative).
        • Acceleration graph a(t): the area under it is the change in velocity.

        Why the area: over a very short time Δt the velocity is almost constant, so the body moves v Δt, a thin rectangle under the graph. Adding all the rectangles gives the area: that's the integral x − x₀ = ∫ v dt (Integrals).

        The picture above is constant acceleration: a flat, v a straight line, x a parabola.

        Constant velocity

        • v = v₀,   a = 0
        • x(t) = x₀ + v₀t

        In words: each second the body moves the same v₀ metres. x₀ is where it is at t = 0 (an initial condition). The position graph is a straight line with slope v₀; the velocity graph is flat, and the rectangle under it is v₀t, the distance moved.

        Short form: starting at the origin, x = vt, so v = x/t and t = x/v.

        From calculus: x = ∫ v₀ dt = v₀t + x₀, with x₀ the constant of integration.

        Constant acceleration: the equations of motion

        • v(t) = v₀ + at
        • x(t) = x₀ + v₀t + (1/2)at²
        • v² − v₀² = 2a(x − x₀)
        • x − x₀ = ((v + v₀)/2) t

        Where they come from: the velocity grows by a every second, so v = v₀ + at. The displacement is the area under the velocity line: a rectangle v₀t plus a triangle (1/2) · t · at. The third equation comes from eliminating t between the first two; it is the one to use when the time isn't given or asked. The fourth says the average velocity is the average of the start and end velocities (true only for constant acceleration).

        Slowing down is the same equations with a of the opposite sign to v₀. Choose the positive direction first and keep it: the signs of v₀, a and x all follow from that choice.

        Free fall

        A body that falls with only gravity acting on it (no air resistance) moves with constant acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s², downward, whatever its mass.

        Signs: with "up" as positive, a = −g; with "down" as positive, a = +g. A ball thrown up keeps the same acceleration all the way: it slows on the way up, stops for an instant at the top (v = 0, but a is still −g), and speeds up on the way down.

        Useful results (dropped from rest, down positive): v = gt, h = (1/2)gt², t = √((2h)/g). Thrown up at v₀: it rises h_(max) = (v₀²)/(2g) and comes back down at the same speed v₀.

        History: Galileo showed that a heavy and a light body fall together (air resistance aside), against the old belief that heavy bodies fall faster. On the Moon, a hammer and a feather dropped together land together.

        3Vectors

        Scalars, vectors and coordinates

        A scalar is a quantity with a size only: mass, time, temperature, energy. A vector has a size and a direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force. "10 km" is a scalar; "10 km to the north-east" is a vector.

        Notation: the book writes a vector in bold, A; here it is A⃗. Its size (magnitude) is A or |A⃗|, always positive or zero.

        Coordinates: in a plane, a point is given by (x, y): x along the horizontal axis (often east), y along the vertical one (often north). In space a third axis z is added. The axes are chosen right-handed: point your right hand's thumb along x, index finger along y, and the middle finger shows z.

        A moving body in a plane is described by two functions, x(t) and y(t). For example x(t) = 0.02t² + t, y(t) = 3t + 1 gives its place at every moment.

        Components, magnitude and direction

        • A_(x) = A cos θ,   A_(y) = A sin θ
        • A = √(A_(x)² + A_(y)²),   tan θ = (A_(y))/(A_(x))
        • A⃗ = A_(x) x̂ + A_(y) ŷ

        In words: the components are the vector's shadows on the axes: how far it goes in x and how far in y. They are numbers that can be negative. θ is measured from the positive x axis, counter-clockwise. The magnitude is Pythagoras (Triangles, Geometry base); the formulas with cos and sin come from the right triangle (Trig base).

        Unit vectors x̂, ŷ, ẑ (the book also writes i, j, k) have length 1 and point along the axes. A⃗ = 3x̂ − 2ŷ means "3 along x, 2 backwards along y".

        The angle trap: arctan only returns angles between −90° and 90°. Look at the signs of the components to see the quarter: A⃗ = −3x̂ + 4ŷ has arctan(−4/3) = −53.13°, but it points up and to the left, so θ = 180° − 53.13° = 126.87°.

        Adding, subtracting and scaling vectors

        • C⃗ = A⃗ + B⃗:   C_(x) = A_(x) + B_(x),   C_(y) = A_(y) + B_(y)
        • C⃗ = A⃗ − B⃗:   C_(x) = A_(x) − B_(x),   C_(y) = A_(y) − B_(y)
        • s A⃗: every component times s

        Drawing it (head to tail): draw A⃗, start B⃗ at the tip of A⃗; the sum goes from the start of A⃗ to the tip of B⃗. Or start both at one point: the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram they make. Both pictures give the same C⃗, and the order doesn't matter: A⃗ + B⃗ = B⃗ + A⃗.

        Subtracting: A⃗ − B⃗ = A⃗ + (−B⃗), where −B⃗ has the same length as B⃗ and the opposite direction.

        Scaling: s A⃗ points like A⃗ (opposite if s < 0) and has length |s| A.

        Magnitudes don't add: walking 3 km east and 4 km north leaves you 5 km from the start, not 7. Add the components, then take the magnitude.

        Position, velocity and acceleration vectors

        • r⃗(t) = x(t) x̂ + y(t) ŷ   (position)
        • d⃗ = r⃗₂ − r⃗₁   (displacement)
        • v_(x) = (dx)/(dt),   v_(y) = (dy)/(dt)
        • a_(x) = (dv_(x))/(dt),   a_(y) = (dv_(y))/(dt)

        In words: in a plane, the motion of one dimension happens in each direction separately: differentiate each component on its own. The velocity vector always points along the path (it is tangent to it); its size is the speed, v = √(v_(x)² + v_(y)²).

        Velocity vs. speed: the velocity is the vector, the speed is its size. A car going round a bend at a steady 50 km/h keeps its speed but changes its velocity, so it is accelerating.
