        Adding velocities: a boat moving at v⃗₁ relative to the water, in water moving at v⃗₂ relative to the bank, moves at v⃗ = v⃗₁ + v⃗₂ relative to the bank (the picture).

        4Scalar and vector products

        The scalar (dot) product

        • A⃗ · B⃗ = AB cos α
        • A⃗ · B⃗ = A_(x)B_(x) + A_(y)B_(y) + A_(z)B_(z)

        In words: the dot product of two vectors is a number (a scalar): the length of one times the part of the other that points along it. α is the angle between them.

        • Same direction (α = 0): A⃗ · B⃗ = AB, as large as it gets.
        • Perpendicular (α = 90°): A⃗ · B⃗ = 0. This is the quick test for "perpendicular".
        • More than 90° apart: negative.
        • A⃗ · A⃗ = A², and the order doesn't matter: A⃗ · B⃗ = B⃗ · A⃗.

        Where it is used: the work of a force along a displacement, W = F⃗ · S⃗ = FS cos θ (Work, later in Mechanics), and the flux of an electric field (Electricity and magnetism).

        The vector (cross) product

        • |A⃗ × B⃗| = AB sin θ
        • (A⃗ × B⃗)_(x) = A_(y)B_(z) − A_(z)B_(y)
        • (A⃗ × B⃗)_(y) = A_(z)B_(x) − A_(x)B_(z)
        • (A⃗ × B⃗)_(z) = A_(x)B_(y) − A_(y)B_(x)

        In words: the cross product of two vectors is a vector, perpendicular to both of them (to the plane they lie in). Its length AB sin θ is the area of the parallelogram they make.

        Its direction (the right-hand rule): curl the fingers of your right hand from A⃗ toward B⃗ through the smaller angle; the thumb points along A⃗ × B⃗. (Or: a standard screw turned from A⃗ to B⃗ moves along it.)

        • The order matters: B⃗ × A⃗ = −A⃗ × B⃗.
        • Parallel vectors (θ = 0): the product is zero; so A⃗ × A⃗ = 0.
        • The unit vectors: x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, ŷ × ẑ = x̂, ẑ × x̂ = ŷ (in a cycle).
        • It distributes: A⃗ × (B⃗ + C⃗) = A⃗ × B⃗ + A⃗ × C⃗.

        Remembering the components: it is the determinant with x̂, ŷ, ẑ in the first row, A's components in the second and B's in the third. Where it is used: torque, angular momentum, the magnetic force on a moving charge.

        5Newton's laws

        Newton's first law (the law of inertia)

        A body stays at rest, or keeps moving at a constant velocity in a straight line, as long as no (net) force acts on it.

        In words: moving doesn't need a force; changing the motion does. For two thousand years people believed the opposite (Aristotle): a cart stops when you stop pushing, so motion seemed to need a force. Galileo saw that it stops because of friction and air resistance, forces that act against the motion. Without them it would roll on forever.

        Inertia is this tendency to keep the same motion. Standing in a bus that brakes, your body keeps going forward: nothing pushed you, you just weren't stopped together with the bus.

        It is a special case of the second law: F = 0 gives a = 0, constant velocity. It is stated on its own because it says something new: rest and steady straight motion are the same "natural" state.

        Newton's second law

        • ∑ F⃗ = m a⃗
        • ∑ F_(x) = m a_(x),   ∑ F_(y) = m a_(y),   ∑ F_(z) = m a_(z)

        In words: the net force (the vector sum of all the forces on the body) gives it an acceleration in the same direction as the net force, proportional to it, and inversely proportional to the body's mass. Twice the force: twice the acceleration. Twice the mass: half.

        Forces add as vectors (Vectors). The law holds separately along each axis, so a problem in a plane becomes two problems on a line: one for x, one for y.

        Only forces acting on this body go into the sum. Forces the body exerts on others belong in their equations.

        Force, mass and the newton

        Mass m is a property of the body itself: how hard it is to change its motion (its inertia), measured in kilograms. Force is something outside acting on it: a push or a pull, measured in newtons.

        • 1 N = 1 kg · m/s²
        • [force] = ([M][L])/([T]²)

        One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s². Holding a 100 g apple still takes about 1 N.

        How a force is measured: a spring stretches in proportion to the force on it (Hooke's law, Equilibrium and elasticity), so a calibrated spring is a force meter.

        Old units: in the cgs system force was in dynes, 1 N = 10⁵ dyn; "kilogram-force" (≈ 9.8 N) is not an SI unit.

        Newton's third law

        If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts on A a force of the same size and the opposite direction: F⃗_(AB) = −F⃗_(BA).

        The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other. The Earth pulls an apple down, and the apple pulls the Earth up just as hard; the apple accelerates a lot, the Earth (huge mass) not measurably.

        Everyday examples: a gun recoils when it fires; a rocket pushes gas backward and the gas pushes it forward; you push the floor backward when you walk, and the floor pushes you forward.

        A trap: a book on a table: its weight (Earth on book) and the normal force (table on book) are equal and opposite, but they are not a third-law pair; both act on the book. The pair of the weight is the book pulling the Earth.

        6Gravitation, weight and density

        The law of universal gravitation

        • F = G (m₁m₂)/(r²)
        • G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²

        In words: every two bodies attract each other, along the line between them, with a force proportional to both masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Twice as far: a quarter of the force. (The picture is in Newton's third law: the two forces are a third-law pair.)

        Why we don't notice it between everyday objects: G is tiny. Two 1000 kg cars 2 m apart attract with about 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ N. Only a huge mass like the Earth makes it big. Cavendish first measured G in 1798 with a delicate torsion balance.

        Spheres: for a uniform ball, r is measured from its centre, as if all its mass sat there. The same law keeps the Moon around the Earth and the planets around the Sun: one law for falling apples and for the sky.

        The acceleration of gravity g

        • g = G M/(R²)
        • g ≈ 9.8 m/s² at the Earth's surface

        Where it comes from: a body of mass m on the Earth (mass M, radius R) is pulled with F = GM m/(R²). By the second law its acceleration is F/m = GM/R²: the m cancels. That is why every body falls with the same g, heavy or light.

        It changes a little from place to place: from about 9.78 at the equator to 9.83 m/s² at the poles (the Earth is not a perfect sphere and it spins), and it drops with height. At a height h, use R + h in place of R.

        Other worlds: the same formula with their own mass and radius: on the Moon g ≈ 1.6 m/s², about a sixth of the Earth's.

        Mass and weight

        W = mg

        Mass and weight are different things. The mass (kg) belongs to the body and is the same everywhere. The weight (N) is the gravitational force on it, so it depends on where it is. A 10 kg body weighs 98 N on Earth and about 16 N on the Moon, but it is 10 kg in both places.

        Everyday language says "I weigh 70 kg"; physics says your mass is 70 kg and your weight about 686 N.

        Weightless astronauts still have their full mass: pushing a heavy object in orbit is just as hard as on Earth, even though it "weighs nothing".

        Density

        • ρ = m/V   (kg/m³)
        • s = ρ/(10³ kg/m³)   (relative density)

        In words: the density is the mass of one unit of volume of a material: how tightly packed it is. Iron is about 7900 kg/m³, water 1000 kg/m³, air about 1.3 kg/m³.

        Relative density compares a material with water, so it has no units: iron 7.9, wood about 0.6. It is also the density in g/cm³.

        Using it: m = ρV and V = m/ρ. A 3 cm wooden cube of 18.9 g: V = 2.7 × 10⁻⁵ m³, ρ = 700 kg/m³.

        7Forces in practice: friction, slopes and pulleys

        Free-body diagrams and the normal force

        A free-body diagram shows one body alone, with an arrow for every force acting on it, starting at the body. It is the first step of almost every mechanics problem.

        • Weight mg: always straight down.
        • Normal force N: a surface pushes back on a body pressing on it, perpendicular to the surface. It is only as big as it needs to be; it is mg on a flat floor only when nothing else pushes or pulls up or down (here the rope lifts a little, so N < mg).
        • Tension T: a rope or string pulls along itself, away from the body.
        • Friction f: along the surface, against the sliding (or the tendency to slide).

        Contact forces (normal, tension, friction) need touching; gravity (and later electric and magnetic forces) act from a distance.

        Friction

        • f_(s) ≤ μ_(s) N   (static: not sliding)
        • f_(k) = μ_(k) N   (kinetic: sliding)

        Static friction holds a body still. It matches whatever force tries to slide it, up to a maximum μ_(s)N; push harder than that and the body starts to slide. Kinetic friction acts while sliding and is constant, μ_(k)N, against the motion.

        The coefficients μ_(s), μ_(k) are pure numbers that depend on the two surfaces, not on the area of contact or (roughly) on the speed. Usually μ_(k) < μ_(s): it is harder to get something moving than to keep it moving.

        Example: a crate on a truck with μ_(s) = 0.4 stays put as long as static friction can give it the truck's acceleration: μ_(s)mg ≥ ma, so up to a = μ_(s)g ≈ 3.9 m/s², whatever the crate's mass. Rolling friction (a wheel rolling) is much smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels work.

        The inclined plane

        • N = mg cos θ
        • a = g sin θ   (no friction)
        • a = g (sin θ − μ_(k) cos θ)   (sliding down, with friction)

        The trick: tilt the axes with the slope: x along it, y perpendicular. Then N and friction lie on the axes and only the weight needs splitting: mg sin θ pulls down the slope, mg cos θ presses into it. (The angle between mg and the y axis equals the slope's angle θ.)

        Nothing moves across the slope, so ∑F_(y) = 0 gives N = mg cos θ; along it, ∑F_(x) = ma. A steeper slope: more pull along it, less pressing (and so less friction).

        When it starts to slide: at the angle where mg sin θ = μ_(s) mg cos θ, that is tan θ = μ_(s). Tilting a board until a coin slides measures μ_(s).

        Tension, pulleys and connected bodies

        • a = ((M − m)g)/(M + m)
        • T = (2M m g)/(M + m)

        A light string (its mass ignored) has the same tension T all along it, and a light, frictionless pulley only turns the string's direction. Bodies tied by a taut string move together: the same size of acceleration.

        How the formulas come out (the Atwood machine, above): one free-body diagram and one second-law equation per body, each in its own direction of motion: Mg − T = Ma for M (going down), T − mg = ma for m (going up). Adding them removes T.

        Checks: equal masses give a = 0; T lies between mg and Mg: less than the heavy weight (so M falls), more than the light one (so m rises).

        8Projectiles and reference frames

        Throwing straight up or down

        • v = v₀ − gt,   y = v₀t − (1/2)gt²
        • t_(m) = (v₀)/g,   y_(m) = (v₀²)/(2g)

        In words: the only force is the weight, so the acceleration is −g (up positive) going up, at the top and coming down. It rises for t_(m) = v₀/g to the height y_(m), and comes back to the start after 2v₀/g, at the same speed v₀, downward.

        Thrown down at v₀: the same equations with −v₀ in place of v₀. Dropped: v₀ = 0. These are the constant-acceleration equations with a = −g (Free fall, Motion in one dimension).

        Throwing horizontally and at an angle

        • x = (v₀ cos α) t,   v_(x) = v₀ cos α
        • y = (v₀ sin α) t − (1/2)gt²,   v_(y) = v₀ sin α − gt

        The key idea: the two directions are independent. Horizontally no force acts (air resistance aside), so the motion is at constant velocity. Vertically only gravity acts: free fall. Solve each one separately; they share only the time t.

        Horizontal throw (α = 0, from a height): x = v₀t, the drop is (1/2)gt². A bullet fired horizontally and one dropped at the same moment hit the flat ground together.

        From flat ground at an angle: it rises for t = (v₀ sin α)/g, reaching h_(max) = ((v₀ sin α)²)/(2g); it lands after twice that time, at the range R = (v₀² sin 2α)/g, the largest at α = 45°. The path is a parabola.

        Inertial frames and fictitious forces

        A reference frame is the "point of view" from which motion is measured: the ground, a train, a ship. An inertial frame is one in which Newton's laws hold as written. Any frame moving at a constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is inertial too.

        Galileo's ship: in a ship sailing smoothly at a steady speed, a dropped stone falls straight down beside the mast, and no experiment inside can tell whether the ship moves. The same in a plane cruising steadily: you pour a drink normally.

        An accelerating frame is not inertial. When a bus brakes, you feel "thrown" forward although no force pushes you: the bus slows and you keep going. Seen from inside the bus, you seem to feel a force F = −ma (a the bus's acceleration): a fictitious force. Such forces have no source and no third-law pair.

        So: solve problems from an inertial frame (the ground) whenever you can; then there are no fictitious forces to worry about.

        9Equilibrium and elasticity

        Equilibrium of forces

        • ∑ F⃗ = 0:   ∑ F_(x) = 0,   ∑ F_(y) = 0

        In words: a body at rest (or moving at a constant velocity) has zero net force: the forces cancel along every axis. This is the second law with a = 0. The branch of mechanics about bodies at rest is statics.

        The knot above is in equilibrium: T₃ = mg (the hanging mass), and along x and y: T₁ cos 60° = T₂ cos 30°, T₁ sin 60° + T₂ sin 30° = mg. Two equations, two unknown tensions.

        A ball hung on a string and pushed sideways by the wind (force F) settles at the angle where T sin α = F and T cos α = mg: F = mg tan α.

        Rigid bodies: translation and rotation

        A rigid body keeps its shape and size whatever forces act on it (an idealisation: real bodies bend a little). Its motion combines two kinds: translation (sliding, every point moving the same way) and rotation.

        • A force acts along its line of action; sliding the force along that line changes nothing.
        • Forces whose lines of action all meet at one point: ∑F⃗ = 0 is enough for equilibrium.
        • Two equal, opposite forces not on the same line (a couple): the net force is zero, yet the body starts to turn. So a rigid body needs a second condition: no net turning effect (torque). Torques: The lever law and torques.

        Hooke's law

        F = kΔL

        In words: stretching (or squeezing) a spring takes a force proportional to how far it is stretched. Twice the force, twice the stretch. k, the spring constant (N/m), says how stiff the spring is. The spring pulls back with the same force, F = −kx (toward its natural length).

        Only up to a limit: stretched too far, a spring (or any material) deforms for good and the law no longer holds. Hooke's law is an observed rule (from 1678), not a basic law like Newton's; it comes from the forces between the material's molecules.

        A spring as a scale: a 30 N weight stretches a spring 6 cm: k = 30/0.06 = 500 N/m.

        Stress, strain and Young's modulus

        • stress = F/A   (N/m²),   strain = (ΔL)/L   (no units)
        • Y = (F/A)/((ΔL)/L),   so ΔL = (FL)/(AY)

        In words: a rod or wire stretches more when the force is bigger, when it is longer, and when it is thinner. Dividing out the size of the sample leaves a property of the material: Young's modulus Y, the stress divided by the strain. Steel: Y ≈ 2 × 10¹¹ N/m².

        Example: a steel wire 2 m long, cross-section 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², pulled with 200 N: ΔL = (200 · 2)/(10⁻⁶ · 2 × 10¹¹) = 2 × 10⁻³ m, two millimetres.

        Other deformations follow the same pattern (stress proportional to strain): squeezing from all sides (a body under water) changes the volume; a sideways force on the top face of a block (shear) slants it.

        10Pressure and fluids

        Pressure and Pascal's law

        • P = F/A   (1 Pa = 1 N/m²)
        • F₂ = (S/s) F₁   (hydraulic press)

        Pressure is force per unit area, the force pressing perpendicular on a surface spread over it. The same force on a smaller area makes more pressure: a knife edge cuts, snowshoes don't sink.

        Pascal's law: pressure applied to a closed fluid (liquid or gas) is passed on undiminished to every part of it. In a hydraulic press, a small force F₁ on a small piston (area s) makes a pressure F₁/s, which pushes the large piston (area S) with F₂ = PS. A 200 N push on a piston 50 times smaller lifts 10 000 N. (The small piston moves 50 times further: nothing is free, see Work.)

        Hydrostatic pressure

        P = P₀ + ρgh

        In words: a liquid presses on everything in it because of its own weight. At depth h, the column of liquid above each square metre weighs ρgh; add the pressure P₀ on the surface (usually the air's). The pressure depends only on the depth, not on the shape of the container, and at a given depth it pushes equally in every direction.

        In water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) every 10 m of depth adds about one atmosphere: at 10 m, P ≈ 1.013 × 10⁵ + 98 000 ≈ 2 × 10⁵ Pa.

        Atmospheric pressure, barometers and manometers

        The air above us has weight too: at sea level it presses with atmospheric pressure P_(a) ≈ 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa (1 atm), about the weight of 1 kg on every square centimetre.

        • Barometer (Torricelli): a tube of mercury turned upside down in a dish. The mercury falls until the column's pressure balances the air's: about 76 cm of mercury (ρgh = P_(a)). With water the column would be about 10 m.
        • Manometer: a U-tube of liquid connected to a gas. The difference h between the two levels gives ΔP = P − P_(a) = ρgh.
        • Absolute vs. gauge pressure: P is the absolute pressure; P − P_(a) (what a tyre gauge shows) is the gauge pressure, which can be negative.

        Archimedes' principle

        • F_(b) = Vρg
        • ∑ F_(y) = Vg(ρ − ρ')

        In words: a body in a fluid is pushed up with a force equal to the weight of the fluid it pushes aside (V the volume under the surface, ρ the fluid's density). ρ' is the body's own density.

        Why: the pressure grows with depth, so the fluid pushes harder on the body's bottom than on its top. That difference is exactly the weight of the fluid that would fill the body's place, since such fluid would just float there.

        • ρ' < ρ: it floats up and settles partly out of the fluid, with the submerged fraction ρ'/ρ (wood of relative density 0.6 floats 60% under water).
        • ρ' > ρ: it sinks (but weighs less in the fluid).
        • ρ' = ρ: it floats at any depth (a fish, a submarine).

        11Work and kinetic energy

        Work

        • W = FS cos θ = F⃗ · S⃗
        • 1 J = 1 N · m

        In words: a force does work on a body when the body moves along the force. Only the part of the force along the displacement counts: F cos θ. Work is a scalar, measured in joules (J).

        • θ = 0 (force along the motion): W = FS, positive.
        • θ = 90° (force across the motion): W = 0. The normal force and the weight do no work on a body sliding on a level floor; carrying a bag along a level road does no work on it either, in this physics sense.
        • θ > 90° (force against the motion, like friction): W < 0.

        Several forces: each one does its own work, and the work of the net force is the sum of them all.

        The work of a varying force

        • W = ∑ F⃗(r⃗_(i)) · Δr⃗_(i)   →   W = ∫_(A)^(B) F⃗ · dr⃗
        • along a line: W = ∫_(x₁)^(x₂) F(x) dx

        In words: when the force changes along the way, cut the path into small pieces on which it is almost constant, add the works of the pieces, and let the pieces shrink: an integral (Integrals). Along a line, the work is the area under the graph of F against x.

        A spring (F = kx to stretch it): the area under the straight line from 0 to x is a triangle, W = (1/2)kx². Stretching 10 cm takes a quarter of the work of stretching 20 cm.

        Kinetic energy and the work–energy theorem

        • K = (1/2)mv²
        • W_(net) = (1/2)mv₂² − (1/2)mv₁² = ΔK

        In words: the kinetic energy is the energy a body has because it moves. The theorem: the work of the net force on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy. Positive work speeds it up, negative work slows it down.

        Where it comes from: for a constant force along the motion, W = FS = ma S; with a = (v₂ − v₁)/t and S = ((v₁ + v₂)/2)t the time cancels and W = (m/2)(v₂² − v₁²). (The same comes out for any force, by integrating.)

        Why it is useful: it connects speeds with distances directly, without the time. Twice the speed is four times the kinetic energy, so a car needs four times the braking distance.

        12Potential energy and conservation of mechanical energy

        Gravitational potential energy and mechanical energy

        • U = m g h
        • E = K + U = (1/2)mv² + m g h

        In words: lifting a body by h takes work m g h against gravity. That work is stored as potential energy: let the body fall, and it gets it back as kinetic energy. h is measured from any level you choose; only changes of U matter.

        Conservation of mechanical energy: when only gravity (or other conservative forces) does work, the sum E = K + U stays the same. Energy only moves between the two forms.

        So its speed at the ground is v = √(2gh) ≈ 9.9 m/s, the free-fall result, found without any time.

        Conservative forces

        A force is conservative when the work needed to move a body from A to B against it depends only on A and B, not on the path. Equivalently: its total work around any closed path is zero.

        Gravity is conservative: lifting a body by h takes m g h, whether straight up, up a ramp or along a winding track (without friction). That is what makes a potential energy possible: it depends only on the position.

        Friction is not: a longer path means more work against it, and around a closed path its work is not zero (it always opposes the motion). The energy it takes doesn't come back as mechanical energy; it turns into heat (Heat and the molecular theory).

        The spring force is conservative too; electric forces are as well (Electricity and magnetism).

        The potential energy of a spring

        • F = −kx
        • U = (1/2)kx²

        In words: a spring stretched or squeezed by x pulls back toward its natural length (the minus sign). The work done to stretch it, (1/2)kx² (the area under F = kx, The work of a varying force), is stored as elastic potential energy and comes back when it is released.

        With a spring: E = (1/2)mv² + (1/2)kx² (+ m g h) is conserved. A spring gun compressed 10 cm (k = 400 N/m) stores 2 J; it launches a 0.2 kg ball at √(2 · 2/0.2) ≈ 4.5 m/s.

        When friction acts

        E_(final) = E_(initial) − f d

        In words: friction (kinetic, constant, over a distance d) takes fd out of the mechanical energy. That energy isn't destroyed: it becomes heat (the surfaces warm up). More generally, the work of the non-conservative forces equals the change in mechanical energy.

        Example: a 20 kg sled slides 10 m down a 30° slope (5 m drop) from rest, μ_(k) = 0.1. Friction 0.1 · 196 · cos 30° ≈ 17.0 N takes ≈ 170 J of the 980 J; it reaches the bottom with 810 J, about 9.0 m/s (without friction 9.9 m/s).

        13Heat and the molecular theory

        Heat is a form of energy

        1 cal = 4.184 J

        In words: when friction stops a sliding body, its mechanical energy seems lost; actually it becomes thermal energy: the bodies warm up. Heat is energy passing from a hotter body to a colder one because of the temperature difference.

        Joule's experiment (1840s): a falling weight turned paddles in water; the water warmed by an amount always proportional to the mechanical energy spent. The old heat unit, the calorie (the heat that warms 1 g of water by 1°C), turned out to be 4.184 joules.

        Food "calories" are kilocalories: a 2,700 kcal daily diet is about 1.1 × 10⁷ J.

        Specific heat and calorimetry

        • Q = mcΔT
        • C = mc   (heat capacity),   Q = CΔT

        In words: the heat Q needed to warm a body by ΔT is proportional to its mass and to the specific heat c of its material: the heat for 1 kg and 1°C (or 1 K: a temperature difference is the same in both).

        Water's specific heat is very large: it takes a lot of heat to warm, and gives out a lot as it cools. That is why the sea keeps coastal climates mild.

        Calorimetry: mix bodies at different temperatures in an insulated vessel (a calorimeter) and they reach a common temperature. No heat leaks out, so the heat given by the hot ones equals the heat taken by the cold ones: ∑ m c ΔT = 0. This is how specific heats are measured.

        Phase changes and latent heat

        Q = mL

        In words: while a substance melts or boils, the heat it takes doesn't raise its temperature: it goes into pulling the molecules apart. The heat per kilogram is the latent heat L (heat of fusion for melting, heat of vaporisation for boiling). Freezing and condensing give the same heat back.

        Water (at normal air pressure): melting at 0°C, L_(f) = 334 kJ/kg (80 cal/g); boiling at 100°C, L_(v) = 2256 kJ/kg (539 cal/g). Boiling points drop with lower pressure: on a high mountain water boils below 100°C.

        Heat conduction and heat of combustion

        Conduction: heat flows through a material from the hot side to the cold side, faster for a bigger area A, a bigger temperature difference and a thinner layer L. The material's thermal conductivity k says how well it conducts: metals (copper 401 W/(m·K)) much better than wood (0.11) or air (0.026). Trapped air makes good insulation (wool, fibreglass, double glazing).

        Heat of combustion: the heat released by burning 1 kg of a fuel: petrol about 4.6 × 10⁷ J/kg, wood about 1.9 × 10⁷ J/kg. Food is "burned" slowly in the body; its calorie value is its heat of combustion.

        The molecular theory of heat

        Matter is made of molecules in constant random motion. Temperature measures their average kinetic energy; heating a body makes its molecules move faster.

        • Gas: the molecules fly freely, far apart, and only collide now and then.
        • Liquid: they stay close and attract each other, but slide past one another.
        • Solid: each one vibrates around a fixed place.

        Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the molecules. Heat taken in raises it. In a phase change the potential part grows (the bonds loosen) while the kinetic part, and so the temperature, stays the same.

        Absolute zero, 0 K = −273.15°C, is where the molecular motion would be the least possible; nothing can be colder. The Kelvin scale starts there: T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15. The theory explains heat conduction too: fast molecules hand on their energy to slower neighbours in collisions.

        14Conservation of energy and power

        The law of conservation of energy

        Energy is neither created nor destroyed. In a closed system (no energy exchanged with the surroundings) the total energy stays constant; otherwise its change equals the energy that came in or went out.

        Energy takes many forms and turns from one into another: mechanical (kinetic and potential), internal (heat), chemical (stored in the bonds of molecules, released by burning or by food), electric, light, nuclear. A power station turns the chemical energy of fuel into heat, then motion, then electricity.

        Mechanical energy alone is conserved only without friction; the total energy always is. The law grew out of the discovery that heat is energy, and it has never been seen to fail.

        Power

        • P = W/t
        • 1 W = 1 J/s,   1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J

        In words: power is how fast work is done (or energy changes form): joules per second, the watt. Two cranes lifting the same load to the same height do the same work, but the faster one has the greater power.

        Units you meet: kilowatt 10³ W, megawatt 10⁶ W (power stations), horsepower ≈ 746 W (engines). The electricity bill counts energy in kilowatt-hours: a 1.5 kW heater on for 2 hours uses 3 kWh.

        Example: lifting a 300 kg lift 20 m in 15 s takes 300 · 9.8 · 20 = 58 800 J: a power of 58 800/15 = 3920 W, about 5.3 hp.

        15Simple machines, the lever law and torques

        Mechanical advantage and efficiency

        • R = (F₂)/(F₁)   (mechanical advantage)
        • E = (W₂)/(W₁) ≤ 1   (efficiency)

        In words: a simple machine (lever, pulley, wheel and axle, hydraulic press) lets a small force F₁ overcome a large load F₂. R says how many times the force is multiplied. E compares the useful work out (W₂ = F₂d₂) with the work put in (W₁ = F₁d₁).

        No machine gives energy for free: without friction W₂ = W₁, so F₁d₁ = F₂d₂: multiplying the force by R means moving R times further. The ideal mechanical advantage is d₁/d₂. With friction some work becomes heat, so E < 1 and the real advantage is smaller.

        Example: a wheel of radius 0.5 m on an axle of radius 0.1 m: ideal R = 5. If lifting a 980 N load actually takes 245 N, the real R = 4 and the efficiency is 4/5 = 80%.

        The lever law

        F₁ℓ₁ = F₂ℓ₂

        In words: a lever (a rigid bar turning about a fixed point, the fulcrum) balances when force times arm is the same on both sides. A long arm lets a small force hold a big load: F₁ = F₂ ℓ₂/ℓ₁.

        Example: a 600 N rock 0.3 m from the fulcrum is lifted by pushing 1.5 m from it on the other side with only 600 · 0.3/1.5 = 120 N. The hand moves 5 times as far as the rock, so the work is the same.

        Everyday levers: a crowbar, scissors, a bottle opener, a wheelbarrow, the forearm.

        Torque (moment of force)

        • M = Fℓ sin θ
        • equilibrium of a rigid body: ∑F⃗ = 0   and   ∑M = 0

        In words: the turning effect of a force about an axis is its torque (the book calls it the moment, M): the force times its lever arm, the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force's line. ℓ is the distance from the axis to where the force acts and θ the angle between the force and that line. Unit: N·m.

        • A force pointing at (or away from) the axis has no turning effect: θ = 0.
        • It turns most when it pushes at right angles, far from the axis: that's why a door handle is far from the hinges.
        • Sign: counter-clockwise positive, clockwise negative (a choice). The lever law is ∑M = 0 about the fulcrum.

        A body at rest needs both: no net force (it doesn't slide off) and no net torque (it doesn't start turning). If the forces balance, the torques can be taken about any point; pick the one where an unknown force acts, and it drops out. Torque is really a vector, M⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗ (Angular momentum).

        16Momentum and its conservation

        Momentum and Newton's second law

        • p⃗ = m v⃗   (kg·m/s)
        • F⃗ = (dp⃗)/(dt)

        In words: the momentum (linear momentum) of a body is its mass times its velocity: a vector pointing along the motion. A slow truck and a fast bullet can have the same momentum.

        The second law in its general form: the net force equals the rate of change of momentum. With a constant mass, dp/dt = m dv/dt = ma, the familiar F = ma; but F = dp/dt also holds when the mass changes (a rocket burning fuel).

        So a force acting for a time Δt changes the momentum by FΔt: a small force for a long time can do what a big force does in a short one.

        The law of conservation of momentum

        P⃗ = ∑ m_(i) v⃗_(i) = const   (no external forces)

        In words: in a system of bodies on which no outside forces act (or they cancel), the total momentum never changes, whatever the bodies do to each other. It holds for each component separately: P_(x), P_(y), P_(z).

        Why: by the third law, every internal force comes with an equal and opposite partner; their momentum changes cancel in pairs.

        Recoil: a 4 kg gun fires a 20 g bullet at 400 m/s. Before, nothing moves (P = 0); after, 0.02 · 400 + 4v = 0, so the gun kicks back at 2 m/s. Two bodies pushed apart by a spring move off with m₁v₁ = −m₂v₂: the lighter one faster.

        Momentum and energy together: momentum is conserved whenever there are no external forces, even with friction or a crash; mechanical energy only without non-conservative forces. Many problems need both.

        Collisions

        • m₁V₁ + m₂V₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂   (always)
        • (1/2)m₁V₁² + (1/2)m₂V₂² = (1/2)m₁v₁² + (1/2)m₂v₂²   (elastic only)

        In words (V before, v after): in a collision the bodies push each other hard for a short time; outside forces are negligible then, so momentum is always conserved. An elastic collision also keeps the kinetic energy (hard balls, billiards). An inelastic one turns some into heat and deformation; a perfectly inelastic one, where the bodies stick together, loses the most.

        The picture: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, elastically: momentum 6 = 2 · 1 + 1 · 4 ✓, energy 9 = 1 + 8 ✓.

        Sticking together, collisions in a plane, changing mass

        • Perfectly inelastic: m₁V₁ + m₂V₂ = (m₁ + m₂)V. A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s hits a 1500 kg car at rest and they lock: V = 8 m/s; the kinetic energy drops from 200 kJ to 80 kJ.
        • Ballistic pendulum: a bullet sticks in a hanging block, which then swings up by h. Two steps: the collision (momentum: mv = (m + M)V) and the swing (energy: V = √(2gh)). Energy is not conserved in the first step.
        • In a plane: momentum is a vector, so it is conserved along x and along y separately: two equations (three with the energy, if elastic).
        • Changing mass (a rocket, a cart filling with rain): ∑ m_(i)(t)v⃗_(i)(t) = const for the whole system, gas or rain included.

        Another frame: the law holds in every inertial frame; sometimes a moving frame (in which the total momentum is zero) makes a problem easier.

        17Circular motion

        Describing circular motion

        • f = 1/T
        • ω = (Δθ)/(Δt) = (2π)/T = 2πf
        • v = (2πR)/T = ωR

        In words: a body going round a circle of radius R at a constant speed (uniform circular motion) takes the period T for one round; the frequency f is rounds per second (Hz). The angular velocity ω is the angle swept per second, in radians per second (Radians, Trig base).

        Linear vs. angular: every point of a turning wheel has the same ω, but points further out move faster: v = ωr. The arc covered is S = Rθ.

        Example: a wheel making 10 turns a second: T = 0.1 s, ω = 20π ≈ 62.8 rad/s.

        Centripetal acceleration

        • a_(R) = (v²)/R = ω²R   (toward the centre)
        • a_(T) = (dv)/(dt)   (along the motion, when the speed changes)

        In words: even at a constant speed, a body on a circle accelerates, because the direction of its velocity keeps turning. That acceleration points to the centre (centripetal, "centre-seeking"), and it is bigger for faster motion and tighter circles. If the speed also changes, there is a second part along the path, a_(T).

        The velocity is always tangent to the circle, at right angles to the radius. Let go of a whirled stone and it flies off along the tangent, not outward.

        Centripetal force

        F = m (v²)/R = mω²R   (net force toward the centre)

        In words: to keep a body on a circle, the forces on it must add up to mv²/R toward the centre (the second law with the centripetal acceleration). It isn't a new kind of force: it is the job done by a tension, friction, gravity or a normal force.

        • A car on a flat curve: static friction supplies it, μ_(s)mg ≥ mv²/R, so v_(max) = √(μ_(s)gR): on R = 50 m with μ_(s) = 0.6, about 17 m/s ≈ 62 km/h.
        • A stone on a string: the tension. 0.5 kg on 0.8 m at 2 turns a second (ignoring gravity): ω = 4π, tension 0.5 · (4π)² · 0.8 ≈ 63 N.
        • The Earth's spin: part of gravity is used up keeping us on our circle, so the measured g is a little smaller at the equator than at the poles.

        Satellites and planets

        • G (Mm)/(r²) = m (v²)/r
        • v = √((GM)/r),   T = (2πr^(3/2))/(√(GM))

        In words: for a satellite on a circular orbit of radius r (from the planet's centre), gravity is the centripetal force. The satellite's own mass cancels. Higher orbits are slower and take longer: T² is proportional to r³ (Kepler's third law).

        Handy: GM = gR² for the Earth. At 400 km up (r ≈ 6771 km): v ≈ 7.7 km/s, one round in about 92 minutes. A geostationary satellite takes exactly a day and stays above one point of the equator: r ≈ 42 000 km, about 36 000 km up.

        "Weightless" astronauts are not out of gravity's reach (it is about 90% as strong at 400 km); they and their ship fall around the Earth together.

        Fictitious forces in a rotating frame

        The Earth turns, so a frame fixed to it is not inertial. Seen from a rotating frame, bodies seem to feel extra (fictitious) forces:

        • Centrifugal force mω²R, pointing outward: what you "feel" pressing you to the door of a car in a curve. From the ground there is no such force; your body just tends to go straight.
        • Coriolis force: acts on bodies moving in the rotating frame, sideways to their motion. It turns winds (to the right in the northern hemisphere), which makes storms swirl around low-pressure areas, and slowly turns the swing plane of Foucault's pendulum, a direct proof that the Earth rotates.

        18Angular momentum, torque and rigid bodies

        Rotational kinetic energy and moment of inertia

        • K = (1/2)Iω²
        • I = ∑ m_(i)R_(i)²

        In words: a rigid body turning at ω has kinetic energy: each small piece m_(i) at distance R_(i) from the axis moves at ωR_(i). Adding (1/2)m_(i)(ωR_(i))² gives (1/2)Iω², where I, the moment of inertia, plays the role the mass plays in (1/2)mv².

        Mass far from the axis counts more (it enters squared). A ring is harder to spin up than a disc of the same mass and size. I depends on the axis chosen. Unit: kg·m².

        Moments of inertia of common bodies

        Where they come from: I = ∑ m_(i)R_(i)² turns into an integral over the body. A ring has all its mass at R: MR². A disc has mass at every distance from 0 to R, so it averages to half.

        Angular momentum and its conservation

        • J = m v r   (a point on a circle),   J⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗
        • J = Iω   (a rigid body about its axis)

        In words: angular momentum is the "amount of rotation", as momentum is the amount of straight motion. The book writes it J. For a body moving past a point O, it is the momentum times the perpendicular distance from O to the line of motion; even a body moving in a straight line has angular momentum about a point not on its line.

        Conservation: with no external torque, the angular momentum stays constant. A spinning skater who pulls in her arms (smaller I) spins faster: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂. From I = 4 to 1.6 kg·m², 2 turns a second become 5. A planet's angular momentum about the Sun is conserved too: it moves faster when nearer (Kepler's second law).

        Energy is not conserved in the skater's case: (1/2)Iω² grows, from about 316 J to 790 J; her arms did that work.

        Torque as a vector

        • N⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗,   N = rF sin θ
        • N⃗ = (dJ⃗)/(dt)

        In words: the torque of a force about a point O is the cross product of the position r⃗ (from O to where the force acts) with the force (Scalar and vector products); its size is the "force times lever arm" of The lever law and torques, and its direction is the axis it tries to turn about (right-hand rule). The book writes it N here (M earlier).

        The rotational second law: torque changes angular momentum, as force changes momentum. No net torque, no change: that is the conservation law above. For a rigid body about a fixed axis, N = Iα with α = dω/dt.

        The centre of mass

        • R⃗ = (∑ m_(i) r⃗_(i))/M
        • F⃗ = M (d²R⃗)/(dt²)

        In words: the centre of mass is the mass-weighted average position of all the parts of a body (or system). Whatever the body does (spinning, tumbling), its centre of mass moves as if all the mass sat there and all the external forces acted there. A thrown hammer wobbles, but its centre of mass follows a clean parabola.

        Gravity acts as if at the centre of mass: lifting it by Δh changes the potential energy by MgΔh. A body hung from a point settles with its centre of mass straight below that point.

        Equilibrium of a rigid body: no net force and no net torque, ∑F⃗ = 0, ∑N⃗ = 0.

        19Harmonic motion

        Simple harmonic motion

        • F = −kx
        • a = −(k/m) x

        In words: a body pulled back toward a point (the equilibrium point, x = 0) by a force proportional to its distance from it oscillates back and forth: harmonic motion. A mass on a spring is the standard example.

        How it goes: released at x = A, it speeds up toward 0 (the force pulls it in), passes 0 at its top speed (no force there, but it keeps going), slows down on the other side and stops at x = −A, then comes back. Without friction it repeats forever. A is the amplitude.

        The equation of motion and its solution

        • (d²x)/(dt²) = −(k/m) x
        • x(t) = A cos ωt,   ω² = k/m
        • T = (2π)/ω = 2π√(m/k)

        In words: the second law gives a differential equation: an equation for the function x(t) itself. Sine and cosine solve it, because differentiating them twice gives back minus themselves times ω² (Differentiation formulas). The starting conditions (here: at rest at x = A when t = 0) pick the cosine.

        The period doesn't depend on the amplitude: a big swing and a small swing take the same time. A heavier mass oscillates slower, a stiffer spring faster. f = 1/T.

        Velocity, acceleration and energy

        • v = −Aω sin ωt,   v_(max) = Aω (at x = 0)
        • a = −Aω² cos ωt = −ω²x,   a_(max) = Aω² (at x = ±A)
        • E = (1/2)mv² + (1/2)kx² = (1/2)kA²

        In words: the speed is greatest in the middle and zero at the ends; the acceleration the other way round. The energy keeps moving between kinetic (middle) and spring potential (ends), and the total stays (1/2)kA².

        Example: 0.5 kg on a spring with k = 200 N/m, amplitude 0.1 m: ω = 20 rad/s, T ≈ 0.31 s, v_(max) = 2 m/s, a_(max) = 40 m/s², E = 1 J.

        A hanging spring and the pendulum

        • x₀ = (mg)/k   (a hanging spring's new equilibrium)
        • T = 2π√(ℓ/g)   (simple pendulum, small swings)

        A spring hanging vertically: the weight stretches it by x₀ to a new equilibrium; around that point the motion is the same harmonic motion, with the same T = 2π√(m/k). Gravity only moves the centre.

        A pendulum (a small mass on a string of length ℓ) swinging through small angles is harmonic too: the restoring force is about mg times the angle. Its period depends only on ℓ and g, not on the mass: a 1 m pendulum takes about 2 s. That is why pendulums kept time in clocks.

        20Viscosity and Stokes' law

        Drag and viscosity

        f_(v) = −Kηv

        In words: a body moving slowly through a fluid feels a resisting force (drag) proportional to its speed and opposite to it. K depends on the body's size and shape; η (eta), the viscosity, is a property of the fluid: how "thick" it is. Honey and glycerin have a high viscosity, water a low one, air much lower still.

        Why: the body drags the fluid next to it along; that layer drags the next one, and so on. Viscosity is the friction between layers of fluid sliding past each other.

        Units: kg/(m·s) (= Pa·s); the old unit is the poise, 1 P = 0.1 kg/(m·s). Viscosity drops quickly as a liquid warms (hot oil flows easily).

        Stokes' law and terminal velocity

        • K = 6πr,   so   f_(v) = 6πηrv   (a sphere)
        • v_(t) = (2r²g(ρ − ρ_(f)))/(9η)

        In words: for a small sphere of radius r, Stokes (1845) found K = 6πr. A ball dropped into a liquid speeds up until the drag (growing with speed) plus the buoyancy balance its weight; from then on it falls at a constant terminal velocity v_(t). Setting mg = buoyancy + 6πηrv with m = (4/3)πr³ρ gives the formula (ρ the ball's density, ρ_(f) the fluid's).

        Example: a steel ball (r = 1 mm, ρ = 7800 kg/m³) in glycerin (η = 1.5 kg/(m·s), ρ_(f) = 1260 kg/m³) sinks at v_(t) ≈ 9.5 mm/s. Timing such a fall measures η. Stokes' law holds only for slow motion; fast bodies (a car, a skydiver) feel a drag closer to v².

        1Basic concepts

        What a wave is

        A wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium (a string, water, air), carrying energy from place to place, while the medium itself only moves back and forth around where it was. Shake one end of a stretched rope once and a single bump, a pulse, runs along it; shake it steadily up and down (harmonic motion) and a sine wave runs along it.

        The medium stays put: a cork on the sea bobs up and down as waves pass under it, but isn't carried along. What travels is the shape of the disturbance and its energy.

        Why it matters: sound, water waves, earthquakes, light and radio are all waves; the same few ideas (wavelength, frequency, speed, interference) describe all of them.

        Transverse and longitudinal waves

        • Transverse: the medium moves across the direction the wave travels (a rope shaken up and down, light).
        • Longitudinal: the medium moves along it, in compressions and rarefactions (a spring pushed and pulled at one end, sound in air).

        Solids carry both; liquids and gases (deep inside) only longitudinal waves, because they can't resist being sheared. In an earthquake the longitudinal wave arrives first: it is faster.

        The superposition principle

        When two waves meet, the displacement at each point is the sum of the displacements each wave would cause alone.

        In words: two pulses running toward each other on a rope add up while they overlap (a tall bump if both are up; they may cancel if one is up and the other down), and then each continues on its way unchanged, as if the other had never been there.

        It explains interference, standing waves and beats, and lets us build any complicated wave as a sum of simple sine waves.

        2Describing a wave mathematically

        Amplitude, wavelength, period and frequency

        • v = λf = λ/T
        • f = 1/T   (Hz)

        The quantities (ψ, "psi", is the displacement of the medium from its rest position):

        • Amplitude A: the largest displacement, from the middle to a crest.
        • Wavelength λ: the distance between two neighbouring crests (or any two points in the same state).
        • Period T: the time for one full oscillation of a point; frequency f: oscillations per second.

        Why v = λf: in one period each point does one full oscillation and the wave moves on by exactly one wavelength. The frequency is set by the source; the speed by the medium; the wavelength follows from both.

        The displacement in space and time

        • ψ(x) = A sin(2π x/λ)   (a snapshot)
        • ψ(t) = A sin(2π t/T)   (one point)
        • ψ(x, t) = A sin(2π(x/λ − t/T))   (moving in +x)

        In words: a photograph of the wave at one moment is a sine of position, repeating every λ; one point watched over time does harmonic motion, repeating every T. Both together give the travelling wave: a minus sign between the two terms means it moves toward +x, a plus sign toward −x.

        Points half a wavelength apart are always opposite (one up when the other is down): they are out of phase by half a cycle.

        Wave speed, dispersion and group velocity

        • v = √(F₀/μ)   (a string: tension F₀, mass per length μ)
        • v = √((λg)/(2π))   (deep-water waves)

        On a string the speed depends only on the string: a tighter string (bigger force pulling each bit back) or a lighter one (less inertia) carries waves faster.

        Dispersion: in some media the speed depends on the wavelength; then a pulse made of many sine waves changes shape as it travels. On deep water long waves run faster, which is why the long swell of a distant storm reaches the beach first. Light in glass disperses too (a prism splits the colours).

        Group velocity: in a dispersive medium the "bunch" of waves (and the energy) moves at the group velocity, which can differ from the speed of the individual crests (the phase velocity).

        The wave equation of a string

        (∂²ψ)/(∂x²) = (1/(v²)) (∂²ψ)/(∂t²)

        In words: Newton's second law for a small bit of the string gives this equation: the curvature of the string (left) decides each bit's acceleration (right). The ∂ means a derivative with respect to one variable while the other is held fixed (a partial derivative).

        Its solutions are exactly the travelling waves: any shape f(x − vt) moving right and g(x + vt) moving left, and their sums, at the speed v = √(F₀/μ). The sine wave is the special case of a harmonic source.

        Energy and intensity; plane and spherical waves

        • I = P/A   (W/m²)
        • I = P/(4πr²)   (a point source in all directions)

        Energy: each bit of the medium oscillates harmonically, with energy (1/2)kA²; so the energy a wave carries is proportional to the square of its amplitude. Twice the amplitude, four times the energy.

        Intensity is the power passing through each square metre across the direction of travel. A plane wave (flat wavefronts) keeps its intensity. A spherical wave from a point source spreads its power over a sphere of area 4πr²: the intensity falls as 1/r², the amplitude as 1/r. A 100 W source gives about 0.88 W/m² at 3 m.

        Wavefronts are the surfaces of equal phase (all the crests); the waves travel perpendicular to them. Circular waves on water, spherical waves in air.

        3Sound

        The speed of sound

        • v = √(B/ρ)
        • B = −(ΔP)/((ΔV)/V)

        In words: sound is a longitudinal pressure wave. Its speed depends on how hard the medium is to squeeze (the bulk modulus B, the pressure change needed per fractional change of volume) and on its density ρ.

        Typical speeds: air about 331 m/s at 0°C and about 340 m/s at room temperature (faster when warmer); water about 1500 m/s; steel about 5000 m/s. Liquids and solids are much denser than air, but far harder to squeeze, and that wins.

        Counting a storm's distance: light arrives almost at once, thunder at about 340 m per second: 3 seconds between flash and bang is about 1 km.

        Loudness: the decibel scale

        β = 10 log(I/I₀)   (dB),   I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m²

        In words: the ear hears intensities from about 10⁻¹² W/m² (the threshold of hearing) to about 1 W/m² (pain): a range of a million million. So loudness is measured on a logarithmic scale (Powers & Logs): every factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB.

        Doubling the intensity (two equal sources instead of one) adds only about 3 dB, not double the decibels.

        Pitch and musical tones

        The pitch of a tone is its frequency: high notes, high frequency. The ear hears about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (less with age). A musical octave is a doubling of frequency: the A above middle C is 440 Hz, the next A 880 Hz.

        Why instruments sound different playing the same note: a string or pipe vibrates at its basic frequency and, at the same time, at whole multiples of it (the overtones, Standing waves). The mix of overtones, the timbre, differs from instrument to instrument.

        The scale: the notes of an octave are chosen with simple frequency ratios between them (9/8 for a whole tone, 16/15 for a semitone in the classic scale); instruments today divide the octave into 12 equal semitones.

        The Doppler effect

        • f' = f (v ± v_(D))/v   (listener moving at v_(D), source at rest)
        • f' = f v/(v ∓ v_(s))   (source moving at v_(s), listener at rest)

        In words: when the source and the listener approach each other the pitch heard is higher; when they move apart, lower. Upper signs: approaching; lower signs: moving apart. v is the speed of sound.

        Why: a listener moving toward the source meets the crests more often. A moving source chases its own waves ahead of it, squeezing them into a shorter wavelength in front (the picture) and stretching them behind. A passing ambulance's siren drops in pitch as it goes by.

        Uses: police radar, measuring blood flow, and (with light) the speeds of stars and galaxies.

        4Reflection and transmission

        Reflection at the end of a string

        • Fixed end (tied to a wall): the pulse comes back upside down: a phase change of half a cycle (180°). The wall pulls back on the string, making an inverted pulse.
        • Free end (a ring sliding on a pole): the pulse comes back the same way up.

        Why inverted at a fixed end: the end can't move, so its displacement must stay 0. Superposition makes that happen if an inverted pulse comes back: the incoming and returning pulses cancel exactly at the wall.

        A sine wave reflected from a fixed end runs back over the incoming one; the two together form a standing wave (next concept).

        Waves crossing into another medium

        Where two media meet (a thin string tied to a thick one, shallow water next to deep), part of the wave is reflected and part is transmitted into the second medium.

        • The frequency stays the same (each bit of the boundary is shaken at the incoming rate).
        • The speed changes (it belongs to the medium), so the wavelength changes: λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁.
        • Going into a slower (heavier) medium, the reflected part is inverted, as at a fixed end; into a faster one, it isn't.

        Refraction of waves

        (sin θ₁)/(sin θ₂) = v₁/v₂

        In words: a wave reaching the boundary at an angle changes direction as it crosses, because the part of each wavefront that enters first changes speed first. Angles are measured from the line perpendicular to the boundary (the normal). Entering a slower medium the wave bends toward the normal; a faster one, away from it. The reflected wave leaves at the same angle it came in.

        Example: water waves cross from deep water (2 m/s) into shallow water (1.2 m/s) at 40°: sin θ₂ = 0.6 sin 40° ≈ 0.386, θ₂ ≈ 22.7°. Waves approaching a beach turn to run in almost straight. The same law for light: Optics.

        5Standing waves

        What a standing wave is

        Two sine waves of the same frequency and amplitude running in opposite directions add up (superposition) to a wave that doesn't travel: a standing wave. Some points, the nodes, never move; between them, the antinodes swing with the largest amplitude.

        • node to node: λ/2;   node to antinode: λ/4

        No energy flows along it: it just sloshes back and forth between the nodes. Every point oscillates at the same frequency, but with an amplitude that depends on where it is.

        A string fixed at both ends

        • L = n λ/2   (n = 1, 2, 3, …)
        • f_(n) = n v/(2L) = n f₁,   v = √(F₀/μ)

        In words: both ends must be nodes, so only a whole number of half-wavelengths fits on the string: these are its modes (normal modes). The lowest, f₁ = v/(2L), is the fundamental; the others are its whole multiples, the harmonics.

        Tuning: a guitarist shortens the string with a finger (higher f) or tightens it (bigger F₀, higher f); thick strings (bigger μ) give low notes.

        Standing sound waves in pipes

        • open at both ends: f_(n) = n v/(2L),   n = 1, 2, 3, …
        • closed at one end: f_(n) = n v/(4L),   n = 1, 3, 5, …

        In words: in a pipe the air oscillates along it. At a closed end the air can't move (a node of motion); at an open end it moves freely (an antinode). An open pipe fits half-wavelengths like a string; a pipe closed at one end fits odd quarter-wavelengths, so its fundamental is an octave lower and only odd harmonics sound.

        Example (v = 340 m/s): a 0.5 m pipe open at both ends: f₁ = 340 Hz; closed at one end: 170 Hz. Organs, flutes and clarinets work this way.

        6Interference and diffraction

        Interference

        • constructive: Δr = nλ
        • destructive: Δr = (n + 1/2)λ,   n = 0, ±1, ±2, …

        In words: two waves of the same frequency from two sources (in step with each other) overlap. Where they arrive crest on crest they reinforce (constructive interference); crest on trough, they cancel (destructive). Which happens at a point depends on the path difference Δr: the difference between its distances from the two sources.

        Example: two loudspeakers in step, λ = 1 m; a listener 3 m from one and 4.5 m from the other: Δr = 1.5 m = 1.5λ, a quiet spot.

        Energy isn't lost: it is moved from the quiet places to the loud ones.

        Two slits

        • bright: d sin θ = nλ
        • dark: d sin θ = (n + 1/2)λ
        • small angles: fringe spacing Δy = λL/d

        In words: a plane wave through two narrow slits a distance d apart makes them two sources in step. Toward a far point at angle θ, the ray from B is longer by d sin θ: whole wavelengths give bright fringes, half-wavelengths dark ones. On a screen at distance L the fringes are evenly spaced.

        Example: d = 0.5 mm, λ = 600 nm, L = 2 m: Δy = 2.4 mm. For light this is Young's experiment, the proof that light is a wave (Optics).

        Diffraction

        Diffraction is the spreading of a wave around obstacles and through openings, into the "shadow" region. Huygens' principle explains it: every point of a wavefront acts as a small source of circular waves, and the new wavefront is their common envelope.

        • Opening much smaller than λ: it acts like a single point source: the wave spreads out in circles in all forward directions.
        • Opening a few wavelengths wide: the waves from different parts of the opening interfere: a strong central beam with weaker side lobes (dark directions where b sin θ = nλ, b the width).
        • Opening much wider than λ: the wave goes straight through with a sharp shadow; diffraction only blurs the edges.

        So we hear around corners (sound: wavelengths of metres) but don't see around them (light: under a micrometre).

        1Light as a wave

        The speed of light

        • c = 299 792 458 m/s ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s
        • in a material: v = c/n

        In words: light in empty space travels at c, about 300 000 km every second: from the Sun to us in about 8 minutes. In air it is very slightly slower; in water or glass noticeably slower (n, the refractive index, in Reflection and refraction).

        How it was measured: Rømer (1676) from the timing of Jupiter's moons; Fizeau and Foucault in the 1800s with fast-turning wheels and mirrors on Earth; Michelson to high precision. Since 1983 the value is exact: the metre is defined from it.

        Particle or wave?

        Newton (1704) thought light was a stream of tiny particles; Huygens, his contemporary, that it was a wave. Both explained reflection and refraction. The wave view won when interference of light was shown: Young's two-slit experiment (about 1801) gives bright and dark fringes, which particles can't do (Physical optics).

        Why light doesn't seem to bend around corners like sound: its wavelength is tiny (under a millionth of a metre), so diffraction only shows at very small openings (Waves, Interference and diffraction).

        The story isn't over: in the 20th century light turned out to also come in packets, photons (Modern physics).

        Electromagnetic waves and the spectrum

        In words: Maxwell (1860s) showed from the laws of electricity and magnetism that changing electric and magnetic fields can travel through space as a wave, at a speed 1/√(μ₀ε₀) that came out equal to the speed of light. So light is an electromagnetic wave. Hertz (1887) made such waves with electric circuits: radio.

        The spectrum: all electromagnetic waves travel at c in vacuum (c = λf) and differ only in wavelength. Visible light is a narrow band, about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Radio waves are metres to kilometres long; X-rays and gamma rays far shorter than atoms.

        2Reflection and refraction

        The laws of reflection and refraction

        • θ₁ = θ₃   (reflection)
        • n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂   (refraction, Snell's law)

        In words: light treated as straight rays (geometric optics, fine when everything is much bigger than the wavelength). At a boundary part of the light bounces back at the same angle, and part goes in, bending: toward the normal entering a denser medium (bigger n), away from it leaving. All angles are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the surface, and all three rays lie in one plane.

        Example: light from air at 42° into crown glass (n = 1.52): sin θ₂ = sin 42°/1.52 ≈ 0.440, θ₂ ≈ 26.1°.

        The refractive index

        n = c/v

        In words: the refractive index says how many times slower light is in a material than in vacuum, which is why it bends at the boundary (Refraction of waves, Waves). It has no units, and is 1 for vacuum.

        Dispersion: n depends slightly on the wavelength (bigger for violet than for red), so a prism spreads white light into its colours, and raindrops make rainbows.

        Total internal reflection

        sin θ_(c) = n₂/n₁   (from the denser medium n₁ to n₂ < n₁)

        In words: going from glass or water into air, the ray bends away from the normal. At the critical angle θ_(c) the refracted ray skims along the surface (θ₂ = 90°); beyond it no light gets out at all: it is totally reflected, with no loss.

        Values: water to air 48.8°, glass to air about 41°, diamond to air 24.4° (that small angle traps light inside a cut diamond and makes it sparkle).

        Uses: prisms in binoculars and periscopes (a 45° prism reflects better than a mirror); optical fibres, thin glass threads that guide light along their length by bouncing it off their walls, carrying telephone and internet signals and letting doctors see inside the body.

        Plane mirrors

        A flat mirror forms an image behind it, as far behind as the object is in front, the same size and the same way up, but left and right swapped. The image is virtual: the reflected rays only seem to come from it; no light is really there, so it can't be caught on a screen.

        Why: by the law of reflection, all the rays from a point of the object leave the mirror as if they came from one point behind it.

        3Spherical mirrors and lenses

        The mirror and lens equation

        • 1/s + 1/p = 1/f
        • m = −p/s

        In words: s is the object's distance from the mirror or lens, p the image's, f the focal length, and m the magnification (image height over object height). The same equation serves mirrors and thin lenses, with these signs:

        • f > 0 for a converging mirror or lens (concave mirror, convex lens); f < 0 for a diverging one.
        • p > 0: a real image (light really meets there; it can be caught on a screen). p < 0: a virtual image.
        • m < 0: the image is upside down; |m| > 1: bigger than the object.

        Spherical mirrors

        f = R/2

        In words: a concave mirror (curved inward, like the inside of a spoon) gathers rays parallel to its axis at the focus F, halfway to the centre of curvature C. A convex mirror spreads them as if from a focus behind it (f < 0).

        Drawing the image takes two of these rays from the object's tip: parallel to the axis → reflected through F; through F → reflected parallel; through C → straight back. Where they meet (or seem to meet) is the image.

        What you get: concave, object beyond F: a real, inverted image (make-up mirrors far away, telescopes). Object inside F: a virtual, upright, magnified image (a shaving mirror close up). Convex: always virtual, upright and smaller, but a wide view (car mirrors, shop mirrors).

        Thin lenses

        • 1/f = (n − 1)(1/(R₁) + 1/(R₂))   (lens maker's formula)
        • D = 1/f   (power, in diopters, f in metres)

        In words: a lens thicker in the middle (convex) is converging; thinner in the middle (concave), diverging. R₁, R₂ are the radii of its two faces (positive for a face bulging outward), n the glass's index: more curved faces or denser glass give a shorter focal length.

        The three rays (the picture): parallel to the axis → through the far focus F₂; through the centre → straight on; through the near focus F₁ → out parallel.

        Example: f = 10 cm, object at 15 cm: 1/p = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, a real image 30 cm behind the lens, m = −2: inverted and twice as big (a projector). Object at 5 cm (inside F): p = −10 cm, m = +2: a virtual, upright magnified image (a magnifying glass).

        4Optical instruments

        The camera and the eye

        A camera is a converging lens that forms a real, inverted, small image on a sensor (or film). Focusing means moving the lens to change p for objects at different distances; the aperture controls how much light enters.

        The eye works the same way: the cornea and lens form an image on the retina. Instead of moving the lens, muscles change its shape (its focal length) to focus near or far (accommodation).

        • Near-sighted (myopia): far objects focus in front of the retina; corrected with diverging lenses.
        • Far-sighted (hyperopia, and with age): near objects focus behind it; corrected with converging lenses. Glasses are labelled by their power in diopters.

        The magnifying glass and the microscope

        • M = d/f   (magnifier, d ≈ 25 cm)
        • M = m₁ M₂   (microscope)

        A magnifying glass is a converging lens held so the object is just inside its focus: you see a virtual, upright, enlarged image. What counts is the angular magnification M: how much bigger the object looks than at the nearest comfortable reading distance d ≈ 25 cm. With f = 5 cm, M = 5.

        A microscope uses two converging lenses: the objective (very short focal length) makes a real, enlarged image m₁ times the object; the eyepiece then works as a magnifier on that image, M₂. The total magnification is their product.

        Telescopes

        M = f₁/f₂

        In words: a telescope also has two converging lenses, but the objective has a long focal length f₁ and the eyepiece a short one f₂; the lenses sit f₁ + f₂ apart. The objective forms a small real image of a far object; the eyepiece magnifies it. The angular magnification is the ratio of the focal lengths: f₁ = 100 cm, f₂ = 2.5 cm gives 40.

        A big objective also gathers more light (faint stars). Large astronomical telescopes use a concave mirror instead of the objective lens. Binoculars are two short telescopes with prisms that turn the image upright.

        5Physical optics

        Two slits and the diffraction grating

        • bright: d sin θ = nλ,   n = 0, ±1, ±2, …
        • dark (two slits): d sin θ = (n + 1/2)λ

        Two slits (Young): light must be coherent (the two slits fed by the same wave) and preferably of one colour (monochromatic); then bright and dark fringes appear, as for any waves (Waves, Two slits).

        A diffraction grating has thousands of equally spaced slits (d apart). The bright lines fall at the same angles as for two slits, but are much sharper and brighter. Since the angle depends on λ, a grating spreads white light into a spectrum of each order; a spectroscope uses this to measure wavelengths and identify the elements in a light source.

        Example: 500 lines per mm (d = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m), λ = 600 nm: sin θ = 0.3, 0.6, 0.9 for n = 1, 2, 3 (about 17.5°, 36.9°, 64.2°); no 4th order, since the sine can't exceed 1.

        Thin films

        • dark (destructive): 2d = (λ/n) m
        • bright (constructive): 2d = (λ/n)(m + 1/2),   m = 0, 1, 2, …

        In words: light reflected from the top and from the bottom of a thin film (a soap bubble, oil on water) interferes. The second ray travels an extra 2d inside the film, where the wavelength is λ/n; the reflection off the top (into a denser medium) also flips it by half a wave. These formulas are for a film surrounded by a less dense medium (a soap film in air).

        Colours: with white light, different thicknesses reinforce different colours, so bubbles and oil slicks shimmer. The thinnest soap film bright in 600 nm light: d = λ/(4n) = 600/(4 · 1.33) ≈ 113 nm. The same effect makes anti-reflection coatings on lenses, and measures tiny thicknesses (interferometers).

        Diffraction and resolution

        Light passing a narrow slit (width b) spreads: a bright central band with dark directions at b sin θ = nλ. The narrower the slit, the wider the spread.

        Why it matters: every lens and the pupil of the eye is an opening, so the image of a point is always a small blurred spot. Two points closer than about that blur can't be told apart: diffraction limits the resolution of every microscope and telescope. A bigger lens (or a shorter wavelength) sees finer detail.

        Polarization

        Light is a transverse wave: its electric field oscillates across the direction of travel. In ordinary light that direction changes at random; in polarized light it stays in one plane.

        A polarizing filter lets through only the light oscillating along its axis. Two filters at right angles block everything. Light reflected off water or a road is partly polarized, so polarizing sunglasses cut the glare. Sound, a longitudinal wave, can't be polarized: polarization is a proof that light is transverse.

        1Electric charge

        Two kinds of charge

        Rub a plastic rod with wool and it attracts bits of paper: it has an electric charge. There are two kinds, called positive and negative. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.

        Where charge comes from: atoms have a small, positive nucleus (protons, with neutrons) surrounded by negative electrons; a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons. Rubbing moves some electrons from one body to the other: the one that gains electrons becomes negative, the other positive.

        History: electricity was a curiosity of rubbed amber until the 1700s; Galvani's frog legs and Volta's first battery (about 1800) led to electric currents, and Maxwell (1864) united electricity, magnetism and light in four equations.

        Conservation and quantization of charge

        • e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
        • q = Ne,   N a whole number

        Conservation: charge is never created or destroyed; the total charge of a closed system stays the same. Rubbing only moves it around.

        Quantization: every charge is a whole multiple of the elementary charge e, the size of the electron's charge (electron −e, proton +e). The SI unit is the coulomb (C), about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons' worth: a huge charge; static charges are usually micro- or nanocoulombs.

        Conductors and insulators

        In a conductor (metals, salt water) some charges move freely: in a metal, the outer electrons of each atom wander through the whole piece. In an insulator (plastic, glass, dry air) every charge stays near its atom.

        • Charging by contact: touch a charged body to a conductor and charge spreads onto it.
        • Induction: bring a charged rod near a conductor without touching: its free electrons shift, one side becomes positive, the other negative. That is why a charged rod attracts a neutral object.
        • Grounding: the Earth is a huge conductor that can give or take any amount of charge.

        2Coulomb's law and the electric field

        Coulomb's law

        • F = k (q₁q₂)/(r²) = 1/(4πε₀) (q₁q₂)/(r²)
        • k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²,   ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²)

        In words: two point charges push or pull each other along the line between them, with a force proportional to both charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance, just like gravity (Gravitation, Mechanics) but much stronger, and it can repel. ε₀ is the permittivity of free space.

        Example: 2 μC and −3 μC 0.3 m apart: F = 9 × 10⁹ · 6 × 10⁻¹²/0.09 = 0.6 N, attractive.

        Several charges: the forces add as vectors (superposition): find each one separately, then add the components.

        The electric field

        • E⃗ = F⃗/q   (N/C)
        • a point charge: E = k q/(r²)

        In words: a charge changes the space around it: any other charge q placed there feels a force qE⃗. The electric field E⃗ is the force per unit of (positive) test charge at each point. It points away from positive charges and toward negative ones, and fields of several charges add as vectors.

        Why a field: it lets us split a problem into two steps: what the charges create (the field), and what the field does to a charge put there. The field is real: it carries energy, and changing fields travel as light (Optics).

        Field lines

        In words: lines drawn so that at every point the field is along the line (tangent to it), pointing the way the arrows go. They start on positive charges and end on negative ones (or go to infinity), and never cross.

        Their density shows the strength: where the lines crowd together the field is strong; spread out, weak. Around a point charge they spread out like the spokes of a wheel, and their density falls as 1/r², exactly like the field. Between two opposite charges they curve from one to the other; between two like charges they push apart.

        Fields of extended charges

        • long straight line, charge λ per metre: E = λ/(2πε₀r)
        • large flat sheet, charge σ per m²: E = σ/(2ε₀)

        In words: a charge spread along a line or over a surface is cut into tiny pieces, each a point charge; their fields are added by integration (Integrals). By symmetry, the field of a long line points straight away from it and weakens only as 1/r; that of a large sheet is the same at every distance. Gauss's law gives these quickly.

        A charge in a uniform field

        In words: between two parallel charged plates the field is uniform (the same everywhere). A charge there feels a constant force qE, so a constant acceleration qE/m: it moves exactly like a ball thrown in gravity (Projectiles, Mechanics), along a parabola. An electron, being negative, is pushed against the field, toward the positive plate.

        Uses: this is how an oscilloscope (and the old TV tube) steers its electron beam to draw on the screen.

        3Gauss's law

        Electric flux

        • Φ = EA cos θ = E⃗ · A⃗
        • Φ = ∫_(A) E⃗ · dA⃗

        In words: the flux through a surface measures how much field passes through it: in the picture of field lines, the number of lines crossing it. A⃗ is a vector perpendicular to the surface with length equal to its area; θ is the angle between the field and that perpendicular. A field along the surface gives no flux. For a curved surface in a varying field, cut it into small pieces and add (integrate).

        Closed surfaces: the perpendicular is taken outward, so lines leaving count positive and lines entering negative.

        Gauss's law

        Φ = Q/ε₀   (Q the total charge inside the closed surface)

        In words: the total flux out of any closed surface depends only on the charge enclosed. Charges outside contribute nothing: every line that enters also leaves. It is one of Maxwell's four equations, equivalent to Coulomb's law, and the easy way to find the field when there is a lot of symmetry.

        How it is used: choose an imaginary closed surface (a Gaussian surface) on which, by symmetry, the field has the same size everywhere and is perpendicular to it. Then Φ = EA, and E = Q/(ε₀A).

        Fields from Gauss's law

        • outside a charged sphere: E = Q/(4πε₀r²)   (as if all at the centre)
        • inside a charged spherical shell: E = 0
        • infinite line: E = λ/(2πε₀r);   infinite plane: E = σ/(2ε₀)

        The sphere: a Gaussian sphere of radius r around it: E · 4πr² = Q/ε₀. Inside a hollow charged shell a Gaussian sphere encloses no charge, so there is no field at all.

        The line: a Gaussian cylinder of radius r and length L around it: E · 2πrL = λL/ε₀. The plane: a box sticking through it, with flux through its two ends: 2EA = σA/ε₀.

        Conductors in electrostatics

        • Inside a conductor in equilibrium the field is zero (otherwise its free charges would still be moving).
        • Any extra charge sits on the surface (a Gaussian surface just inside encloses none).
        • Just outside, the field is perpendicular to the surface, with size σ/ε₀; charge crowds at sharp points, where the field is strongest (lightning rods).

        Shielding: a closed metal box keeps outside fields out (a Faraday cage): you are safe in a car struck by lightning, and a phone in a metal box loses signal.

        4Energy and potential

        Electric potential energy

        U = k (qQ)/r

        In words: the electric force is conservative (like gravity): the work to move a charge from one place to another doesn't depend on the path. So a charge in a field has potential energy. For two point charges it is k q Q/r, with zero when they are far apart; positive for like charges (work was needed to push them together), negative for unlike ones.

        Energy is conserved: a charge released in a field gains kinetic energy as it loses potential energy.

        Electric potential and voltage

        • V = U/q   (volt, 1 V = 1 J/C)
        • point charge: V = k Q/r;   several: V = k ∑ (Q_(i))/(r_(i))
        • W = qΔV

        In words: the potential at a point is the potential energy per unit charge there: a property of the place, set by the surrounding charges. The potential difference (voltage) between two points is the work per coulomb to carry a charge between them. Potentials are numbers (scalars), so several charges' potentials simply add, which is easier than adding fields.

        The electron-volt: the energy an electron gains crossing 1 V, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. An electron accelerated through 1000 V reaches about 1.9 × 10⁷ m/s.

        Field and potential

        • E = −(dV)/(dx)
        • uniform field: V = Ed

        In words: the field points "downhill" in potential, from high to low, and is as strong as the potential changes per metre. That's why the unit of field is also V/m. Between two plates d apart with a voltage V across them, E = V/d: 400 V across 2 cm is 2 × 10⁴ V/m.

        Equipotential surfaces connect points of equal potential; they cut the field lines at right angles, and moving a charge along one takes no work. Around a point charge they are spheres; between parallel plates, planes. A conductor's whole body is one equipotential.

        5Capacitance and energy of a charged conductor

        Capacitance
