        • C = Q/V   (farad, 1 F = 1 C/V)
        • a conducting sphere: C = 4πε₀R

        In words: charging a conductor raises its potential in proportion to the charge; the ratio, the capacitance, says how much charge it holds per volt. It depends only on its size and shape. A metal ball of radius 10 cm has about 11 pF; even the whole Earth only about 7 × 10⁻⁴ F: a farad is huge.

        Capacitors (two conductors close together, Direct current) reach far bigger capacitances.

        The energy of a charged conductor

        W = (1/2)QV = (Q²)/(2C) = (1/2)CV²

        In words: charging a conductor takes work, because each new bit of charge is pushed onto charge already there. Since the potential grows from 0 to V during the charging, the average is half of it, hence the 1/2. The work is stored in the electric field around the conductor.

        Example: the 10 cm ball charged to 10 kV holds Q = 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ C and about 5.6 × 10⁻⁴ J. A Van de Graaff generator builds up such charges by carrying them on a moving belt into a large metal sphere.

        6Current, resistance and Ohm's law

        Electric current

        • I = Q/t,   I = (dq)/(dt)   (ampere, 1 A = 1 C/s)

        In words: an electric current is charge flowing: the amount of charge passing through a cross-section of the wire each second. In a metal wire it is electrons drifting; in salt water or a battery, ions. A current of 25 mA carries about 1.6 × 10¹⁷ electrons a second.

        Direction: by convention the current flows the way positive charges would move: from the high-potential end to the low one, out of the battery's + terminal. Electrons actually move the other way, but in almost every calculation it doesn't matter.

        Direct current (DC) keeps one direction and size (a battery); alternating current comes later.

        Ohm's law and resistance

        • I = V/R,   V = IR   (ohm, 1 Ω = 1 V/A)
        • R = ρL/A   (a wire: resistivity ρ, length L, area A)

        In words: in a metal conductor the current is proportional to the voltage across it (Ohm, 1827); the constant ratio is its resistance R. 12 V driving 60 mA through a wire means R = 200 Ω.

        What resistance depends on: a longer wire resists more, a thicker one less, and the material counts through its resistivity ρ (copper about 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m): 10 m of copper wire 1 mm² thick has 0.17 Ω. Resistance usually grows with temperature.

        Not a law of nature: Ohm's law holds for metals (at a steady temperature), not for diodes, lamps that heat up, or gases. A device obeying it is called ohmic.

        Conduction in materials

        • Metals: free electrons; the field drives them, collisions with the vibrating atoms hold them back. Their average drift is slow (fractions of a millimetre per second), though the field travels almost at light speed.
        • Semiconductors (silicon, germanium): few free electrons; adding traces of other elements (doping) controls the conduction. The basis of diodes, transistors and chips.
        • Superconductors: some materials, cooled far enough, lose all resistance.
        • Liquids (electrolysis) and gases (sparks, neon lamps) conduct by moving ions.

        7DC circuits

        Resistors in series and in parallel

        • series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …
        • parallel: 1/R = 1/(R₁) + 1/(R₂) + …

        Series (one after the other): the same current flows through each, and the voltages add, so the resistances add: the total is bigger than any one.

        Parallel (side by side between the same two points): each has the same voltage, and the currents add, so the reciprocals add: the total is smaller than the smallest. Two in parallel: R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Household devices are in parallel, so each gets the full voltage.

        Example: 6 Ω and 12 Ω on 1.5 V: in series 18 Ω, I ≈ 0.083 A; in parallel 4 Ω, 0.375 A (0.25 A through the 6 Ω, 0.125 A through the 12 Ω).

        Electromotive force and internal resistance

        • ε = W/q
        • I = ε/(R + r),   V = ε − Ir

        In words: a battery or generator pushes charge around a circuit, doing work W on each charge q; its electromotive force (emf, ε) is that work per coulomb, in volts. Inside, the source has its own internal resistance r, so the voltage at its terminals drops when it delivers current. Only with no current is V = ε.

        Example: a 12 V battery with r = 0.5 Ω on a 5.5 Ω load: I = 2 A, terminal voltage 11 V. Cells in series add their emfs and their internal resistances; identical cells in parallel keep the emf and share the current.

        Kirchhoff's rules

        • Junction rule: the currents into any junction add up to the currents out: ∑ I = 0 (charge is conserved).
        • Loop rule: around any closed loop, the voltage changes add up to zero; equivalently, the emfs equal the IR drops: ∑ ε = ∑ IR (energy is conserved).

        Why: charge can't pile up at a junction, and a charge that goes round a loop comes back to the same potential. These two rules solve any circuit, even when series and parallel don't apply (two batteries in different branches). Choose a direction for each current; a negative answer means it flows the other way.

        Measuring: ammeters and voltmeters

        An ammeter measures the current through a branch and goes in series with it; it must have a very small resistance so it doesn't change the current. A voltmeter measures the voltage between two points and goes in parallel with them; it must have a very large resistance so it draws almost no current.

        8Power in a circuit

        Electric power

        • P = IV
        • a resistor: P = I²R = (V²)/R

        In words: each coulomb crossing a voltage V gives up the energy V joules; I coulombs cross per second, so the power is IV. In a resistor that energy becomes heat (Joule heating): a heater, a toaster, a light bulb filament. A source supplies Iε, of which I²r is lost inside it.

        Example: a 60 W lamp on 230 V draws 60/230 ≈ 0.26 A and has R = 230²/60 ≈ 882 Ω when lit.

        Energy bills count kilowatt-hours: a 2 kW heater for 3 hours uses 6 kWh (Power, Mechanics).

        Why power lines use high voltage

        The power sent is IV; the loss in the wires is I²R. Sending the same power at a higher voltage needs a smaller current, and the loss drops with its square: ten times the voltage, a hundredth of the loss. That is why electricity travels at hundreds of kilovolts and is stepped down near homes (transformers, Alternating current).

        9Capacitors and dielectrics

        The parallel-plate capacitor

        • C = Q/V
        • C = ε₀ A/d

        In words: a capacitor is two conductors close together, charged +Q and −Q. For two flat plates of area A a distance d apart, the field between them is uniform, E = σ/ε₀, and V = Ed, which gives C = ε₀A/d: big plates close together hold a lot. Plates of 0.01 m² 5 mm apart: about 18 pF.

        Uses: storing energy (a camera flash), smoothing voltages, timing circuits, tuning radios.

        Capacitors in series and in parallel

        • parallel: C = C₁ + C₂ + …
        • series: 1/C = 1/(C₁) + 1/(C₂) + …

        In words: the opposite of resistors. In parallel they share the voltage and their charges add, so the capacitances add (like one bigger plate). In series each carries the same charge and the voltages add, so the reciprocals add: 2, 3, 6 μF in series make 1 μF; in parallel 11 μF.

        Energy stored in a capacitor

        • W = (1/2)QV = (1/2)CV² = (Q²)/(2C)
        • energy per volume of field: u = (1/2)ε₀E²

        In words: moving each new bit of charge dq across the growing voltage q/C takes work dW = (q/C)dq; adding it all up (the area under the straight line V against q) gives Q²/(2C). The energy is stored in the field between the plates.

        Dielectrics

        • C = κC₀ = κε₀ A/d
        • at a fixed charge: V = V₀/κ, E = E₀/κ

        In words: filling the gap with an insulator (a dielectric) raises the capacitance by its dielectric constant κ: glass about 4–6, water about 80, air practically 1. The field polarizes the material's molecules (their charges shift slightly), which weakens the field inside and so lowers the voltage for the same charge.

        The same effect explains why a charged comb attracts a neutral scrap of paper: it polarizes it, and the near side is pulled harder than the far side is pushed.

        Charging and discharging through a resistor

        • discharging: q(t) = Q e^(−t/(RC))
        • charging: q(t) = Cε(1 − e^(−t/(RC)))

        In words: a capacitor doesn't charge or empty at once: the current through the resistor is large at first and dies away. The charge changes exponentially (Powers & Logs) with the time constant τ = RC: after one RC a discharging capacitor keeps about 37% of its charge (a charging one reaches about 63%). R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 μF: τ = 1 s.

        10The magnetic field and moving charges

        Magnets and the magnetic field

        Every magnet has a north and a south pole; like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Cutting a magnet in two gives two smaller magnets: a single pole has never been found.

        The magnetic field B⃗ fills the space around a magnet. A small compass needle turns to point along it; field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole. The Earth is a huge magnet, which is why a compass points (roughly) north.

        The source of all magnetism is moving charge (Ørsted, 1820: a current turns a compass). In a magnet it is the electrons' motion and spin (Magnetic fields in matter).

        The force on a moving charge

        • F⃗ = q v⃗ × B⃗
        • F = q v B sin θ   (tesla, 1 T = 1 N/(A·m))

        In words: a magnetic field pushes only on moving charges, and sideways: the force is perpendicular both to the velocity and to the field (the cross product, Scalar and vector products). A charge moving along the field feels nothing. For a negative charge the force is reversed.

        Sizes: the Earth's field is about 10⁻⁴ T (1 gauss); a fridge magnet about 10⁻² T; strong lab magnets a few tesla.

        It does no work: the force is always across the motion, so it can bend a path but never change the speed.

        Circular motion in a magnetic field

        • R = (mv)/(qB)
        • T = (2πm)/(qB)

        In words: a charge moving across a uniform field feels a force of constant size, always toward one centre: it goes round a circle (Circular motion, Mechanics: q v B = mv²/R). Faster or heavier particles make bigger circles; the time for one round doesn't depend on the speed.

        Uses: a mass spectrometer sorts ions by their radius (so by their mass); cyclotrons accelerate particles round and round. A proton at 2 × 10⁶ m/s in 0.5 T circles with R ≈ 4.2 cm.

        11Forces on currents

        The force on a current-carrying wire

        • F⃗ = I L⃗ × B⃗
        • F = I L B sin θ

        In words: a current is moving charge, so a wire carrying current I in a field feels the sum of the forces on all its charges. L⃗ points along the wire, in the current's direction. A 0.2 m wire carrying 5 A across a 0.4 T field: F = 0.4 N.

        Direction (right-hand rule): fingers along I, curl them toward B⃗; the thumb gives the force.

        The torque on a coil: motors and meters

        N = N I A B sin θ   (N turns, area A)

        In words: in a field, the two sides of a current loop are pushed in opposite directions, so the loop turns until its plane is perpendicular to the field. The torque is largest when the plane is along the field. A 100-turn coil of 5 cm × 10 cm with 2 A in 0.3 T: up to 0.3 N·m.

        Uses: an electric motor reverses the current every half turn (a commutator) so the coil keeps turning; a moving-coil meter turns against a spring by an amount proportional to the current. A loop behaves like a small magnet (a magnetic dipole).

        12The magnetic field of a current

        A long straight wire

        • B = (μ₀I)/(2πr)
        • μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A

        In words: the field lines of a straight current are circles around the wire, getting weaker as 1/r. Right-hand rule: thumb along the current, the fingers curl the way the field goes. 10 A, 5 cm away: B = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T, about the Earth's field.

        Where it comes from: the Biot–Savart law gives the field of each small piece of wire; adding them along a long wire gives this result.

        A loop and a solenoid

        • centre of a circular loop: B = (μ₀I)/(2R)
        • inside a long solenoid: B = μ₀nI   (n turns per metre)

        A solenoid (a long coil) makes a strong, uniform field inside, along its axis, and almost none outside: like a bar magnet with poles at its ends. 1000 turns per metre with 2 A: B ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻³ T. With an iron core inside it is an electromagnet, many times stronger.

        Ampère's law

        ∮ B⃗ · dl⃗ = μ₀I   (I the current through the loop)

        In words: going round any closed path, the sum of the field along the path equals μ₀ times the current passing through it. It plays the role Gauss's law plays for electric fields: with symmetry it gives the field at once. A circle of radius r around a wire: B · 2πr = μ₀I, the wire's formula. A rectangle half inside a solenoid: BL = μ₀n L I.

        The force between two currents

        F/L = (μ₀I₁I₂)/(2πd)

        In words: each wire sits in the other's field. Parallel currents attract; opposite currents repel (the reverse of charges). 10 A and 20 A, 10 cm apart: 4 × 10⁻⁴ N per metre.

        The ampere was defined this way: the current that gives 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre between two wires 1 m apart.

        13Electromagnetic induction

        Magnetic flux

        • φ_(B) = BA cos α   (weber, 1 Wb = 1 T·m²)
        • φ_(B) = ∫ B⃗ · dA⃗

        In words: the magnetic flux through a surface measures how much field passes through it, exactly like the electric flux (Gauss's law): field times area times the cosine of the angle between the field and the surface's perpendicular.

        Faraday's law and Lenz's law

        • ε = −(dφ_(B))/(dt)   (a coil of N turns: × N)
        • I = ε/R

        In words: whenever the magnetic flux through a loop changes, an emf appears around the loop, equal to how fast the flux changes (Faraday, 1831). It doesn't matter how: moving a magnet, changing a current nearby, turning or stretching the loop.

        Lenz's law (the minus sign): the induced current flows so that its own field opposes the change that made it. Push a magnet's north pole toward a coil and the coil's near end becomes a north pole, pushing back. Otherwise energy would come from nothing.

        Example: a 200-turn coil of 0.01 m² while the field drops from 0.5 T to 0.1 T in 0.2 s: ε = 200 · 0.4 · 0.01/0.2 = 4 V.

        Motional emf and the generator

        • a rod sliding across a field: ε = B L v
        • a coil turning at ω: ε = N B Aω sin ωt

        In words: a conducting rod moving through a field has its charges pushed along it (q v B), so an emf appears: 0.5 m at 3 m/s in 0.4 T gives 0.6 V. A coil turning in a field sees its flux go up and down: a sine-shaped emf. That is the generator, the source of almost all our electricity: mechanical energy (steam, water, wind) turned into electrical energy.

        Example: 100 turns, 0.02 m², 0.2 T, 50 turns a second: peak emf ≈ 126 V.

        Self-inductance and eddy currents

        A coil's own changing current changes its own flux, so it induces an emf in itself that opposes the change: ε = −L dI/dt, L the inductance (henry). A coil resists sudden changes of current, the way mass resists sudden changes of velocity; it stores energy (1/2)LI² in its field.

        Eddy currents: a changing field induces swirling currents in any nearby metal; they heat it (induction cookers) and brake moving metal (train brakes). Transformer cores are made of thin insulated sheets to stop them.

        14Alternating current

        AC voltage and current, rms values

        • V(t) = V₀ sin ωt,   I(t) = I₀ sin ωt
        • V_(rms) = V₀/√2 ≈ 0.707 V₀,   I_(rms) = I₀/√2
        • P_(av) = I_(rms)V_(rms) = (1/2)I₀V₀

        In words: a generator gives a voltage that swings back and forth as a sine, and the current through a resistor follows it. The rms ("root mean square") value is the steady DC value that would deliver the same average power; with rms values the DC formulas V = IR and P = IV = I²R = V²/R still hold for resistors.

        Household electricity: "230 V" is the rms value; the peak is 230 √2 ≈ 325 V, alternating 50 times a second (60 in some countries). A 50 Ω heater on it uses about 1060 W.

        The transformer

        • V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁
        • I₁V₁ = I₂V₂   (ideal)

        In words: two coils on one iron core. The alternating current in the first makes a changing flux, which induces a voltage in the second (Faraday's law) in proportion to the turns. Few turns on the second coil step the voltage down; many turns step it up. The power in and out is nearly the same, so stepping the voltage up steps the current down.

        Example: 230 V into 1000 turns, 50 turns out: 11.5 V; a 2 A load there draws only 0.1 A from the mains. Transformers only work with AC (a steady current gives no changing flux): that's why the grid is AC (Why power lines use high voltage).

        Coils and capacitors in AC circuits

        A capacitor blocks steady current but passes AC: it lets more through at higher frequencies. A coil passes steady current easily but resists fast changes: it lets less through at higher frequencies. In both, the current and voltage are out of step by a quarter cycle, and on average they use no power.

        Together (an LC circuit) they resonate: energy sloshes between the capacitor's field and the coil's at f = 1/(2π√(LC)), like a mass on a spring. Tuning a radio means adjusting C so that this frequency matches the station.

        15Electromagnetic waves and magnetism in matter

        Maxwell's equations and electromagnetic waves

        • c = 1/(√(μ₀ε₀)) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s
        • E = cB,   c = λf

        In words: four laws describe all of electricity and magnetism: Gauss's law for E⃗, Gauss's law for B⃗ (no single poles), Faraday's law (a changing B⃗ makes E⃗), and Ampère's law completed by Maxwell (a changing E⃗ also makes B⃗). Together they allow fields that keep each other going and travel through empty space: an electromagnetic wave, at a speed that comes out exactly c, the speed of light.

        The wave: E⃗ and B⃗ oscillate at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel (a transverse wave), in step. Any accelerating charge sends one out: an antenna drives electrons up and down to broadcast. FM radio at 100 MHz has λ = 3 m. The spectrum: Electromagnetic waves and the spectrum (Optics).

        Magnetic fields in matter

        • Diamagnetic materials (water, copper) are weakly pushed out of a field.
        • Paramagnetic materials (aluminium, oxygen) are weakly pulled in: their atoms are tiny magnets that partly line up with the field.
        • Ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) are strongly pulled: their atomic magnets line up together in regions (domains), and can stay lined up: a permanent magnet. Heating above a certain temperature (the Curie point) destroys it.

        The atomic magnets come from the electrons' orbits and their spin (Modern physics).

        1The structure of matter

        Atoms, elements and molecules

        All matter is made of atoms. A substance made of one kind of atom is an element (about 92 occur in nature: hydrogen, carbon, iron…). Atoms join into molecules: water is two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, H₂O.

        How we know: chemists found that elements always combine in fixed whole-number proportions (Dalton, about 1808), which only makes sense if matter comes in small, identical pieces. Brownian motion (pollen grains jittering in water, explained by Einstein in 1905) showed the molecules' blows directly.

        Sizes: an atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m across; a water molecule has a mass of about 3 × 10⁻²⁶ kg.

        The mole and Avogadro's number

        • N_(A) = 6.022 × 10²³ per mole
        • n = m/M   (moles = mass ÷ molar mass)

        In words: a mole is a fixed number of particles, N_(A), chosen so that a mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its molecular (or atomic) mass: 12 g of carbon, 18 g of water, 32 g of oxygen gas O₂. It lets us count atoms by weighing.

        Example: 18 g of water is 1 mol, 6.0 × 10²³ molecules; each has a mass of 0.018/N_(A) ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg.

        2The kinetic theory of gases

        The gas laws and absolute temperature

        • PV/T = const   (a fixed amount of gas)
        • PV = n R T,   R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
        • T(K) = t(°C) + 273

        In words: for a gas, squeezing it at a steady temperature raises its pressure in proportion (Boyle); heating it at a steady volume raises its pressure in proportion to the absolute temperature (Charles, Gay-Lussac). Together: the ideal gas law. Extending the straight lines back, the pressure would reach zero at −273°C: absolute zero, the start of the Kelvin scale.

        Example: a closed can of air at 0°C and 1 atm, heated to 100°C: P = 373/273 ≈ 1.37 atm. A mole of any gas at 0°C and 1 atm fills about 22.4 L.

        Pressure from molecular collisions

        • P = (1/3)ρ v̄²   (v̄² the mean of the squared speeds)
        • (1/2)m v̄² = (3/2)kT,   k = R/N_(A) = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K

        In words: the kinetic theory pictures a gas as a huge number of tiny molecules flying around and bouncing off the walls. Each bounce hands the wall momentum 2mv_(x); added over all the molecules hitting each second, it gives the steady push we call pressure. Comparing with PV = n R T shows what temperature is: the average kinetic energy of the molecules. Boltzmann's constant k is the gas constant per molecule.

        Speeds: v_(rms) = √((3RT)/M): at room temperature nitrogen molecules move at about 520 m/s, hydrogen at about 1900 m/s. Their average kinetic energy at 300 K is 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J, whatever the gas.

        3Electricity and the building blocks of the atom

        Faraday's laws of electrolysis

        • m = (Q/F)(M/z)
        • F = N_(A)e ≈ 96 500 C/mol   (the faraday)

        In words: passing a current through a solution of a salt deposits the metal at one electrode. The mass deposited is proportional to the charge passed, and to the element's molar mass divided by its valence z (the charge of its ion in units of e). It was the first hint that charge comes in fixed packets: each ion carries a whole number of them.

        Example: 2 A for one hour (7200 C) through a silver solution (z = 1, 107.9 g/mol) deposits about 8.05 g of silver.

        Discovering the electron

        In a glass tube with almost no air, a high voltage makes "cathode rays" stream from the negative electrode. J. J. Thomson (1897) bent them with electric and magnetic fields (Electricity and magnetism) and measured their charge-to-mass ratio e/m: the same for every metal, and about 1800 times that of a hydrogen ion. They were particles far lighter than any atom: electrons, part of every atom.

        Millikan (1909) measured the charge itself by balancing tiny charged oil drops in an electric field: always whole multiples of e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Then m_(e) = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

        The nucleus and isotopes

        Rutherford (1911) fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but a few bounced back. So the atom's positive charge and almost all its mass sit in a tiny nucleus, about 10⁻¹⁴ m across (a hundred-thousandth of the atom), with the electrons around it. The atom is mostly empty space.

        Isotopes: the mass spectrograph (ions sorted by the radius of their circle in a magnetic field) showed that atoms of one element can have different masses: neon has atoms of mass 20 and 22. The nucleus holds protons (their number Z fixes the element) and neutrons (discovered in 1932), whose number can vary.

        4Special relativity

        Classical and modern physics

        By 1900 Newton's mechanics and Maxwell's electromagnetism (classical physics) explained almost everything, but a few facts didn't fit: light's speed came out the same for every observer, hot bodies glowed with the "wrong" colours, and atoms should have collapsed. Two new theories fixed this: relativity for the very fast, quantum mechanics for the very small. Classical physics remains correct for everyday speeds and sizes.

        Einstein's postulates

        • The laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame (Inertial frames and fictitious forces, Mechanics).
        • The speed of light in vacuum is the same, c, for every observer, however the source or the observer moves.

        In words: the second postulate (confirmed by Michelson and Morley's experiment) breaks everyday intuition: chasing a light beam at half of c, you still measure it moving away at c. Einstein (1905) took both seriously, and time and length had to give way.

        Time dilation and length contraction

        • γ = 1/(√(1 − v²/c²))
        • Δt' = γΔt   (a moving clock runs slow)
        • L' = L/γ   (a moving rod is shorter along its motion)

        In words: Δt is the time between two events measured by a clock that is present at both (its own, "proper" time); any observer who sees that clock moving measures a longer time. L is the length measured at rest with the object; moving, it is shorter. γ is practically 1 at everyday speeds, and grows without limit near c.

        Example: muons made high in the atmosphere live 2.2 μs in their own frame; at 0.98c (γ ≈ 5) we see them live about 11 μs, long enough to reach the ground, as measured.

        Nothing with mass can reach c: the energy needed grows without limit. No signal travels faster than light.

        Mass and energy

        • E₀ = mc²   (rest energy)
        • E = γmc²,   p = γmv

        In words: mass is a form of energy. A body at rest has energy mc²; moving, its total energy is γmc² (kinetic energy (γ − 1)mc², which is (1/2)mv² at low speeds). A gram of matter is 9 × 10¹³ J; nuclear reactions turn a small part of the mass into energy (The nucleus).

        The electron's rest energy is about 0.511 MeV.

        5Photons: the particle nature of light

        Planck's quanta and the photon

        • E = hf = (hc)/λ,   h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s
        • λ(nm) = 1240/(E(eV))

        In words: to explain the colours of light glowing from hot bodies (black-body radiation), Planck (1900) had to assume that light energy is given out only in packets, quanta, of size hf. Einstein (1905) went further: light itself travels as such packets, photons. Higher frequency (bluer light) means more energetic photons.

        Handy: in electron-volts (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) and nanometres, E·λ ≈ 1240: red light (700 nm) photons carry about 1.8 eV, blue (450 nm) about 2.8 eV. A 100 W lamp giving 5 W of 550 nm light sends out about 1.4 × 10¹⁹ photons a second, which is why the graininess of light isn't noticed.

        The photoelectric effect

        K_(max) = hf − W

        In words: light shining on a metal knocks electrons out. Experiment showed what the wave picture could not explain: below a certain frequency no electrons come out, however bright the light; above it, they come out at once, with an energy set by the frequency and not the brightness. Einstein's photons explain it: each electron absorbs one photon; it needs at least the work function W to escape, and keeps the rest as kinetic energy. Brighter light means more photons, so more electrons, not faster ones.

        Example: a metal with W = 2.3 eV in 400 nm light (3.1 eV photons): electrons leave with up to 0.8 eV. Light above 539 nm frees none.

        The dual nature of light

        Light shows both natures: interference and diffraction (Optics) are wave behaviour; the photoelectric effect and the way light is absorbed one photon at a time are particle behaviour. Neither picture alone is complete; which one shows up depends on the experiment. The same turns out to be true of electrons and all matter (Quantum mechanics).

        Photons have momentum p = h/λ: light pushes on what it hits (Compton scattering of X-rays off electrons, solar sails).

        6The Bohr model

        Atomic spectra

        A hot gas glows only at certain sharp colours, its line spectrum, different for every element: a fingerprint used to find what stars are made of. Hydrogen's visible lines (the Balmer series, 656 nm red, 486 nm blue…) fit a simple formula that classical physics couldn't explain; nor could it explain why the electron, circling the nucleus, doesn't radiate its energy away and spiral in.

        Bohr's model of hydrogen

        • L = m v r = n h/(2π),   n = 1, 2, 3, …
        • E_(n) = −(13.6 eV)/(n²),   r_(n) = n² · 0.0529 nm
        • hf = E_(n) − E_(m)

        In words: Bohr (1913) assumed the electron can circle only on orbits whose angular momentum is a whole multiple of h/2π, and doesn't radiate while on one. So the atom has only certain energy levels; it gives out (or absorbs) light only when the electron jumps between two levels, as one photon carrying the difference.

        It works: from level 3 to 2, 13.6(1/4 − 1/9) ≈ 1.89 eV, a 656 nm photon: the red Balmer line. Removing the electron from the lowest level (ionization) takes 13.6 eV. The model fails for atoms with more electrons; quantum mechanics replaced it, keeping its energy levels.

        Many-electron atoms and the periodic table

        In bigger atoms the electrons fill shells (levels) from the lowest up. Each state holds at most one electron (Pauli's exclusion principle), so a shell holds a fixed number: 2, 8, 18…

        Chemistry follows: elements with the same number of outer electrons behave alike, which is why the periodic table repeats in rows. Full shells (helium, neon, argon) are inert; one extra electron (sodium) is easily given away; one missing (chlorine) is eagerly taken.

        X-rays and lasers come from jumps between levels too: deep inner levels give X-ray lines; in a laser, many atoms are made to jump down together, in step.

        7Quantum mechanics

        Matter waves

        λ = h/p = h/(mv)   (de Broglie)

        In words: if light waves act as particles, de Broglie (1924) proposed that particles act as waves, with a wavelength set by their momentum. Electrons through a crystal make diffraction patterns, just like X-rays: confirmed in 1927. An electron accelerated by 100 V has λ ≈ 0.12 nm, about an atom's size; a thrown ball's wavelength is about 10⁻³⁴ m, far too small ever to notice.

        Use: the electron microscope, whose short wavelength sees details far finer than light can (Diffraction and resolution, Optics).

        The wave function and the uncertainty principle

        • |ψ|² = probability density of finding the particle
        • Δx Δp ≥ h/(4π)

        In words: a particle is described by a wave function ψ, found from the Schrödinger equation (the quantum "law of motion"). It doesn't tell where the particle is, only the probability of finding it at each place. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: position and momentum can't both be known exactly: squeezing one makes the other spread.

        A particle in a box of width L can only have energies E_(n) = n²h²/(8mL²): confinement by itself makes the energy come in levels. An electron in a box the size of an atom (0.1 nm): E₁ ≈ 38 eV. That is why atoms have energy levels.

        Energy levels, quantum numbers and spin

        Solving Schrödinger's equation for hydrogen gives Bohr's energies, and labels each state with quantum numbers: n (the shell, the energy), l (the orbital angular momentum, 0 … n − 1), m (its direction). Electrons also have an intrinsic angular momentum, spin, with two possible values ("up" and "down"), and with it a small magnetic moment: the source of magnetism in matter (Electricity and magnetism).

        Counting states: shell n has n² orbital states, times 2 for spin: 2n² electrons (2, 8, 18…), the shell sizes behind the periodic table.

        8The nucleus

        The structure of the nucleus

        A nucleus is made of protons and neutrons (together, nucleons). Z, the number of protons (atomic number), fixes the element; A, the number of nucleons (mass number), the isotope: written ^(A)_(Z)X, e.g. helium-4 has Z = 2, A = 4.

        Size: about 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ A^(1/3) m, so all nuclei have about the same density, enormous: a teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh billions of tonnes. Masses are given in atomic mass units, 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, worth 931.5 MeV.

        Nuclear forces and binding energy

        • ΔE = ΔMc²
        • ΔE(MeV) = ΔM(u) × 931.5

        In words: protons repel each other electrically, yet nuclei hold together: a much stronger, very short-range nuclear (strong) force binds the nucleons. A nucleus weighs less than its separate protons and neutrons; the mass defect ΔM, times c², is the binding energy: the energy needed to pull it apart. Helium-4: ΔM ≈ 0.0304 u, about 28.3 MeV, 7.1 MeV per nucleon.

        The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron: light nuclei release energy by joining (fusion), heavy ones by splitting (fission).

        Models of the nucleus

        No simple theory describes the nucleus completely; two models each explain part of it. The liquid-drop model treats it like a drop of charged liquid: it explains why the binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant and how a heavy nucleus can wobble and split (fission). The shell model puts nucleons in energy levels, like electrons in an atom: nuclei with certain "magic" numbers of protons or neutrons (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) are especially stable.

        9Radioactivity

        Alpha, beta and gamma

        • Alpha (α): the nucleus throws out a helium nucleus; Z drops by 2, A by 4. Stopped by a sheet of paper.
        • Beta (β⁻): a neutron turns into a proton, emitting an electron (and an antineutrino); Z rises by 1, A stays. Stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
        • Gamma (γ): a high-energy photon from a nucleus settling to a lower level; nothing else changes. Needs thick lead or concrete.

        In every decay charge, the number of nucleons and energy are conserved: check that the Z's and the A's balance on both sides. Discovered by Becquerel (1896) and the Curies.

        The decay law and half-life

        • N(t) = N₀ e^(−λt) = N₀ (1/2)^(t/T_(1/2))
        • T_(1/2) = (ln 2)/λ
        • activity R = λN   (becquerel, 1 Bq = 1 decay per second; 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq)

        In words: each nucleus decays at random, with the same chance every second whatever its age; so the number left falls exponentially. The half-life is the time for half of them to decay: after 3 half-lives, an eighth is left. It is fixed for each isotope (from fractions of a second to billions of years) and nothing (heat, pressure, chemistry) changes it.

        Carbon dating: living things keep a steady share of carbon-14 (half-life 5730 years); after death it decays. A sample with a quarter of the living level is about 11 500 years old.

        10Fission, fusion and elementary particles

        Fission and fusion

        Fission: a heavy nucleus (uranium-235) absorbs a neutron and splits into two middle-sized nuclei plus 2–3 neutrons, releasing about 200 MeV. The new neutrons can split more nuclei: a chain reaction, controlled in a reactor, uncontrolled in a bomb. A kilogram of uranium-235 releases about 8 × 10¹³ J, as much as burning thousands of tonnes of coal.

        Fusion: light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) joining into helium release even more energy per kilogram. It powers the Sun and stars, but needs temperatures of millions of degrees to push the nuclei together against their repulsion; controlled fusion on Earth is still being developed.

        Elementary particles

        Protons and neutrons are not elementary: each is made of three quarks. Today's Standard Model has a small set of elementary particles: six quarks, six leptons (the electron, its heavier cousins the muon and tau, and three neutrinos), and the particles that carry the forces (the photon for electromagnetism, gluons for the strong force, W and Z for the weak force behind beta decay), plus the Higgs boson.

        Antiparticles: every particle has one, of the same mass and opposite charge (the positron for the electron). A particle and its antiparticle meeting annihilate into energy, E = mc², exactly as relativity predicts.
